fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurr ed on the ISS. None of these events spread into a real
fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of fa ilures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown
that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of
spacecraft fire detection is critically needed.6
Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al. 5 found that the particulate produced
by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity.
Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment 5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity
from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while
solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient
data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detec

ger than 1 µm while
solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient
data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited
results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g
combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft.
II. SAME Experiment
To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate,
another experiment was developed: the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The SAME experiment
sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit
with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol
instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and some systems require
substantial sample return to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used
three discrete instruments to measure separate moments

provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution. The measurements were made using smoke generated by
overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature,

deviation.

Calibration of the moment instruments was essential to properly interpret the flight data and was performed on
the ground before the flight. Calibration was accomplished using two different aerosol generators one using mono-
disperse particle generation using dioctyl phthalate (DOP) according to the appro ach by Mulholland and Liu 11 and
the other using polystyrene spheres. The monodisperse droplet generator functioned by producing a spray of DOP
diluted with isopropanol which is then evaporated and recondensed producing monodisperse droplets. The droplet
size is controlled by the DOP dilution level. The generator will operate stably for tens of minutes. The aerosol from
the generator was sampled simultaneously by the SAME instrument under test and a reference instrument. For the
number count, the reference instrument was a TSI 3022A pa rticle counter, for the mass concentration, a Tapered
Element Oscillating Microbalance and for the first moment a TSI Electrical Aerosol Detector was used. The results
for the P-Trak are shown in Fig. 4. As the number concentration increased, the effect of the particle diameter
became more evident. Separate correlations were devel oped for each part

G. Experimental Results
Over 100 sample materials were tested. These were comprised of samples of 6 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™,
Pyrell™, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. The test
conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates. The baseline air flow rate was 8 cm/s with
runs conducted at rates down to 2 cm/s with a limited set conducted with no airflow while the sample was heated.
The sample temperatures were based on the pyrolysis properties of the material and were thus material specific. The
baseline temperature was selected to produce 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 seconds and have reasonable signal on
each of the moment instruments. To examine the effect of sample temper ature, additional higher temperature
conditions were also selected that would not saturate th e moment instruments. The TEM girds recovered from the
thermal precipitators on SAME-1 were unfortunately cont aminated with extraneous particles whose origin is
currently under investigation. For SAME-2 more rigorous assembly controls were followed and numerous good
particle images were obtained. For typical runs, the partic le concentratio

2. MPASS Results
The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector.
Because of how they are used, a smoke detector is not calibrated for speci fic materials and instead has a single
calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or
the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a se lected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration). The
approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from
the MPASS output. This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass
concentration) as a reference. A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal
to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time).

The results are shown in figures 9 and 10, for prediction of the mass concentration and the number
concentration, respectively. Ideally th ese response graphs should be horizont al lines. The norm alized output is
plotted along with the normalized correlation result as a function of geometric m ean diameter. Ideally the
normalized result should be horizontal lines. The uniformity of response (scatter) is expressed by the least squares
variance relative to the mean ( Δ) and is shown in the legend. Both figures show that the correlation decreases the
relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor.
The resulting variance for the mass response is substantially lower than for the number concentration. This is
consistent with the fact that the original optimizati on of the MPASS was to mass concentration not to number
concentration. Thus with appropriate processing, the MPASS output can be proportional to either the number
concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions. This
independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its respon

concentration or the mass concentration over a wide range of particle sizes and material compositions. This
independence demonstrates that by combining 2 moments the MPASS is able to scale its response to the particle
size being sampled giving a more accurate indication of the amount of smoke present than a single moment detector.
The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke
concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can
minimize false smoke detector alarms.

3. TEM Results
Overall, 72 particle samples were taken on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids using the thermal
precipitator. These samples were imaged with a TEM to evaluate the particle morphology as a function of flow
conditions, material and heating level. Overall, silicone rubber and DBP presented no particles that were visible via
TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the
TEM. Figure 11 presents typical images for the major materials.

As seen in Table 1, aging did increase the average partic le size, however this level of change is not readily
visible in the TEM images, instead the mo st visible change is the disappearance of the smallest particles. (Fig 12)
As described in the discussion of Table 1, this is consistent with expectations since the smaller particles have the
highest mobility and consequently are readily incorporated in to the larger particles. Particularly for the semi-liquid
particles, this absorption of the smallest particles into larger particles is expected to have little or no apparent effect
on the size of the larger particles b ecause the diameter is the cube root of the volume. In th e case of non-liquid
particles, the smallest particles will ne vertheless be unlikely to be visible via TEM when they are attached to larger
particles.

4. Impact of flow on particle morphology
As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are
released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the
reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species
concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the
decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage
and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the
condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the
order of ms or less. Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian
motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue
for time scales of up to 103 s. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and
form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig.
11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an
agglomerate structure compos

This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig.
11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an
agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal-
like structure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11).

A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow. The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is
controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases
would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would
correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in
the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial
concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case. This is expected to
lead to more coagulation and a larger particle size. It is found for all of the materials the
diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow
tests.

The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined
for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very
high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the
aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the
smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume. As a
result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles. It is
important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed
the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing
zone. So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to
consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles.

For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection.
This is likely to result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8
cm/s air flow. A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of
the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow
of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13).

The results from the SAME experiment indicate that su bstantial differences in the size distributions of the
smoke particles are evident for the five spacecraft material s that were tested. For the conditions of the SAME
experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an
ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results sugg est that some materials such as silicone rubber can
produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques. The zero flow conditions produced
smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate. Since spacecraft
fire conditions include an even wider array of materials than those tested here and a broader range of flow and
temperature conditions, broad smoke aerosol size distributions can be expected from credible pre-fire overheat
events. These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution
may show more successful detection and false alarm rejec tion than single moment detectors. The results from the
prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this res

size distribution
may show more successful detection and false alarm rejec tion than single moment detectors. The results from the
prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect with the technique showing real
potential as a means to respond to a broad particle range while avoiding excessive false alarms from nuisance
sources. The TEM result demonstrated that fire particulate can be expected to have a broad range of morphologies
influenced by heating rate, material and flow conditions.

text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A
2.2 SAME Experiment Background
Since the very beginning of the manned space flight program, NASA engineers and scientists have gone to great lengths to
prevent fires from occurring on spacecraft. They have done this by adapting fire safety systems and procedures developed
on Earth to the unique conditions and operating environment of spacecraft. However, microgravity combustion experiments
have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a
spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth.
In 2000, NASA's Bioastronautics Initiative began with the objective of ensuring and enhancing the health, safety, and
performance of humans in space. As part of this effort, the Life Support and Habitation Branch at NASA Glenn Research
Center is responsible for developing and implementing a research plan to significantly improve fire safety on spacecraft and
in space habitats. This goal will be achieved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the
experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions.
Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:7:1
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
ved by applying a significant amount of fundamental knowledge and the
experimental capability of microgravity research to spacecraft fire safety questions.
Spacecraft smoke detectors must detect smoke with a variety of particulate types. Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot,
while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke
that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products. Differences in the nucleation and growth processes
for these different types of smokes create particles that have different sizes and properties.
The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the smokes
with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created
in normal Earth gravity. This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration
smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that
experiment.
To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles th

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:7:2
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that
experiment.
To develop smoke detectors that are sensitive to the type and size of smoke particles that will be encountered in
microgravity and to allow them to distinguish between dust and smoke, better knowledge of the size distribution and
morphology of the particulates is required.
2.3 SAME Experiment Objectives
The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to
relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. This will
be accomplished by extending the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) concept to provide a particulate count and mass
density determination to the diagnostic array used to analyze these liquid smokes. The experimental design and practical
application of this data will be enhanced by the development of a numerical code that will predict the smoke droplet growth
as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
The SAME experiment has the following (listed) obje

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:7:3
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
ct the smoke droplet growth
as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
The SAME experiment has the following (listed) objectives:
1. Make measurements of three moments of the particle size distribution for the μg smoke from several
materials found in spacecraft considering the effects of sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time
(near the source) and smoke aging. The primary targets are materials that produce liquid smoke particulate
but solid smoke producers will also be considered.
2. Make measurements of the effect of µg and 1-g on the size distribution of liquid aerosol smokes (using an
idealized smoke e.g. DBT) to provide data for numerical model comparison.
3. Evaluate the performance in µg of the two existing U.S. spacecraft smoke detector designs for the test
conditions.
4. Evaluate other smoke detection/sensing devices at NASA’s request for the test materials
2.4 SAME “Firsts” for NASA
• Measurements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure
particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively. Both devices are manufactured by

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:7:4
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
surements of microgravity smoke: Diagnostics such as the P-Trak and the DustTrak will be used to measure
particle count and particle mass concentration, respectively. Both devices are manufactured by TSI. With the aid of
these instruments (and others), microgravity smoke will be characterized.
• The use of rapid prototype materials for manned flight experiment hardware.
• Use of an automatic, remotely adjustable, ‘particulate friendly’ dilution system.

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:8:0
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A
2.5 The SAME Risk mitigation experiment – DAFT
The objective for the risk mitigation experiment, DAFT (Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test), is to provide a
microgravity technology demonstration of the P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Counter manufactured by TSI. The P-Trak is a
hand held air quality monitor which is capable of counting particles whose mean diameter is in the range of 1.0 to 0.05
microns.
After extensive market research performed by both the Engineering and Science teams, it has been determined that the P-
Trak is the only commercially available hardware that can perform this particle count while maintaining the weight,
resource, and space limitations for an MSG experiment.
P-Trak measures particle number concentrations in real-time while storing that data in a memory maintained by an on-
board battery. These measurements are made in units of particles per cubic centimeter (pt/cm3) versus traditional aerosol
measurements of milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter). These droplets have many times the avera

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:8:1
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
eter (mg/m3) made by photometers. P-Trak operates by using the particles in the
aerosol as seeds to condense droplets of alcohol (a condensate nuclei counter). These droplets have many times the average
diameter of the original particles, and may, therefore, be easily counted with standard optical techniques. The potential
problem is that these droplets are directed through a nozzle to facilitate the counting, and some of these droplets (a
predictable percentage) collide with the walls and form a film. In a gravity environment, this film is recycled by ‘falling’
down hill.
In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle,
effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics. Furthermore,
there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be
counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count.
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:8:2
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
gh count.
The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were
machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which
the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence,
inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit.
The modifications to account for and eliminate this problem have been devised and implemented, however, it is not possible
to test the effectiveness of these modifications in any of the available ground based facilities and/or the KC-135 due to the
duration of the nominal operation time required (minutes per instance). This testing, and the verification of the accuracy of
the instrument functions on orbit, are the core of the DAFT experiment.
Two P-Trak units are included in DAFT flight hardware, one being only flight hardened, and the other with the modified
condenser and flight hardened.
To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail
here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This h

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:8:3
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
ified
condenser and flight hardened.
To successfully accomplish P-Trak functional demonstration, additional hardware (which will not be explained in detail
here) has to be delivered to the ISS. This hardware includes a dust concentration monitor (DustTrak), data cables, fill
assembly, sample bag assemblies, sample holders, virtual impactor, alcohol reservoir, battery packs, a HEPA filter
assembly, and appropriate tubing.
The P-Trak utilizes isopropyl alcohol as a condensate, and its use must therefore, be carefully monitored and requires a
specific agreement for that use on the ISS which is contained within a Volatile Usage Agreement (VUA) created for the
experiment.

4.0 SAME CREW INTERFACES
4.1 Hardware Subsystem Description
The major planned components of SAME are as follows. They are organized by the assembly level, and the order in which
they are currently planned to be installed into the MSG.:
1. Fluids Control Box Assembly (67198MABA220)
The Fluids Control Box (FCB) installs on the back wall of the MSG in the upper left section. It is a fan cooled
enclosure made from aluminum that contains most of the fluids control devices and monitoring devices including
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG
fluids resources (VES and GN2) a
subject: PSI-102

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:9:1
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
uids control devices and monitoring devices including
solenoids, pressure regulator, pressure transducers and mass flow controller. It interfaces directly with the MSG
fluids resources (VES and GN2) and the Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU), and distributes the fluids
resources accordingly. Please refer to the SAME Fluids Schematic (67198PABA000) for more information on its,
and the other fluids system functions.
2. Sample Plate Assembly (Experiment Support Plate Assembly) 67198ABA100
This assembly, when fully integrated, contains all of the major functional systems of SAME. It is a mounting plate
which includes the mounting hardware for the Sample Carousel, the Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU), the
Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) and the Aging Chamber Assembly (ACA). Permanently mounted to it
are:
• The Smoke Generation Tube
• The Video Camera and Controller
• The Sample Positioning system including:
o the Sample Turning Module
o the sample engagement mechanism
o the sample position indicator
o the sample positioning lock mechanism
o the Sample Carousel mounting system

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:10:0
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A
3. Dynamic Diagnostics Assembly (DDA) (67198MDBA165)
The DDA is attached to the Sample Plate Assembly and the Aging Chamber Assembly by the crew and contains:
the ISS and STS smoke detectors and the sampling ports that supply the P-Trak Enclosure and the Commercial
Diagnostics Enclosure (and port(s) added for any additional diagnostics required). The DDA has a very low
internal volume, and the flow of the sample aerosol through it is controlled by regulating and balancing the
requirements of the active diagnostics in the DDA with the exhaust rate of the Aging Chamber piston, as
controlled by its mass flow controller. It also contains a port, protected by a HEPA filter, that is connected to the
VES for exhaust and purging.
4. Aging Chamber Assembly (67198MABA150)
The Aging Chamber Assembly contains the cylindrical, metallic Aging Chamber, the pneumatically activated
Inlet and Outlet Gate Valves and the Inlet and Outlet Elbows, which connect to the Smoke Generation Tube and
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:10:1
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
be and
the DDA, respectively. A Rulon piston, internal to the chamber, moves the sample into and out from the internal
volume, and that flow is controlled by a mass flow controller which regulates the pressure or vacuum flow
accordingly. Sampling ports are provided in the elbows for use by the Thermal Precipitator, and the unit contains
a Mixing Fan to insure that the contents are homogenous before disbursal to the DDA.
5. Data Acquisition and Control Unit (DACU) (67198EABA660)
The DACU is the central control unit for SAME. The baseline software is resident there, and, although many of
the other packages contain their own relay and control cards, ultimately it is the DACU that interfaces with the
Ethernet and the MLC to orchestrate the performance of the experiment. It also collects and stores data for
subsequent downlink through the MSG systems, and controls the MSG Video Recorder to provide a taped record
of the pyrolysis event.
6. P-Trak Enclosure (67198MABA500)
The P-Trak Enclosure is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the
Fl

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:10:2
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
is a flight hardened assembly containing a TSI P-Trak modified to take advantage of the
VES system and to function in a microgravity environment. Although it interfaces with the DDA, the DACU, the
Fluids Control Unit and the Power Distribution and Control Unit, it is basically a smart box that can operate
independently and store its own data.
7. Commercial Diagnostics Enclosure (CDE) (67198MABA600)
The CDE houses two of the SAME diagnostics, the TSI DustTrak and a First Alert ionization smoke detector.
Both units have been hardened for flight and have been modified to utilize the VES to drive the sample. The
DustTrak has also been modified to utilize MSG air to provide its ‘sheath air’ in order to decrease the amount of
aerosol required by the unit. Like P-Trak, the DustTrak portion of this device can operate independently and store
its own data. The modified First Alert cannot.
8. Dynamic Diluter (DD) (67198MABA180)
The DD is a custom designed component that provides dilution of the aerosol from the DDA before its
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure
the amount of sample being introduced and using that i

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:10:3
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
aerosol from the DDA before its
introduction into the P-Trak (and possibly the DustTrak). It works by utilizing a laminar flow element to measure
the amount of sample being introduced and using that information (from a differential pressure transducer) to
increase or decrease the diluent flow to achieve the desired concentration. The dilution setpoint may be altered by
software and adjusts to the desired setting in approximately 5 seconds.
9. Power Distribution and Control Unit (PDCU) (67198EABA680)
The PDCU is the central disbursement point for the commands, power distribution and data collection for SAME.
It contains the power converters, main relays and terminal data connections for the entire system and interfaces the
DACU with the various systems and devices constituting the experiment.

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:11:0
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
SAME-DOC-001 Rev. A
10. Sample Carousel Assembly (67198MABB400)
The Sample Carousel Assemblies (5) each contain six (6) Sample Tubes that interface the samples to the Smoke
Generation Tube and allow the capture of the smoke in the Aging Chamber. Sample Carousels are sequentially
installed onto the mounting locations on the Sample Plate Assembly, and the mechanisms contained by it identify
the individual sample numbers, rotate the carousel to the correct position and engage the Sample Tube, which
allows the sample to be in a position to be energized. The samples themselves are composed of five (5) materials:
Teflon, Kapton, Silicone, Cellulose and DiButyl Phthalate (which being a liquid, is contained within a small
section of cotton lampwick) in small, cylindrical sections, that are wrapped with coils of wire (baseline: stainless
steel) that both provides the heat energy to the sample when energized and measures its temperature (by its
varying resistance).
These samples are removed from the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis.
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MA

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:11:1
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
the tubes for weighing, both before and after the experiment (before launch and
after being downmassed) to quantify the actual mass loss during pyrolysis.
11. Thermal Precipitator Unit (TPU) (67198MABB300)
The TPU is a device that captures actual samples of the aerosol particulate on Transmission Electron Microscope
(TEM) grids for examination when returned from the ISS. The units (4) are number matched to the samples in the
carousel, to take samples from both the Inlet and Outlet Elbows leading to and from the Aging Chamber.
12. Alcohol Wick Storage Container (67198MABD700)
The Alcohol Wick Storage Container is a custom manufactured aluminum vessel to contain the alcohol wick
required by the P-Trak during the time (launch, non-ops) when it is not in direct use. Only one is nominally
required, but two are included to provide one as a backup.
13. Hoses
SAME utilizes ISS GN2 and the VES system both as resources for the experiment process and as systems to
power its devices. These resources are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic
hoses and

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:11:2
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
ces are distributed to the components from the FCU via the hoses, which are
nominally operated at +/- 15 psig. In order to conserve weight and volume, and provide ease of operation, acrylic
hoses and quick disconnects will be used for the distribution of pressure and vacuum throughout the system (not
typical Teflon with stainless steel overbraid).
14. Harnessing
All harnessing will conform to applicable standards and be designed to minimize the crew time needed to make
the required experiment connections, without sacrificing reliability.
15. SAME Service Kit
This is a place holder. SAME has not yet defined any servicing requirements.
4.2 Video Recording Devices
Video recordings of the smoke evolution process are very important for establishing proper operation of the test apparatus
and for debugging the system operation. Furthermore, the video provides a helpful demonstration of the variability in
smoke evolution. Experience with CSD showed dramatic cases where clearly visible smoke streams were not always
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered ligh

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:11:3
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
reams were not always
detectable by the smoke detectors while invisible smoke streams were readily detected. Normal video resolution is
acceptable if the smoke is illuminated by forward scattered light from an appropriate light source. Video will be viewed on
and recorded by the MSG video Monitor/Recorder.
4.3 On-Orbit Crew Operational Functions
The crew will be asked to assemble the experiment from provided subsections, load software, reload Sample Carousels,
Thermal Precipitator Modules, and alcohol for the particle counter, enter parameters, initiate the experiment, and
disassemble the experiment.

5.0 SAME SOFTWARE CONTROL
5.1 Software Controlled Operational Functions
The DACU is the central point for SAME control. It is ultimately responsible for all experiment operations and interfacing
with the environment external to SAME. It contains all of the logic necessary to autonomously operate the experiment as
well as receive, validate, and process commands from the MSG. The DACU periodically transmits the status of the Smoke
system to the MSG, which then forwards it to the ground. The software can autonomously control the progress of
preprogrammed test, manage and store all science and system files on the local data storage medium, control the MSG
video recorder capturing Smoke images, and copy the files to the MLC for downlink. The software inside the DACU is
also responsible for providing diagnostic information and manual control of all sensors and controls using the GSE port.
Please refer to the SAME Baseline Software Requirements Document (SAME-DOC-004) for more detail.
5.2 Data Collection
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information. The Thermal Precipitator Module,
which collects samples of the smoke, will be ba

more detail.
5.2 Data Collection
Data is collected and stored in the DACU until it is time to downlink the information. The Thermal Precipitator Module,
which collects samples of the smoke, will be bagged and returned for analysis. Sample Carousels are retained so that the
samples can be weighed after return to Earth.
6.0 SAME OPERATIONS
6.1 Operations Flow
1. Experiment Setup- The experiment will be shipped in individual subassemblies that will be assembled inside of
the MSG. Parts will be inserted through the MSG side ports starting with the upper, back components. After
the MSG ports are covered and the rack is returned to nominal position, the Experiment Software is installed
onto the MSG Laptop.
2. Perform Experiment- The first steps in performing the experiment are to load the desired Sample Carousel, load
or replenish the alcohol wick in the particle counter, and install a new Thermal Precipitator Module. Next, the
start-up check out routine is performed. After the uplink parameters are sent, the experiment is initiated. Then,
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again
until all six samples in the Sample

id: PSI-101:doc:PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf:12:2
file: PSI-101_Science Documents_SAME_Baseline Concept Description Document_001 Rev A.pdf
text:
ters are sent, the experiment is initiated. Then,
the baseline uplink parameters are modified, as required, for the next test and the experiment is initiated again
until all six samples in the Sample Carousel have been used. The next number matched Sample Carousel and
Thermal Precipitator Module will then be loaded and the experiment will continue as such until complete.
3. Shutdown and Repack Experiment- When all the Sample Carousels have been used and all the experiments
have been performed, the final Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator Module will be capped and bagged.
In reverse order of installation, the experiment hardware will be repackaged for downmassing.
6.2 Detailed Operations
Please refer to the SAME Operations Concept Document (SAME-DOC-009) for a more detailed description of all
Operations functions.
6.3 Timeline
Since the experiment is designed for operations controlled from the ground, once the components have been installed in the
MSG, timeline concerns have mainly to do with the acquisition of command windows and with weekly or semi weekly
service sessions by the crew.
SAME will follow the standard ISS procedures for scheduling activities aboard the station i

service sessions by the crew.
SAME will follow the standard ISS procedures for scheduling activities aboard the station including OCR and iURC
submittals and conferences with the ISS Cadre.

7.0 SAFETY CONCERNS & PREVENTATIVE MEASURES
7.1 Overall Strategy
Safety analysis is being performed for the SAME (formerly Smoke) hardware in accordance with the safety policies and
safety requirements for flight hardware (NSTS1700.7B and ISS Addendum). This assessment is being prepared using
NSTS 13830C as a guideline for data submittal. Hazards not eliminated by design are addressed in either the latest revision
of standardized hazard control report JSC Form 1230 for ISS and launch/landing phase of the mission or in a Unique
Hazard Report, JSC 542B. For the most part, the SAME experiment uses generic hazard controls for electrical power
hazards, sharp edges, EMI (te

7.2 Pressurized Systems
The pressure system includes the aging chamber, the system for moving the piston in the aging chamber (valves, regulator,
lines, hoses, relief devices) and the Dynamic Diluter. All of the parts will be designed to meet the requirements of
NSTS1700.7 ISS addendum, NASA-STD-5003, SSP 30558, and SSP 52005 for pressurized hardware. Pressurized lines
and fittings will be designed to a factor of safety of 4.0 X System MDP of 200 psid (ISS N2 limiting pressure). Pressurized
system components will be designed to a factor of safety of greater than or equal to 2.5 X System MDP of 200 psid. Down
stream of the pressure reduction the MDP is 20 psig. These components are designed with the same factors of safety. See
table of components and factors of safety and hazard report SMOKE-04. Materials will be selected and evaluated for stress
corrosion and/or fluid compatibility in accordance with SSP 30233, Space Station Requirements for Materials and
Processes. In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will
not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SD

In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will
not over pressurize. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001) specifically hazard report
SMOKE-04.
7.3 Structures
The SAME experiment is launched in stowage and contained in MSG for on orbit use. The structural aspect of SAME is
primarily sealed containers and vented containers. Pressure systems are covered in section 1.2. SAME structural failure is
addressed in Hazard Report SMOKE STD 01 in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).
7.4 Materials
The ZIN Tech Engineering Team will assure that reasonable measures have been taken with regard to material selection for
the experiment‘s design, and selected materials are safe for the intended manned space flight application in their respective
usage environment. A material flammability assessment will be performed per NSTS 22648. The flight unit will be offgas
tested. The SAME Project Team will prepare the standard Materials Identification & Usage List (MIUL) and MUA’s. ZIN
Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to
NASA/GRC/SMAD for con

Engineering will review and approve material evaluation prepared by the SAME Project, and submit it to
NASA/GRC/SMAD for concurrence. Upon material evaluation approval, NASA/GRC/SMTD will issue the Material
Certification Letter in accordance with the guidelines established in the applicable Material and Processes (M&P)
Intercenter Agreement prior to flight hardware fabrication. Further information can be found in Hazard Report SMOKE

7.5 Frangible Materials (Glass)
All of the hardware which contains glass will undergo a vibration test in the stowed configuration at workmanship or
protoflight levels and a post-test visual inspection to verify ability to survive launch loads. The duct with the video camera
lens and LEDs installed will be stowed with clear plastic for crew inspection after launch.

The P-Trak needs a cartridge with an alcohol-saturated wick for its operation; therefore, a risk of contaminating the ISS
environment has to be considered. The amount of alcohol released will be carefully

7.7 Non-Ionizing Laser Radiation
The ISS Smoke Detector, the P-Trak and the DustTrak contain lasers as a part of their diagnostics systems. These lasers are
of Class 1 lasers, and the laser beams are fully contained. These items are not removed from their original housings and are
used in the applications for which they are intended. There is no crew access to the lasers at any time. The lasers meet
ANSI Z136.1-2000 standards for Class 1. More detail can be found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).
7.8 Ionizing Radiation
The STS Smoke detector and the First Alert Smoke Alarm each contain 1 micro curie of Americium-241. These items are
not removed from their original housings and are used in the applications for which they are intended. More detail can be
found in the safety date package (SAME-SDP-001).

5.0 RUNNING A TEST
5.1 Initialization
Select the Initialize button on the System tab, sending the Initialize command, and wait until the Run
Mode changes from Unitialized to Ready.
5.2 Setting parameters
From the Testing tab, select Change… to change to the set of test parameters you want to look at. Create
a new test by selecting the CreateNew button. Select Set anywhere in the window to change the
parameter for the selected test.
The Test Setup group box is the way to choose which di agnostics to use. Select the Pri. or Sec. radio
button to see the difference in setup between primary and secondary aging.
Heater Control Setpoint should be set after knowing the unheated resistance of a sample, a.k.a. R0.

To find the R0 of a sample, engage the sample to th e inlet tube either by manual blocking or using the

5.4 Running the Test
From the Testing tab select Start… and enter the test number to run, if it hasn’t already been entered in
the field, and select Send.
After sample positioning and aging chamber setup has occurred the test will pause so you can examine
the log for any warnings or errors. Then send the Resume button. The test should proceed to finish. You
can abort anytime by sending the Abort command. An abort causes all valves to be turned off as well as
all diagnostics.

restart of low rate telemetry packets and updating GMT. If the system restarts, select Shutdown again or
send the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’.

7.3.2 Sample Heating Start Time
Ideally, the start of sample heating is calculated so that the end of sample heating occurs before the piston
reaches the top of the chamber. Actually, even before that, so that most of the smoke in the inlet tube at
the end of heating enters the chamber as well. And really, even before that, so that some clean air follows
the ‘last’ of the smoke and more of the smoke enters the chamber. The amount of the latter clean air is
determined by the BackEndCleanAirOffset registry value.
Because there is no direct physical measurement of where the piston is in the middle of its stroke, the
software must estimate when the stroke begins and how long the stroke will take. Then it can back off
from there to determine sample heating stop and start times. The registry values, FillWaita.b, where a.b is

7.3.3 Secondary Aging Volume
When a secondary aging period and volume are speci fied, the piston must stop a percentage of the
distance between the top and bottom of the chamber. There is no direct physical measurement of the
running distance, therefore it is estimated from th e exhaust rate over time. The registry value,
ExhaustPercentageCorrectionFactor, is applied to the running percentage. To adjust this value,
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber to a specific percentage. For best results use the
exhaust rate and secondary volume that will be used during the actual test. Or use 5 LPM and
50%.
- Perform a SelfTest to exhaust the chamber the rest of the way. Use the same rate and 100%.
- Calculate the time taken for each portion using log messages or pressure data and figure the
percentage of total time taken by the second exhaust. Adjust the registry value and repeat until
this percentage is within the desired accuracy of the secondary aging volume percentage.

7.5 Description of HeaterCorrectOffset Utility
Sample heater offset correction is a feature of the sample heater microcontroller that reduces
measurement error by automatically removing off set voltages from the signal path. After offset
correction is performed, all subsequent resistance me asurements will include the o ffset correction. Until
the system is powered off, that is. At power up the offset correction is zero. Offset correction should be
run for each sample while the sample is engaged with the inlet tube and sample heater contacts.
Occasionally the offset correction circuitry produces a co r

8.0 KNOWN ISSUES
- Aborting a test occasionally causes the software to restart. If this should happen you’ll need to
reissue the Initialize command.
- Try to avoid running a test sequence through the change of hour (i.e. 12:45-13:05). Transfer of
the housekeeping file at the top of the hour takes a good bit of processor time and the processor is
close to 100% capacity, possibly affecting diagnostic measurement retrieval.
- It is recommended that the system be gracefully shut down using the Shutdown button on the
System tab, then cut power about 2 minutes later. However, about 20% of the time the software
will hang or restart before completely shutting down. If it restarts, issue the Shutdown command
again or issue the OS command with parameter, ‘/bin/shutdown –b’. If it hangs (you may only
know this if you have a monitor connected to the GSE port) a hard power off will have to suffice.
The operating system will clean up any file ‘litter’ on the next power up.
- Maximum inlet velocity with the FillLeakRateLPM registry value equal to 0.30 is 9.8 cm/sec.
Above this the software does not correctly use the FillWait registry values to time chamber fill

2005-01-2930
Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires
David Urban, DeVon Griffin, Gary Ruff
NASA Glenn Research Center
Thomas Cleary, Jiann Yang, George Mulholland
National Institute of Standards and Technology
Zeng-guang Yuan
National Center for Microgravity Research
Copyright © 2005 SAE International
ABSTRACT
The history and current status of spacecraft smoke detection is discussed including a review of the state of understanding of the effect of gravity on the resultant smoke particle size. The results from a spacecraft experiment (Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)) which measured microgravity smoke particle sizes are presented. Five different materials were tested producing smokes with different properties including solid aerosol smokes and liquid droplets aerosol smokes. The particulate size distribution for the solid particulate smokes increased substantially in microgravity and the results suggested a corresponding increase for the smokes consisting of a liquid aerosol. A planned follow on experiment that will resolve the issues raised by CSD is presented. Early results from this effort have provided the first measurements of the ambient aerosol environment on the ISS (In

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
nned follow on experiment that will resolve the issues raised by CSD is presented. Early results from this effort have provided the first measurements of the ambient aerosol environment on the ISS (International Space Station) and suggest that the ISS has very low ambient particle levels.
INTRODUCTION
The non-buoyant microgravity environment causes substantial changes in flame structure and consequently changes the properties of the produced smoke. In particular, the increased residence time in the high temperature zone where the smoke is formed, increases the opportunity for growth in the size of the smoke particulate. This change has hampered the rational implementation of spacecraft smoke detectors because there is very little data concerning the resultant size of microgravity smoke particulate and the background dust aerosol size distribution. In the absence of any reference data, the ISS and STS (Space Transportation System or Space Shuttle) Orbiter smoke detectors each were designed using different detection technologies which have very different particle size sensitivities.
SMOKE BACKGROUND – Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ned using different detection technologies which have very different particle size sensitivities.
SMOKE BACKGROUND – Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid, hydrocarbon soot, condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Ash particles and soot particles are the dominant particulate in established fires while early ignition and fire establishment periods tend to produce higher concentrations of unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments. Given the constrained environment on any spacecraft the target for any detection system is necessarily the early ignition period and not after the fire has become established, consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot and ash.
PRIOR SPACECRAFT SYSTEMS - In the earliest missions (Mercury, Gemini and Apollo), the crew quarters were so cramped that it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors (Friedm

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ew quarters were so cramped that it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors (Friedman, 1992). These devices were limited to line-of sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms.
Space Shuttle Detectors - The Space Shuttle Orbiter was developed in a time (1970’s) of rapid progress in smoke detection for terrestrial applications (Bukowski and Mulholland, 1978). At the time, ionization detectors were becoming readily available but photoelectric (scattering or obscuration detectors) were generally unavailable due to the difficulty of producing stable light sources. There was no data available concerning the smoke particle size distribution in low-gravity and the database of normal-gravity smoke characteristics was a fraction of what is available today. There was also no data on spacecraft dust particle size distributions but the absence of gravitational settling suggested that there would be more large particles than are seen on earth. Consequently it is understandable that the Orbiter design (figure 1) employed a variant of the accepted ground based ap

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text: tling suggested that there would be more large particles than are seen on earth. Consequently it is understandable that the Orbiter design (figure 1) employed a variant of the accepted ground based approach (ionization detectors). The Orbiter has 9 particle-ionization smoke detectors in avionics cooling air return lines in the mid-deck and flight deck and SpaceLab had six additional particle-ionization smoke detectors in the avionics lines. (Martin and DaLee 1993) While the design rationale is not completely known, Celesco™ (later Brunswick Defense™) based their design on data that suggested incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 to 0.7 m range (L.G. Barr in National Research Council 1975). Use of a pump provided the opportunity to employ a particle separator allowing rejection of particulate larger than 1μm consistent with their understanding that incipient smoke particles were smaller than 1 m. Furthermore, since the response from ionization chambers is affected by the ambient air velocity, implementing an ionization detector in a flow duct was probably facilitated by the use of an air pump to control the air flow through the smoke detector

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ambers is affected by the ambient air velocity, implementing an ionization detector in a flow duct was probably facilitated by the use of an air pump to control the air flow through the smoke detector. This air pump increased the power requirements and reduced the operational life for the detectors.
Figure 1: Brunswick Defense™ smoke detector used in the NASA orbiter fleet. The inlet is on the right and the gas is expelled out the small plate on the top.
ISS Detectors - At the time the International Space Station (ISS) was being developed, stable laser-diode light sources were readily available. Consequently, terrestrial smoke detectors using light scattering were becoming more readily available. This provided the opportunity to produce a detector that required substantially less power, (1.5 Watts versus 9 Watts for the orbiter detector) (Steisslinger et al., 1993) and, with no moving parts, was quieter with a much longer operational life. The choice was supported by data indicating that early smoldering fires produce larger particulate than established flaming fires (Bukowski and Mulholland, 1978). The designated detectors (figure 2) for the ISS are laser-diode, forward-scattering

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
at early smoldering fires produce larger particulate than established flaming fires (Bukowski and Mulholland, 1978). The designated detectors (figure 2) for the ISS are laser-diode, forward-scattering, smoke or particulate detectors. Their sensitivity is greatest for particles larger than 1 m with sensitivity extending down to 0.6 m. The current requirements for the ISS call for two detectors in the open area of the module, and detectors in racks that have cooling air-flow (McKinnie, 1997).
The design developed for the ISS by Allied Signal™ (figure 2) consists of a 2-pass laser diode to sense forward scattered light (30 degrees). There is also a zero degree obscuration system that is used as a measure of the beam strength. The system is designed to alarm based on the magnitude of the scattered light signal referenced to the beam intensity. Some level of dust discrimination is provided based on frequency analysis of the scattered light signal. The system is less sensitive to particles smaller than the wavelength of the laser (near IR) than it is to larger particles. The minimum reported sensitivity is 0.3 m (Steisslinger et al 1993). It draws relatively little power (1.5 W) and i

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
smaller than the wavelength of the laser (near IR) than it is to larger particles. The minimum reported sensitivity is 0.3 m (Steisslinger et al 1993). It draws relatively little power (1.5 W) and it has a long operational life. The current alarm value of 2 volts is calibrated to 3.3% obscuration / meter (1% obscuration / foot) of visible light for punk type smoke in a UL smoke box. In this standard smoke detector qualification method, the detector is placed in a chamber filled with smoke which is adjusted to achieve a target level of attenuation of visible light passing between a lamp and a photocell in the box (Underwriters Laboratory, UL-268, 2003).
Figure 2: Allied Signal/Honeywell light-scattering smoke detector used in the ISS. The near IR laser beam emerges from the enclosure into the top assembly (A) and is reflected by two mirrors (one visible at top right (B)) and is then reflected back to the sensors in the enclosure (C). One sensor detects the forward scattered light and is referenced by another sensor that looks directly at the incident beam.
It is interesting to note that the ISS and the Orbiter detectors have particle sensitivities that are nearly mutually exclusiv

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
is referenced by another sensor that looks directly at the incident beam.
It is interesting to note that the ISS and the Orbiter detectors have particle sensitivities that are nearly mutually exclusive. In both cases the designs were based upon the best available data however, due to the complete absence of low-g data concerning the nature of particulate and radiant emission from incipient and fully developed low-g fires, different conclusions were drawn concerning the optimal design for spacecraft fire detection.
As described by Friedman (1994) there have been six overheat and failed component failures in the NASA Orbiter fleet (Space Transportation System or STS). None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is critically needed (Ruff et al., 2005).
BACKGROUND IN LOW GRAVITY SMOKE – Other than the results reported here, the only combustion-generated particulate samples that have collected near the flame zone for well-developed mi

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
f et al., 2005).
BACKGROUND IN LOW GRAVITY SMOKE – Other than the results reported here, the only combustion-generated particulate samples that have collected near the flame zone for well-developed microgravity flames have been soot sampled from the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) experiment (Urban et al. 1998). All of the other data either came from drop tower tests and therefore only corresponded to the early stages of a fire or were collected far from the flame zone. The fuel sources in the drop tower tests were restricted to laminar gas-jet diffusion flames (Ku et al. 1995) and very rapidly overheated wire insulation (Paul et al. 1993) and Srivastava, McKinnon and Todd (1998). The gas-jet tests indicated, through thermophoretic sampling, that soot primaries and aggregates (groups of primary particles) in low-gravity may be significantly larger than those in normal gravity (1-g). This raises new scientific questions about soot processes as well as practical issues for particulate size sensitivity and detection/alarm threshold levels used in on-orbit smoke detectors. The overheated wire insulation tests in the 2.2 second drop tower suggest that particulate generated by overheated wi

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text: sensitivity and detection/alarm threshold levels used in on-orbit smoke detectors. The overheated wire insulation tests in the 2.2 second drop tower suggest that particulate generated by overheated wire insulation may be larger in low-g than in 1-g (Paul et al. 1993). One of the most surprising results was the determination by Srivastava, McKinnon and Todd (1998) that the Teflon wire coloring agent had a very strong effect on the particle size distribution and morphology. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids downstream of the fire region in the Wire Insulation Flammability experiment (Greenberg, Sacksteder and Kashiwagi 1995) as well as visual observation of long string-like aggregates, further confirm this suggestion. Subsequently, the LSP experiment sampled soot from ethylene and propane gas jet diffusion flames in long-term low gravity (Urban et al, 1998) the soot primary particles were typically twice the size of soot from similar normal gravity flames and the aggregates were more than an order of magnitude larger. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combus

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
re more than an order of magnitude larger. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft.
SPACECRAFT ATMOSPHERE DUST BACKGROUND – Any effort to detect fires must be able to discriminate against the ambient background and nuisance signals. In the case of smoke detection the background dust aerosol conditions must be considered. The only spacecraft background aerosol particulate measurements to date were made on the Orbiter on STS 32 in 1990 (Liu et al. 1991). These measurements included the results from two cascade impactors and a light scattering device. The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 2.5 to10 m and >100 m ranges. The other two ranges <2.5 m and 10 to 100 m were very lightly populated (Table 1). Each impactor samples approximately 15 m3 of air over approximately 30 hours. These results showed substantially higher concentrations than typical indoor measurements. These data were supported by the light scatterin

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ples approximately 15 m3 of air over approximately 30 hours. These results showed substantially higher concentrations than typical indoor measurements. These data were supported by the light scattering instrument which made 17 measurements in 12 locations, all of these reported mass concentrations ranging from 50 to 70 g/m3.The low particle levels in the < 2.5 m bin suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection since typical normal gravity fires produce substantial particulate in this size range (Bukowski et al. 2003, Bukowski and Mulholland 1978), and the average sizes that were recorded by CSD (below) are in this size range. However more complete particle size statistics are needed.
Table 1: Airborne Particle Mass Concentration: Comparison of STS-32 to Indoor Environments (from Liu et al., 1991)
CSD Experiment
The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment was conceived as an opportunity to examine smoke detection from conditions resembling incipient fires in low-gravity. Materials representative of those used in spacecraft (paper, Teflon™, Kapton™ and silicone rubber, and candle wax (representative hydrocarbon)) were heated or ignited in a few cases to produce

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ravity. Materials representative of those used in spacecraft (paper, Teflon™, Kapton™ and silicone rubber, and candle wax (representative hydrocarbon)) were heated or ignited in a few cases to produce three types of smoke (soot, recondensed liquid pyrolysis products and recondensed solid pyrolysis products). The smoke from these sources was exposed to spacecraft smoke detectors and physically sampled for Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) analysis. As will be described below the tests were generally successful and produced unique results. The CSD experiment flew in the Orbiter mid-deck on the US Microgravity Laboratory-3 (USML-3) mission (STS-75).
CSD EXPERIMENTAL CONCEPT - The CSD experimental hardware consisted of two modules named the Near-Field Module and Far-Field Box as shown in figure 3. The Near-Field Module (figure 4) was installed inside the Glovebox and contained the sample and the near field diagnostics. The Far-Field Box (figure 5) was external to the Glovebox and contained two spacecraft smoke detectors. Products from the near field tests were transported to the Far-Field Box and subsequently back into the Glovebox via Teflon hoses which entered the Glovebox throu

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ained two spacecraft smoke detectors. Products from the near field tests were transported to the Far-Field Box and subsequently back into the Glovebox via Teflon hoses which entered the Glovebox through ports in the airlock door. All of the combustion products were contained in either the Glovebox or the Far Field Box; by the time the experiment was completed, all of the products were returned to the Glovebox.
Figure 3: CSD Hardware: The Near Field Module is to the back left and the Far Field Box is to the right. Connecting hoses and thermophoretic sampler are in the front.
The Near-Field Module (figure 4) consisted of a small test chamber fitted with a sample carrier that held the sample being tested. A small fan blew air from the Glovebox into the right side of the chamber past the sample and out the left side where it entered the hose to the Far-Field Module. The sample was ignited or overheated by a resistively heated Kanthal™ wire. The smoke particulate was sampled by a rake of thermophoretic probes and smoke production was detected by a laser light extinction system.
The Far Field Box (figure 5) contained a duct and a fan to transport the smoke from the Near Field Module to t

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ermophoretic probes and smoke production was detected by a laser light extinction system.
The Far Field Box (figure 5) contained a duct and a fan to transport the smoke from the Near Field Module to two spacecraft smoke detectors, one matching the STS detector and the other identical to the ISS detector except that its signal was amplified by a factor of 6.6 over the ISS standard (due to misdiagnosed low-signal from a prior engineering model). The analog signals from the various instruments were displayed by digital readouts on the Far Field Box where they were recorded by a video camera for later transcription.
Figure 4: Near Field Module: Deployed thermophoretic probe on left and a sample card holding a candle to the right.
Figure 5: Interior of Far Field Box: Visible is the interior duct with the ISS detector on the right and the STS detector in the center.
CSD EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE - The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period o

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
ebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined.
CSD EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS - In all, 25 tests were performed, the bulk of which were overheated material tests in which the heating level was established to produce a target weight loss rate without causing the sample to develop a sustaining combustion reaction. The intent of these tests was to produce smoke typical of an incipient fire where much of

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
to produce a target weight loss rate without causing the sample to develop a sustaining combustion reaction. The intent of these tests was to produce smoke typical of an incipient fire where much of the material is being heated but has not yet ignited. The candle tests and one of the paper tests were combustion tests where the samples were ignited so the combustion products could be observed.
As discussed in the introduction, smoke encompasses various types of aerosol materials. In this experiment, the smoke sources can be divided into three types based upon the type of smoke that they emitted: the candle and burning paper produced soot, the Teflon™ and Kapton™ produced particles composed of solid, recondensed, pyrolysis products and the silicone rubber and pyrolyzing paper produced liquid droplets of pyrolysis products. TEM images of the solid particulate are presented below and will be discussed later. For the candle tests, the duct air flow was used to drive the candle flame past the smoke point, causing it to emit soot. These soot tests produced varied results between the two detectors as shown below (figures 6 and 7). In figure 6, both detectors showed rapid detection of the

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
he smoke point, causing it to emit soot. These soot tests produced varied results between the two detectors as shown below (figures 6 and 7). In figure 6, both detectors showed rapid detection of the soot. In the case of figure 7, the STS detector shows a strong signal while the ISS detector signal is quite weak considering this signal has a higher amplification level than the standard detector.
Figure 6. CSD results from candle test 16: Traces of smoke detector signals as a function of time for a candle test 16. The initial peak on both detectors is wax vapor released by the ignition process. The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.
Testing with the Teflon™ and Kapton™ produced lower overall smoke concentrations. In the case of the Kapton tests, the STS detector showed an early peak followed by a rapid return to baseline while the ISS detector reported signal for another minute (figure 8). This result may be an artifact of the flow environment or a result of the fact that the Kapton wire used on the Orbiter uses a combination of Kapton™ and Teflon™ layers and so the STS detector may be respo

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
result may be an artifact of the flow environment or a result of the fact that the Kapton wire used on the Orbiter uses a combination of Kapton™ and Teflon™ layers and so the STS detector may be responding to only one of these materials. Similar results were seen with the Teflon™ testing (figure 9).
Figure 7. CSD results from candle test 6: Traces of smoke detector signals as a function of time for a candle test 6. The initial peak on both detectors is wax vapor released by the ignition process. The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.
Figure 8. CSD results from Kapton™ test 9: Traces of smoke detector signals as a function of time for a Kapton™ test 9. The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.
The liquid smoke producing samples produced very different results as seen in figure 10 for the silicone rubber. Despite producing dense smoke that was clearly visible, the STS detector showed virtually no signal while the ISS detector saturated.
The approach for the pyrolyzing paper samples was to heat them below

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
spite producing dense smoke that was clearly visible, the STS detector showed virtually no signal while the ISS detector saturated.
The approach for the pyrolyzing paper samples was to heat them below the ignition temperature so they produced smoke without ignition. This produced similar results to the silicone rubber with virtually no signal on the STS detector and a strong signal on the ISS detector. Notably in one test the sample ignited and the STS detector signal changed from the baseline to a substantial peak (figure 11) presumably because the smoke now contained soot in addition to the condensed pyrolysis products.
Figure 9. CSD results from Teflon™ test 13: Traces of smoke detector signals as a function of time for a Teflon™ test 3. The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.
Figure 10. CSD results from silicone rubber test 7: Traces of smoke detector signals as a function of time for a silicone rubber test 7. The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.
Figure 11. CSD results from paper test 15: Trace

file: PSI-102_Presentations_Detection of Smoke from Microgravity Fires_paper.2005.docx
text:
cone rubber test 7. The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.

The STS detector (solid line) shows downward deflection with increased smoke level, the ISS detector (dashed line) deflects upward.
