Another proof of burner emulation was demonstrated by Bustamante et al. (2012) by comparing the
flame standoff distance in the laminar region for burning of inclined flat plates. A pure methane
flame was used in a porous plate burner and compared to a methanol flame on a fuel-soaked wick
plate. Results showed the similarity in the flame shape along the surface oriented at different angles
from a ceiling fire, to a vertical wall fire, to a pool fire. Also the onset of transition to turbulent flow
was matched. The paper noted a difference of fire size in the turbulent over-fire region due to a
mismatch between the heats combustion of methane and methanol.
3. Experimental Method
A BRE burner has been designed and constructed, inspired by the de Ris burner. Its size has been
selected based on our flight and drop tower tests, and the burner size used by Brahmi et al (2005).
The BRE burner has a face of 50 mm in diameter. Owing to the anticipated heat flux variation over
the surface while burning in microgravity or normal gravity, two sensors are used. An appropriate
averaging of the two heat fluxes provides the needed average heat flux for computing the heat of
gasification. The thermoc

rning in microgravity or normal gravity, two sensors are used. An appropriate
averaging of the two heat fluxes provides the needed average heat flux for computing the heat of
gasification. The thermocouples at the operating face record the surface temperature, allowing the
re-radiation heat flux to be estimated. Glass beads provide a porous matrix for fuel flow, ensuring a
uniform fuel flux, and porous brass screen serves as its face and internal layers. Figure 1 shows the
BRE burner with heat flux sensors at the center and near the edge.

Validation in 1-g. A series of tests were performed to assess burner’s ability to emulate condensed-
fuel combustion. It was reasoned that fuel properties that control the burning rate are (1) the heat of
combustion, especially controlling flame height; (2) the heat of gasification, an approximation to
evaporative condensed-phase fuels; (3) the surface temperature or corresponding re-radiation; and
(4) the smoke point, which determines flame radiation. These properties must reasonably match
those of the condensed fuel of interest.
The burning rate of the condensed fuel is determined by a load-cell measurement of a pool fire. Then
literature values are established for the four fuel properties as described above. Two of the four
properties – heat of combustion and smoke point – are matched by selecting the proper gaseous fuel.

The other two properties – heat of gasification and surface temperature – indicate the burning
condition. We wish to match these properties with a gaseous fuel mixture having the same mixture
flow rate as the pool fire to evaluate the concept of BRE.
We tested the BRE to see if it could emulate a 50 mm pool of methanol burning steadily. The mass
loss rate of methanol was measured and the flame was photographed. To match the methanol with
the BRE we would need to use a gaseous fuel with the same flow rate. To match the flame height
and consequently the heat flux, the fuel must have the same heat of combustion. In addition,
consideration of the sooting tendency led to the choice of methane as the gaseous fuel. Nitrogen was
added to the fuel stream to match the heat of combustion of methanol, 19.1 kJ/g (Tewarson, 2002).
The gas burner BRE used a fuel mixture of 52% (volume) methane with 48% nitrogen. The flow rate
of the mixture was 33 cc/s to match the burning rate of the methanol, 11g/m2-s.
If the BRE concept is correct, the two flames should be nearly identical in appearance and heat flux
distribution. The measured heat fluxes in the BRE are 5.5 and 21.3 kW/m2 for the heat flux gag

4. Applications of the BRE
Having demonstrated the BRE’s capability to emulate the combustion of various fuels in normal
gravity, extensions of its use can be considered. In addition to steady burning, the conditions of
ignition and extinction can be examined relative to condensed-phase fuels. By the determination of
these conditions, a mapping of the properties that allow burning with boundaries of ignition and
extinction can be produced. This conceivably can be done in normal as well as microgravity.
Moreover the conditions of burning can be efficiently established in microgravity using the BRE.
Some preliminary results in this regard are examined below.

properties of fires. Yet their evaluation for materials is difficult to capture with current experimental

could be clearly identified by increasing the flow rate of fuel gradually until the establishment of the

6. Conclusions
1. We are able to match the burning rate and flame characteristic of a condensed-phase fuel by
matching the heat of combustion and smoke point of the condensed fuel with a gaseous fuel and
inert in the BRE. This has been demonstrated for pool fires of methanol, heptane and PMMA.
2. By adjusting the fuel flow rate to match the burning rate of the pool fire with the selected gas
mixture, the BRE flame yields similar burning conditions as the pool fire of 50 mm diameter, not
only in the fuel property (heat of gasification), but also in the flame appearance. Although the
surface temperature was not perfectly matched, the results were reasonable.
3. Extinction and ignition conditions for the burning of condensed-phase fuels can be studied much
more easily and accurately with the BRE.
4. The success in validating the emulation ability of BRE burner would justify its usage in studying
the burning behavior of condensed fuels of interest by using a simulation gaseous fuel. We hope
to use this to explore microgravity fires.
5. Preliminary drop test results using a 50 mm BRE appears to yield nearly steady burning
conditions. While these conditions may not all correspond to real

1. Introduction
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s BRE experiment to facilitate its
analysis. The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of soot or the
combustion gases. For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-imaging
measurements. Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational
logs provide information that can support the analysis.

It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the BRE data begin by familiarizing themselves
with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the BRE Final Report or the more
comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation document.

Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document. To interpret the non-imaging data,
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 19039A1_data.csv, which has

2. BRE Overview
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/BRE Final Report, which also provides descriptions of the
science, preliminary results, and more. It is strongly suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in
analyzing the BRE data.

The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS).

The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G. Quintiere of the Department of Fire
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is),
namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global,
retired). The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student
in the Fire Protection Engineering department.

Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME
including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam
who are also with CWRU.

The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64.
More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Feb. to April 2019, while the second-
round testing occurred from Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021. The first round of tests was limited to ethylene and
the 25-mm BRE burner, while the second round also included tests with methane and the 50-mm burner
(although not together).

3. Tests Conducted
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/BRE – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments
Report for ISS Increment 64 (which is included in the ACME/s-Flame Final Report). A minor correction was
made to Table 1 in which 19094 is now identified as April 4. It had accidentally been identified as April 5
in the 30-day reports, although the testing did extend past midnight in Cleveland, OH so the final tests

ACME/BRE Data Interpretation 4 August 2022

were conducted on April 5. Nonetheless, the BRE (and more generally ACME) test days and numbers are
identified by the date on which the test day began, even if they occurred after midnight (whether on the
ISS or in Cleveland).

The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 45
flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, when an
additional 17 flames were ignited. BRE’s second-round flame testing began in Sept. 2020, during
Increment 63, in which 47 flames were ignited. The second and final round of tests was
completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames were ignited. As a result,
62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and second rounds of testing for a total
of 194 flames.

The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI
team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests
to maximize its scientific outcome. However, the break was longer than had been planned
because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew availability. As a result, BRE’s
second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds of the preceding ACME experiment,
Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), was completed, where that
occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was the delayed start of commercial crew
launches and understanding that crew availability would be limited until such crew launches
entered an operational, rather than demonstration, phase.

All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene
(C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range of chamber
pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in
future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric
conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen.
In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any combustion products (e.g., water
vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the
chamber atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But during tests
days, the atmosphere was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests.
Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and 50 mm,
and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen. Therefore, the
second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than investigated during the first
round. However, in contrast to the first round most of the round 2 tests were

h nitrogen. Therefore, the
second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than investigated during the first
round. However, in contrast to the first round most of the round 2 tests were carried out at
roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary effect on flames. Meanwhile, the tests in
this round were carried out at various oxygen concentrations as in the first round but were more
often conducted with ~40% oxygen, where oxygen of course has a strong effect on combustion.

BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are independently
conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple
hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4) is the primary
component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-
carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting because of its carbon

ACME/BRE Data Interpretation 4 August 2022

double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen, where the fuel
and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch for some cases. But the ACME
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-
orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.

There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all ISS results are electronically
transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME
experiments.

1. Data Output File
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D). The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and
test (a letter and single-digit number). As such, the example, 19039A1 is test A1 conducted
on the 39th day of 2019. But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 40th) day because
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day.

Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 19039B1, 19039B2, and 19039B3) are
typically similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or
repeat. Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0. While initially used
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a related
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not
conducted at all. The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted
alphabetically. However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter.

The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The first row is a header and provides a limited
summary of the hardware and operational conditions. The header is explained in Section 10.1

B. Image Files
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras:
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera
ACME Data Camera (DataCam)
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package

The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used
for BRE or most of the current ACME experiments. Of the ACME investigations, the LLL-UV camera
was only used by the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) study.

1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera. Its primary
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is
also often referred to as the operations or ops camera.

The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps. It is not recorded on the space station
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/. That software
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making
measurements of flame dimensions.

2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam)
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. It is equipped with a motorized lens with
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for
imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.

Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often
downlinked during a test day. Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon
object (HOBJ) format, which is not readily opened with typical image processing software.
The image data was made available in that raw format and later in a converted TIFF format,
where the NASA conversion was carried out without each of the following:
• color balancing (to avoid possible saturation as subsequently discussed)
• dark frame subtraction
• removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage)
Furthermore, the NASA conversion employs a standard bilinear demosaicing process which is
detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) as it
will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers. The priority in the NASA conversion
was to make the images more readily accessible, not to meet all needs.

Most ACME investigators are processing the raw HOBJ files using the OMA2 software
developed by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment. The
OMA2 software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the
latter can be used with both PC and Linux operating systems. A tutorial was prepared by Dr.
Jesse Tinajero on the use of OMA2 to process ACME’s HOBJ image files, where it can be found
at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMtu3KEXNiI. It has also been broken up and posted
in three parts in which the image resolution may be better:
Part 1 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdQHeQwokvY
Part 2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mua_8CfqhfM
Part 3 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BGRqgbIxZL4

The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten by Tinajero as a Python function, where
Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for MacOS, Linux,

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021

and Windows operating systems. The Python script to open the HOBJ files can be downloaded
from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample. A tutorial for this function may be found at
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wbgWeJSilc.

The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji
variant, where both can be freely downloaded. In either software package, the HOBJ files can
imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings:
Image type 16-bit unsigned
Width 1360
Height 1024
Offset to first image 6244
However, imported DataCam images will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) is subsequently implemented. It
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion. As another option,
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions.

To use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements, it is critical to avoid saturation,
for example by using a camera gain of zero. Another employed approach was to not use the
camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and 1.68,
respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation. Such multiplication can be
done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the white
balancing is accomplished with the commands:
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68
clip 4095
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software
because the color balancing was at least generally not done with the hardware to avoid the
risk of saturation.

However, in carrying out color-ratio pyrometry calculations for the ISS data from ACME’s CLD
Flame experiment, the investigators determined that the three color ratios (e.g., blue/red)
didn’t result in the same temperature profile until the green channel was adjusted by 10%.
This notably differs from the camera’s default of multiplication by 1 (i.e., no multiplication)
for the green color plane.

For Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP): “After rigorous testing, it was determined [by Tinajero and
Long] that a modified version of the bilinear method could be used to optimize the conversion
of raw fiber images to full resolution color images. This modified version biases the linear
interpolation along the length of the fiber. This method combined with moderate use of
defocusing was found to reduce artifacts created by standard demosaicing algorithms and
was used in all of the fiber measurements described below.”
Jesse Tinajero and Marshall Long. “Dilution Limits of Coflow Laminar Methane and
Ethylene Flames in Microgravity Versus Normal Gravity,” 12th U.S. National Combustion
Meeting, 24-26 May 2021.

Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format
with 12-bit image data. As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced. Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021

susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit. As a result, the images feature hot pixels which
increase in number over the months and years in space. As such, it will appear as if there is a
star field within the combustion chamber. Therefore, the images should ideally be processed
to remove the bright outlying hot spots. Radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera
imaging.

Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames. As a
result, the framing rate was typically far less. Different exposures are often selected for
different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate
may not be consistent. Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under
uncertain or varying flame intensities. Bracketing can also used to simultaneously accomplish
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame.

In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file
which should be available for each successful flame test, e.g., to verify the exposure duration.
These files are in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet
software or alternately as a text file. Column headings are found in the first row of such files.

Again, it is very important to understand that the exposure time, in microseconds, trumps the
specified framing rate (in fps), i.e., where long exposures will lead to a shorter actual framing
rate. In this example case, the 0.1-s exposure time means that the framing rate (at the test’s

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021

start) was nominally 10 fps rather than the 30 indicated by FrameRate. It is furthermore
important to understand that the exposure time (and thus actual framing rate) was often
varied during the test, where that could be seldom or often if bracketing was employed, i.e.,
where a repeated sequence of images was taken at different exposures.

Unfortunately, it has been seen during bracketing that the reporting of exposure times in the
metadata files is, or at least can be, offset. Therefore, it is important to identify the brightest
images, for example, in an image sequence to determine which had the longest of the
bracketed exposure times.

The parameter files, with names like ‘as run21028C1.txt,’ control the DataCam exposures and
much more. However, these files have not always saved as intended and were sometimes
corrected after the fact. In contrast, the text-file logs, with names such as 2021-01-28_12-
28_ACME.log, are a reliable source for the parameters which specified the imaging settings
and much more. There is a single file of this type for each test day (at least normally) and the
parameters are a small fraction of the automated log content, but one can search for a test
by its number. Log files like this are discussed in section 4.C.5 of this document.

Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward. In
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s
long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis. This is contrary to an ACME
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format. In this regard, the science requirements were not
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs.

There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely
reproducible. Therefore, the scaling of the image data should ideally be established for each
subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a test day. The scaling can
typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin Filament
Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions.
Meanwhile, the other cameras used in ACME testing had fixed lenses.

3. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera
During ACME testing, this intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass
filter and was generally archived at 23 fps.

The grayscale image files are in a Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) format and can be opened
readily, where brightness/contrast adjustment may again be required.

Note that this camera’s Field of View (FOV) is partially blocked by the arms of the fiber array
for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) when it is moved to position the fibers across the flame.

As with the ACME DataCam, it might be useful to check the metadata for the CFI intensified
camera, which is in a comma-delimited (CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet
software or alternately as a text file.

4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR’s
collimated illumination package. The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter, but it may also be useful for
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction. However, the camera’s red filter,
corresponding to the red illumination, appears to be broad enough to permit significant soot
incandescence to pass through the filter. As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions. After post-processing on the ground,
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened. The
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps.

It is important to understand that this camera’s images are of limited value for BRE because
of the general lack of soot with exception of ignition. But even considering that, the soot
volume fraction can be computed using images from the ACME DataCam as discussed in that
camera’s section.

In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, this
monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera
is nearly insensitive to blue. The red filter was installed on 5 March 2018 and used throughout
all subsequent ACME testing.

C. Test Parameters and Other Files
Files discussed in this section include the following:
CIR chamber calculator file
Test parameter file

1. CIR chamber calculator file
In great contrast to other file types, there is just a single file for each of BRE’s two rounds of
testing:
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2019-01-31 to 2019-04-09.xlsx
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2020-07-22 to 2021-02-03.xlsx
which provide estimates of the composition of the combustion chamber before and after each
BRE test, and more generally for every Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) action
involving gas flow into or out of the chamber. As a result, this includes filling and venting
operations, plus recirculation of the chamber contents through the adsorber cartridge filled
with 13x molecular sieves.

More specifically, the chamber calculator provides the chamber pressure before and after
each operation involving flow into or out of the chamber. While the standard ACME data
output files (discussed in section 4.A.1) provide the chamber pressure throughout each test,

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021

that measurement is from a pressure transducer that hasn’t been calibrated in years.
Meanwhile, the calibrations of the corresponding CIR pressure transducers are checked every
six months and those calibrations are updated if needed. Therefore, the chamber calculator
is the more reliable source of the chamber pressure.

The pressure in the CIR chamber is measured by four different CIR pressure transducers, of
which one (PT29) is a different model used for safety. The output of the other three
transducers were used to obtain an average chamber pressure. However, the output of one
of those (PT28) was clearly an outlier from the other two (PT16 and PT17) as well that of PT29.
Therefore, the average pressure recorded in the chamber calculator file was later based on
just PT16 and PT17.

For BRE, the chamber calculator also provides concentration estimates of the following gases
within the chamber before and after each test and FOMA operation:
Oxygen & nitrogen: O2, N2
Fuels: CH4, C2H4
Combustion products: CO2, H2O
The latter are based on telemetry from the three Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) on the ACME
chamber insert for the flow of fuel, oxygen (or inert), and nitrogen.

In a test, the chamber calculator assumes either complete combustion or no combustion,
where in the former case the reactant flowing from the burner is transformed into carbon
dioxide and water vapor (or water vapor alone if the fuel was hydrogen). Failed or
unsustained ignitions were typically set to assume no ignition. Short-lived flames were often
treated as having complete combustion, even if a significant fraction of the reactant didn’t
burn. However, adjustments can be made to account for partial combustion by appropriate
selection of the ‘Burn Fraction’ in column AL.

With recirculation of the chamber contents, the calculator assumes that the carbon dioxide
and water vapor are completely adsorbed, i.e., removed from the chamber. Meanwhile, it
assumes that any unburnt fuels are not adsorbed.

Researchers can of course make their estimates of the chamber contents where the chamber
calculator should nonetheless be referenced for its record of fills, venting, and recirculation.
Note that the chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed
hardware. Unfortunately, it is not yet possible to compare chamber calculator estimates with
measurements that were sometimes made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph
Instrumentation Package (GCIP). Concentrations from the latter are not yet available as
explained in section 4.A.3 of this document.

2. Test parameter file
Each BRE test was controlled by a software script and corresponding parameter file, named
for example ‘as run21028C1.txt,’ specifying settings for imaging, ignition, gas flow, and more.
The parameter file and script are discussed extensively in the ACME/BRE Experimental
Procedure document, which should be referred to for information on this file type. But note
that the ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the as-run test parameters, where
the separate parameter files are unfortunately not completely reliable. They have not always

ACME/s-Flame Data Interpretation 20 September 2021

been saved and when the file saving was automated, they have still sometimes had missing
entries.

3. Notes
Notes of various types are available for test days, where not all types were collected or
necessarily prepared for each test day. It is important to understand that the notes, whether
handwritten or typed, may include mistakes. It is better to rely on automated logs, metadata
files, and parameter files or of course the measurements themselves when possible.

The daily test point logs, with names such as ‘19039 daily test point log.pdf,’ chronologically
list the tests and the image data acquired which was to be downlinked. Typically, image data
was not downlinked without successful, i.e., sustained, ignition. As an example, image data
wasn’t downlinked if the test aborted prior to ignition. However, the reverse is not always
true. Image data was sometimes downlinked when ignition was unsuccessful and as a result
the test point log is only a clue as to what transpired. Furthermore, note that image data
from certain selected cameras, e.g., the HiBMs camera, was sometimes not downlinked due
to the limit of how much data could be reasonably downlinked in a subsequent two-shift day.

Notes with names such as ‘19039 flow traces.pdf’ include preliminary plots of the flow rates
(as seen on a console during testing) and other flame diagnostics, typically along with
additional information about the tests.

The test parameter notes, with names such as ‘19039 test parameter notes.pdf,’ show the
parameter values which were planned in advance of the test day and the changes made
during the test day.

The test sheets, with names such as ‘19039 test sheets.pdf,’ are summary notes about the
conduct of each tests conducted that day.

Relationship to NASA Flammability
Tests 1 and 2
• The Upward Flame Propagation (Test 1) is the dominant
test for material flammability by NASA.

– It tests the flame propagation of a vertical sample 30 × 6.4 –
7.5 cm wide, under a small electric source heat flux of 75
kW/m2.
– The atmospheric conditions are controlled.
– Burn length and time are recorded.
– It is considered a pass-fail type test.

• The NASA Test 2: Cone Calorimeter with external heat
fluxes of 25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement information gained
from Test 1.

Background of Combustion in
Microgravity
• Experiments in Skylab (Ross, 2001; Kimzey, 1974) indicated sustained
burning of thin paper and plastics.
• More recent experiments indicate flame spread on thin paper and plastic
thin cylinders in microgravity (Ross, 2001).
• Opposed flow spread in a quiescent atmosphere has been shown to
depend on material, thickness, and oxygen concentration (Ross, 2001).
• The burning of candle flames on the MIR (Ross, 2001) last for periods
ranging from about 100 s to more than 45 minutes. A spherical flame
formed around the wick.
• Droplet experiments by Kumagai and others (Ross, 2001).
• Small diameter jet flames of 0.4 – 2.7 mm yielded spherical flames of
durations from 150 – 300 s (Ross, 2001).
• Sunderland et al. (1999) recorded flames for port diameters up to 3.3 mm,
and Re from about 10 – 1700 in microgravity.
• Brahmi et al. (2005) used a gaseous burner to simulate burning in g. They
burned ethane over a 60  60 mm sintered bronze plate in O2-N2 flowing
at velocities of 10 – 150 mm/s.
• Bustamante (2012) aircraft and drop data on flat liquid-fueled wicks.

Knowledge Lacking and Knowledge
to be Gained by Flight Tests
• The proposed tests aboard the ISS will establish the
range of steady burning conditions for condensed fuels
in microgravity. We will identify the associated material
properties and the real materials that are represented.

• Once established based on fuel properties, NASA Test 2
could be used as a basis for establishing comparable
properties for real materials. This could elevate the role
of NASA Test 2 over Test 1. This would close the loop of
using a ground-based test to assess the true
flammability of materials in microgravity.

Science Data End Products
Objective
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity
for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular
burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2
ambients with various pressures and ambient O2
concentrations and pressures. Emphasize conditions that
can be related to diverse condensed fuels.

2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of
O2/CO2 (desired).
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction
limits.

Science Data End Products
Science Data End Products
• Color flame images and shapes.
• UV images.
• Surface temperatures and incident flame heat flux measurements.
• Radiation from the flame to the surroundings to estimate radiative
flux.
• Flammability mapping of quasi-steady burning as a function of heat
of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface temperature.
• Quasi-steady burning flux (burning rate per unit area) as a function
of significant properties, e.g., heat of gasification, heat of
combustion, and smoke point.
• Contour plots of soot temperature and filament temperature.
• Contour plots of soot volume fraction.
• Plots of radiant emissions versus time.
• Plots of chemiluminescent emissions versus time.

Justification for Extended-
Duration Microgravity
• The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft
owing to considerable g-jitter disturbances.

• Testing in NASA 5.2-s drop facility indicated possible approach to
steady burning.

• The longer duration testing in the ISS will facilitate the efficient
operation of the BRE to exploit a relatively quick record of results
over a range of flow rates. This will insure a complete
flammability map in microgravity.

BRE Operational Sequence
Action Approx.
Time
1. Ensure that the appropriate burner is installed. Preflow the
burner fluent gas at the composition of the upcoming test point
to flush the plumbing system.
2. Establish chamber conditions. These consist of a set point
pressure and species compositions, as specified in the test
matrix. Conditions are obtained in four ways: from cabin air
(desired); from the preceding test; from scrubbing and
replenishing; or from a complete evacuation and recharge.
3. Allow chamber contents to reach equilibrium. A hold time of
5 minutes is required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed
conditions.
4. Take reference images (if applicable). Establish framing rates for
video cameras. Begin color imaging. Begin monitoring
measurements and wait 15 s.

BRE Operational Sequence
Action Approx.
Time
5. Commence fluent flow at a value to be uplinked. The initial
value should correspond to about 1 g/m2-s of hydrocarbon fuel.
Energize igniter to ignite the flame and then retract the igniter.
If ignition does not occur within 5 seconds, shut off the flow. A
new value of flow rate will be specified by uplink. If the flame
ignites, proceed to Step 6. Otherwise proceed to Step 7.
6. Set the flow rate to the test flow rate. Anytime during this step,
if the flame extinguishes, or either heat flux sensor exceeds a
critical temperature, stop the fuel flow. Continue until the
surface burner temperatures become quasi-steady. Then
reduce the flow rate in 10% increments of the test flow rate,
hold for 15 s, and continue such reductions until extinction.
7. Stop fluent flow. Record reference images (if applicable). After
60 s terminate color imaging and monitoring measurements.

Heat flux measurement
• The incident heat flux is conductive and radiative.
• Heat flux gages in the surface will record incident
heat flux.
• Thermocouples in the surface will record the Ts
distribution.
• Surface reradiative flux scales with Ts 4.
• Flow rate will be varied to obtain a wide range of L.

Motivation
• Many condensed fuels have a critical heat flux (CHF)
below which ignition and spread is impossible.

• This CHF depends on the surface heat loss rate.

• Buoyant cooling occurs in 1g, so CHF is lower in g.

• BRE will identify g CHF for condensed fuels.

Condensed fuel ignition in g will generally be easier
than on Earth.

NASA Test 1
• The Upward Flame Propagation
(Test 1) is NASA’s main test for
material flammability in
spacecraft.
• It tests the flame propagation of a
vertical sample 30  6.4 – 7.5 cm.
• Burn length (15 cm threshold) and
time are recorded.
• It is a pass-fail test.
• It is similar to UL-94, whose
performance scales with hc / L .

NASA Test 2
• Ohlemiller (1992) found that NASA Test 1 results did not
correlate with NIST flammability tests of ignition, burning
rate, and opposed flow flame spread.
• He recommended that Test 1 be modified to include the
addition of external radiant heating.
• NASA Test 2 uses a cone calorimeter with heat fluxes of
25 – 75 kW/m2 to supplement Test 1.
• Tests 1 and 2 do not explicitly predict performance in g.
Ohlemiller recommended g tests,
stating “Without such information
spacecraft designers are confronted
with unquantifiable risks regarding
fire safety.”

Relating material properties to g flammability
Can 1g properties be related to g flammability?

• This works for to UL-94 in 1g, whose performance
scales with hc / L .
• If it works in g, a limited number of g tests could
be used to predict ignition, burning, and extinction
behavior of many materials.

A BRE goal is to furnish g measurements relating
ignition, burning, and extinction to material properties
that are obtainable in 1g.

g combustion surprises
• Quasisteady burning of condensed fuels in g has
rarely been observed.
• Several surprises were seen in tests of g droplets
and flame spread, including those associated with
3D effects, flaming fire brands, radiative extinction,
etc.
• The effects of radiative feedback have not been
explored.

The MIR fire
• In the MIR fire a solid propellant oxygen generator
ignited, producing a 1 m flame.
• If this flame had impinged on other materials, could
they have burned self-sustained?
• Material flammability in space must be better
understood.

Past condensed fuel combustion in g
• Experiments in Skylab indicated sustained burning
of thin paper and plastics.
• Spread on 4.5 mm diameter rods of Delrin, PMMA
and HDPE was achieved in opposed flows down to
1 cm/s.
• Opposed flow spread in quiescent g depends on
material, thickness, and oxygen concentration.
• Droplet flames of Kumagai, Williams, and co-
workers.

Candles in g
• Candle flames on MIR survived from 1 – 45
min. Hemispherical flames were observed.
• Dietrich and T’ien’s glovebox tests had
much shorter durations.
• The MIR flights had XO2 = 0.22 – 0.25 and a
metal screen enclosure.
• The glovebox had XO2 = 0.217 and a
perforated plastic enclosure.
Sustained burning of condensed fuels in g without
external radiation is confirmed.

Flame shape in g
• Sunderland and co-workers found g gas jet flames
to be spherical at low Re, and longer than 1g
flames.
• Candle and droplet flames also are spherical in g.
• Planar surfaces in g can produce spherical flames.

• Torero and co-workers
burned ethane in a 60  60
mm porous burner in g.
• Oxidizer flow rates were 10
– 150 mm/s.
• Three flame shape regimes
were observed: elliptical (I);
parabolic (II); and flat (III).
• BRE is likely to encounter
all 3 shapes.

sintered metal burners for studying the steady
burning of planar condensed fuels.
• The fuel flux was uniform across the burner
surface. Water cooling was used.
• They successfully emulated burning rate and flame
shape for a wide range of B numbers:

• The proposed ISS tests will establish the range of
ignition, steady burning, and extinction for diverse
condensed fuels in g.

• Effects of incident radiation will be considered by
scaling the test results.

• Follow-on tests could incorporate the effects of
convection and other extinguishing agents.

Knowledge lacking and
to be gained by flight tests
• BRE will identify flammability maps for:
L = 0.5 – 5 kJ/g
hc = 5 – 50 kJ/g
= 0 – 20 kW/m2

• Where unknown, these properties can be
measured in 1g for diverse materials using NASA
Test 2.

• This will close the loop of using a ground-based
test to assess the flammability of materials in g.
"
rrq

Experimental Objectives
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration g for
CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on 25 and 50 mm
porous circular burners. Consider O2/N2 ambients
with various XO2 and p. Emphasize conditions that
can be related to diverse condensed fuels.
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for
ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for
ignition limits.
4. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for
extinction limits.

Summary of approach for ISS tests
• Burn tests. The chamber contents will be set. Fuel flow
will commence followed by ignition. The flames will be
observed without varying the fuel or its flow rate. Ts and
L will vary, allowing diverse conditions to be observed.

• Ignition tests. The chamber contents will be set. Fuel
flow will commence followed by attempted ignition.

• Extinction limit tests. The chamber contents will be set.
Flames will be ignited followed by a gradual reduction in
fuel flow rate until extinction.

Plans for ground-based research
• Measurements to establish flammability
maps in normal gravity will continue,
using gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.

• Development of detailed analysis tools
will continue.

• Modeling using FLUENT is planned.

Science Data End Products
Objective Science Data End Products
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration
microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2
mixtures on 25 and 50 mm porous circular
burners. Consider O2/N2 ambients with
various XO2 and p. Emphasize conditions
that can be related to diverse condensed
fuels.
Color flame images
UV images
Ts and incident flame heat flux
measurements
Soot temperature
Soot volume fraction
Gas phase point measurements
Radiant emissions
Chemiluminescent emissions
Gas Composition
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for
ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
Same as for Objective 1.
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2
for ignition limits.
Ignition limit map.

4. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2
for extinction limits.
Extinction limit map.

Justification for extended-duration g
• NASA Tests 1 and 2 are inadequate for analyzing
material fire hazards in spacecraft.
• Past and planned g tests of condensed fuels are
insufficient to cover the diverse condensed fuels
used in spacecraft.
• The BRE tests cannot be performed in parabolic
aircraft owing to g-jitter. Drop tower times are too
short compared to the characteristic times for the
gas phase (~20 s) and Ts (~40 s).
• Only long-duration g tests will allow the
establishment of g flammability maps.

Requirements discussion
• Most of the BRE experiment requirements fall
within the ACME ISRD requirements.
• Details are provided next.

Requirements discussion
BRE Burners
• The burners shall involve round porous frits of 25
and 50 mm diameters.
• Each burner shall contain two heat flux meters flush
with the frit surface and facing outward.
• The heat flux meters shall be maintained at 65 – 85
°C to avoid condensation.
• The burners shall be positioned such that the burner
axis is coincident with the CIR chamber axis and
orthogonal to the CIR chamber window axes.
• The plane of the CIR chamber window centers shall
be 10±2 mm downstream of the frit surface.

ISRD Section 1.1: Accepted
ISRD Sections 1.2-1.7: Not Applicable

Requirements discussion
Burner Gas Delivery
Required flow rates for BRE are:
• Fuel: 0 – 0.1 slpm (N2 basis)
• Oxidizer: Not applicable
• Inert: 0 – 2 slpm (N2 basis)

These requirements were established by
observations of flames in 1g, in the 5 s drop
facility, and on the parabolic aircraft.

ISRD Section 1.8: Accepted.
ISRD Section 1.9: Accepted for the above flows.

Requirements discussion
Ignition
• Ignition disturbances should be minimized
to allow undisturbed burning quickly.
Ignition should occur ~ 3 mm from the frit
surface.
• BRE is unique among ACME experiments
in its interest in ignition limits. Thus the
igniter conditions must be highly repeatable.

ISRD Section 1.10: Accepted with the above
qualifications.

Requirements discussion
Ambient Environment
• Prior to each test, the chamber shall contain the
specified gas composition within ±0.01 mole fraction. A
cylindrical free area that is (1) at least 200 mm in
diameter, (2) at least 100 mm downstream of the frit
surface, and (3) at least 50 mm upstream, shall be kept
clear of solid objects. The temporary insertion of the
igniter and probes are allowed exceptions.

• Suggested methods to decrease bottled gas
consumption rates include, as available, partial venting
and filling, and scrubbing for CO2 and H2O.

ISRD Section 1.11: Accepted

Requirements discussion
Data Recording
• Data recording is required for the two
BRE heat flux sensors, one at the center
of the burner and the other midway
between the center and the periphery.

• Data recording is required for the two
thermocouples attached to the frit surface.

ISRD Section 1.12: Accepted with the above
additions.

Requirements discussion
Monitoring Measurements
• The BRE monitoring measurements shall include:
chamber p; chamber XO2; gas flow rates; burner p;
and acceleration.
• These shall be initiated before test operations begin
and continue sufficiently past flame extinction to
allow a baseline measurement.

ISRD Sections 2.1-2.3: Accepted
ISRD Sections 2.4 and 2.5: Not Applicable
ISRD Section 2.6: Accepted

Requirements discussion
Science Diagnostics
• Measurements shall include: color imaging for
operations; color imaging for data analysis; UV
imaging; Ts at 2 locations with a range of 30 – 500 °C;
T in hot soot-containing regions; T in hot soot-free
regions; T in far-field; soot volume fraction; radiant
emission; chemiluminescent emission; and post-test
gas composition.

ISRD Sections 3.1-3.3: Accepted.
ISRD Section 3.4: Accepted, with specific locations to
coincide with the two heat flux measurements. Two K-
type thermocouples will measure Ts from 30 – 500 °C.
ISRD Sections 3.5-3.9: Accepted.

Operational sequence for ignition,
burn, and extinction tests
Action Time
1. Install burner and flush the plumbing.
2. Establish chamber conditions (p and species).
3. Allow 5 mins for chamber contents to reach equilibrium.
4. Take reference images. Begin color imaging. Begin
monitoring measurements and wait 15 s.
5. Ignition test: Commence fluent flow, energize igniter, and
retract igniter. If flame ignites, proceed to Step 6 or Step
7. Otherwise proceed to Step 8.
6. Burn test. Allow the flame to burn until extinction or
quasisteady. Detect extinction with a PMT or with near
real-time video. Reduce flow rate to confirm extinction.
7. Extinction test. Burn for 20 s then reduce flow rate
gradually until extinction.
8. Record reference images. After 60 s terminate color
imaging and monitoring measurements. Select data for
downlink and downlink data.

ignition, burning, and extinction tests for
25 mm burner at 1.01 bar.
Evacuate and recharge chamber.
2 O2/40 C2H4/100 0.025 Ignition, burning and extinction test.
3 0.050 Ignition, burning and extinction test.

6 0.050 Ignition, burning and extinction test.

Test matrix
Test Notes
11– 19 Repeat Tests 2 – 10 for an ambient of O2/30.
20 – 28 Repeat Tests 2 – 10 for an ambient of O2/21.
29 – 55 Repeat Tests 2 – 28 for CH4.
56 – 82 Repeat Tests 2 – 28 for 50 mm burner.
83 – 91 Repeat Tests 2 – 10 for an ambient of O2/15
(desired).
92 – 100 Repeat Tests 110 – 118 for CH4 (desired).
101 – 135 Repeat Tests 2 – 28 and 110 – 118 at 2.02 bar
(desired).
136 – 142 Repeat Tests 110 – 118 for 50 mm burner
(desired).
143 – 177 Repeat Tests 2 – 28 and 110 – 118 with ambients
of O2/CO2 (desired).

Test matrix notes
• Many tests shown will not ignite.
• Chamber contains O2/N2, except tests 143 – 177, which
involve CO2 in the chamber and N2 in the burner stream.
• Different fuel and oxidizer mole fractions may be specified
during uplink.
• If scrubbing is available, the CO2 and H2O will be scrubbed
after some tests, and reactants replenished as needed.
• Estimated video downlink time for BRE is 50 minutes. Full
downlink will be required for the first few flames. Otherwise
downlink will include 15 s intervals around ignition and
extinction and occasional 2 s intervals.

Science success criteria
Minimum Success

• Obtain color video, Ts, and burner heat flux for one
C2H4 flame that burns for at least 20 s and then
extinguishes.

Science success criteria
Complete Success (i.e., completion of required matrix)

All of the above plus:
• Perform Tests 1 – 82 or a similar set of tests.
• Obtain flammability maps for C2H4 and CH4.
• Measure peak T as a function of time for at least 5
flames.
• Measure T distributions at quasi-steady conditions and
near the extinction limit for at least 5 flames.
• Measure soot volume fraction profiles at quasi-steady
conditions and near the extinction limit for at least 5
flames.

Science success criteria
Superior Success (desired)

All of the above plus:
• Perform Tests 83 – 177 (including O2/15; CH4; 2.02
bar; 50 mm burner; and O2/CO2).

Post flight data analysis plan
• Much post-flight data analysis will occur during mission
ops. Analysis will include: plots of Ts, incident flame heat
flux, and L versus time; and analysis of other discrete
signals for evidence of quasi-steadiness.

• Extensive image analysis will be performed and, where
possible, compared with g images of condensed fuel
flames.

• We will map out the flammable conditions and burning
rates of diverse condensed fuels. Flammability maps for
each ambient condition will be prepared on 3-axis plots,
where the axes are hc, L, and reradiation heat flux.

Flying 250 miles above the Earth, the International Space Station (ISS)
provides a platform for research to improve life on Earth, enable space
exploration, and understand the universe. This Researcher’s Guide is
intended to help potential ISS combustion science researchers plan
experiments utilizing the microgravity environment in order to understand
how heat and mass transport phenomena coupled with chemistry affect
combustion behavior and fire safety. It covers the nature of the acceleration
environment on ISS, available facilities for conducting combustion research,
examples of previous microgravity investigations, and current combustion
science and fire safety projects being developed for execution on the ISS.
The Lab is Open

1. Microgravity, or weightlessness, alters many observable phenomena
within the physical and life sciences. Systems and processes affected by
microgravity include surface wetting and interfacial tension, multiphase
flow and heat transfer, multiphase system dynamics, solidification, and
fire phenomena and combustion. Microgravity induces a vast array of
changes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans, including global
alterations in gene expression and 3-D aggregation of cells into tissue-like
architecture.
2. Extreme conditions in the ISS environment include exposure to extreme
heat and cold cycling, ultra-vacuum, atomic oxygen, and high-energy
radiation. Testing and qualification of materials exposed to these extreme
conditions have provided data to enable the manufacturing of long-
life, reliable components used on Earth as well as in the world’s most
sophisticated satellite and spacecraft components.
3. Low-Earth orbit at 51 degrees inclination and at a 90-minute orbit
affords ISS a unique vantage point with an altitude of approximately 240
miles (400 kilometers) and an orbital path over 90 percent of the Earth’s
population. This can provide improved spatial resolution and

Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water
and heat. For the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy
in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting
systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation
to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture).
These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards
currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury
contamination from coal, and wild-land fires).
Despite being the subject of active research for over 80 years, combustion processes
remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact
on human health, comfort and safety. This is because the simplest combustor
(e.g., kitchen stove) remains beyond our detailed numerical modeling capabilities.
Typically, the combustion process involves a large number of chemical species
(hundreds) and reactions (even thousands). It is these species and reactions
that determine flammability limits (combustor operating ranges) and pollutant
emissions. Much of combustio

chemical species
(hundreds) and reactions (even thousands). It is these species and reactions
that determine flammability limits (combustor operating ranges) and pollutant
emissions. Much of combustion research involves developing a comprehensive and
predictive quantitative understanding of this complex process. This understanding
usually occurs in smaller, bench-scale experiments that are amenable to detailed
study and modeling. In these bench-scale experiments, however, buoyant forces,
created by gravity and the large temperature differential between the flame and
the ambient gas, dominate and frequently obscure the physical and chemical
phenomena of interest, and hence, complicate analyses. In the absence of gravity,
buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler one-
dimensional systems.
To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the
density gradients in flames. Typical flame temperatures are on the order of 2,300
degrees Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees
Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter.
The resultant density gradient induces a strong ve

Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees
Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter.
The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but
the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward.
The resultant flow instabilities cause the flicker typical of flames on Earth. Figure 1
contains a gallery of 1-g to 0-g comparison flames.
By varying or eliminating the effects of gravity, we can extract fundamental data
that are important for understanding combustion systems. This approach has
been implemented to some extent in existing terrestrial reduced-gravity platforms,
but the experimental time scales and sizes have been limited. Long-duration
Why Conduct Combustion
Research in Microgravity?

experiments using realistic sizes are essential for a comprehensive understanding of
the combustion phenomena and are possible only in the microgravity environments
offered by space facilities.
Besides terrestrial applications of combustion, gravity-related combustion research
issues are also of crucial importance to NASA’s manned and unmanned missions.
Fire safety is an important operational element of human space exploration
missions to minimize the likelihood and impact of accidental fires in spacecraft
and human habitats. The effects of these environmental changes on combustion
in reduced gravity are unclear and need to be better understood for all mission-
relevant scenarios. Every aspect of fire prevention, detection and suppression is
Figure 1. 1-g and 0-g comparison flames. Left to right, top to bottom: ethane jet flames, ethylene jet flames, candle
flames, burning heptane droplets and flame spread over a butanol pool. (Image credit: NASA)

fundamentally different in space than on Earth. Thus, an improved knowledge of
combustion in reduced gravity is essential to adapt fire safety concepts and systems
to the more stringent conditions of the space environment.
Benefits of conducting combustion research in microgravity can thus be
summarized as:
• R emoval of the complex interaction between the buoyant flow and the energy
feedback to the flame.
• R ealistic simulation of the fire risk seen in manned spacecraft.
• P ractical simulation of the gravitational environment seen for reacting systems
in future spacecraft.

Over the past two decades, microgravity combustion research has focused primarily
on increasing our understanding of fundamental combustion processes (e.g.,
droplet combustion, soot production, flame spread, smoldering and gas jet flames).
This research program has been highly successful and was aided by synergistic
programs in Europe and in Japan. Overall improvements were made in the ability
to model droplet combustion in spray combustors (e.g., jet engines), predict flame
spread, predict soot production, and detection and prevention of spacecraft fires.
Some of the findings from past microgravity combustion research are presented
below. Current ongoing flight projects on the International Space Station (ISS) are
given in each area.
Droplet Combustion
The availability of a long-duration, high-quality microgravity environment allows
researchers to study the textbook problem of a spherical droplet surrounded by a
spherical flame in an infinite, quiescent, ambient atmosphere. A cadre of researchers
from academia, industry and federal laboratories has successfully established this
simple geometry as an excellent test bed to study fundamental combustion science
problems and other topi

researchers
from academia, industry and federal laboratories has successfully established this
simple geometry as an excellent test bed to study fundamental combustion science
problems and other topics of applied combustion research. Through a robust
program, researchers gained insight into wide-ranging problems of interest in
combustion science. These programs included ground-based experimental work in
drop towers and aircraft flying parabolic trajectories (and normal gravity; i.e., 1-g,
test laboratories), numerical and theoretical modeling, and ultimately experiments
in space-based facilities. The programs provided the opportunity to investigate
phenomena such as:
• D epartures from quasi-steady combustion.
• T ransition from diffusive to radiative extinction.
• Liquid-phase transpor t.
• The influence of conv ection on flame dynamics (refer to Figure 2).
• The dynamics of soot formation and destr uction (refer to Figure 3).
• The behavior of multi-component fuels.
• D roplet-droplet interactions and flammability limits.
Results from Past and
Recent Research

The droplet combustion community is fortunate to currently have the Combustion
Integrated Rack (CIR) and a CIR insert called Multi-user Droplet Combustion
Apparatus (MDCA) available to study droplet combustion aboard the ISS. This
facility is currently operational and allows the dispensing, deployment and ignition
of droplets ranging in size from 1 to 5 mm (either free floating or fiber supported)
in a 0-3 atm ambient environment of up to 40 percent oxygen by volume (balance
of a range of inert gases and inert gas mixtures).
Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
The objective of the FLEX is to study heptane and methanol droplets in ambient
mixtures of oxygen and nitrogen diluted with a second inert gas (nitrogen, carbon
dioxide, helium or xenon). The goal of the research is to examine how the addition
of an inert gas suppressant influences the flammability limit of the two fuels. The
application is an improved quantitative understanding of how flammability limits
change in reduced gravity as it relates to fire safety. The research to date has shown
that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity. The implication is that
terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in l

vity as it relates to fire safety. The research to date has shown
that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity. The implication is that
terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same
margin of safety as in normal gravity.
The FLEX is of interest for terrestrial applications as well. The physical and
chemical kinetic models of heptane and methanol combustion are the building

burning in 70 percent carbon dioxide, 21 percent
oxygen, balance nitrogen and translated to the right

Figure 3. Comparison of sooting propensity in different
diluents with ethanol burning in 30 percent oxygen at pressure of
2.4 atm. (Image credit: NASA, FLEX-2 experiment)

blocks for more complex models of practical liquid fuels such as diesel and jet fuel.
The long-duration experiments on the ISS provide benchmark data that researchers
can develop, improve and ultimately validate detailed theoretical and numerical
models of liquid hydrocarbon fuel combustion. The FLEX experiments performed
to date demonstrated radiative and diffusive extinction, combustion instabilities,
lower flammability limits and recently explained cool flame phenomenon after
visible flame extinction. Comparison with theoretical and numerical models
validated aspects of the models while identifying areas that require improvement.
FLEX-2, the follow-on experiment, builds upon FLEX. It studies a range of fuels
including mixtures of pure fuels, real fuel surrogates, soot formation, slow sub-
buoyant, convective flow effects and droplet-droplet interactions. International
collaborations extend this to study flame propagation in droplet arrays and
investigate the combustion of liquid, biologically derived fuels.

Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame)
Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed
that our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes
of fuel dilution, namely for sooty, pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are
near extinction. The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the
range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and
experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels. The
dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be
carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions.
Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames
in an air coflow. Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid
flame dependence on heat loss to the burner. The results of this experiment will be
directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion,
ignition, flame stability and more.

Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)
Electric fields can strongly influence flames because of their effect on the ions
present as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the
induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits,
direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission. The purpose of the E-FIELD
Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame-ion production
and investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames. Outside
reviewers recently concluded that the experiment “… will contribute to our critical
understanding to our knowledge of combustion processes in the presence of electric
fields.” The experiment will be conducted with a normal coflow flame (as in the
CLD Flame experiment) or perhaps with a simple gas-jet flame where there is no
surrounding coflow. An electric field will be generated by creating a high-voltage
(up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat, circular mesh suspended
above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of field

differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on Earth. On Earth
it is understood that the best results are generally obtained when the extinguisher
“attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and the point

microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment

The goal is to measure flame spread rate across a representative, thick, solid fuel

Super-Critical Processes
Because of its unique and significant advantages, Super-Critical Water Oxidation
(SCWO) was identified by NASA as a potential technology for use in closed-loop,
life-support systems addressing waste management and resource reclamation needs.
Initial efforts in applying SCWO to solid waste management were conducted at
NASA’s Ames Research Center in the 1990s in ground-based laboratories. These
early tests were designed to look at oxidation rates and destruction efficiencies for
cellulosic material as a function of particle size, mixing, temperature and pressure.
Results from these tests provided empirical correlations for use in reactor design.
In 2004, an investigation to assess the impact of buoyancy on SCWO processes
was initiated as part of GRC’s microgravity combustion program. The SCWO

Well over 200 principal investigators have utilized reduced-gravity facilities to
study fundamental combustion phenomena in the areas described above. Most of
the research was conducted in drop towers and aircraft, and the most promising
experiments, after a thorough scientific and engineering review process, were
selected for conduct in space-based facilities. The investigations led to numerous
discoveries, highlighted the importance of frequently neglected phenomena,
improved our understanding and predictive capabilities for all combustion systems,
and enhanced our ability to detect and prevent spacecraft fires. Some of the most
pertinent highlights and lessons learned are presented below.
Flame Existence
One of the most seemingly simple, but long-standing, questions addressed by
microgravity testing involved whether flames could even exist without buoyancy.
Many researchers, including notable experts, argued openly in the scientific
literature that, in the absence of convection, a steady flame could not exist;
diffusive transport alone could not sustain a flame. Two spaceflight experiments
demonstrated conclusively the fallacy of such arguments.

Low-Stretch (Low-Velocity) Flames
Reduced-gravity facilities offer the opportunity to study flames where the
characteristic velocities are much lower than typical buoyancy-induced gas
velocities, approximately 1 m/s in the candle flame in Figure 1. These low-speed
flows result in flame stretch or strain rates that are unachievable in terrestrial,
bench-scale experiments. Conventional theories of flame limits all predicted that,
as the flame stretch characteristic velocity decreased, the oxygen concentration
that would support steady or quasi-steady-state combustion would monotonically
decrease.
This was not the case, however, as several classes of experiments demonstrated. At
low-characteristic velocities (low-flame stretch), radiative loss begins to dominate,
eventually leading to flame extinction at sufficiently low velocities or stretch rates
(e.g., Olson et al., 1988). Figure 8 shows this schematically. For flame spread across
solid materials, the ordinate in Figure 8 is the ambient oxygen mole fraction and the
abscissa the gas velocity across the solid surface. The boundary represents limit of
steady flame spread. Outside of this boundary, steady flame spread does not occur;

Another common class of flames in combustion research is gaseous jet flames (a

the details of soot production and destruction. For bench-scale laminar gas-jet

and space-based facilities show striking differences (in comparison to normal-

jet Reynolds numbers (e.g., Hegde et al., 1994; Urban et al., 1998). The onset of

Flame Stability
In normal gravity, flames that approach their flammability limit are frequently
“blown off” by the large buoyancy-induced flow. These same near-limit flames in
microgravity exhibit very different and unique behaviors in many cases. The simple
microgravity candle flame in Figure 1, as it depleted the ambient oxygen and
neared extinction, exhibited flame oscillations in most tests (Dietrich et al., 2000).
These oscillations increased in magnitude until the flame finally extinguished, but
they could exist for prolonged periods of time (over one minute in extreme cases).
Similar flame oscillations occur during spherically symmetric droplet combustion
(Dietrich et al., 1996).
Instabilities also occur during flame spread over solid and liquid surfaces. Over
solids, a complex fingerlike smoldering front occurs during near-limit flame spread
under certain conditions (Olson et al., 1998). A pulsating gas-phase flame spread
occurs as a flame spreads across a liquid pool under selected ambient conditions (e.g.,
Miller et al., 2000). Finally, microgravity experiments involving premixed flames
demonstrate instabilities in both low- and high-Lewis-number gas mixtures (e.g.,

These instabilities, obscured in normal gravity by the strong buoyant flow, highlight

Cool Flames
Recent spaceflight experiments (FLEX) involving single alkane droplets burning in
a quiescent ambient uncovered unexplained and unexpected behavior. For the large
alkane droplets, after ignition the droplet burns for a short time with a typical hot
flame. As expected, the hot flame extinguished when the radiative loss reduced the
flame temperature below a critical value. Inexplicably after hot flame extinction,
however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period
and then suddenly stopped

ced the
flame temperature below a critical value. Inexplicably after hot flame extinction,
however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period
and then suddenly stopped vaporizing at a finite droplet size. The plateau in
vaporization occurred coincident with the formation of a large vapor cloud. This
vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that
forms after visible flame extinction. The vaporization stops when the cool flame

extinguishes and the vapor cloud forms because the cool flame only burns a fraction
of the fuel vaporized from the droplet surface.
This cool flame supported droplet combustion was not only unexpected, but also
thought to be impossible by many in the peer community (it took a year for the
team to convince themselves and then another year to convince the skeptical peer
community). Cool flames form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and
oxidizer, but should not form after a hot flame extinguishes. The FLEX tests showed
that the cool flame can burn for a prolonged period of time. The microgravity
droplet combustion tests offer a unique platform to study these low temperature
chemical reactions. Cool flame chemistry is very important in internal combustion
engines and a predictive understanding of their chemistry is critical in developing the
next generation engines with higher efficiency and lower emissions.

Spacecraft Fire Safety
The 1967 tragic accident of Apollo 1, in which three NASA astronauts lost their
lives when a cabin fire broke out during a launch pad test, and the near-tragedy
of Apollo 13 in 1970, when an oxygen tank exploded during transit to the moon,

highlight the hazard posed by accidental fires on spacecraft. A fire or explosion
requires all elements of the “fire triangle” to be present: fuel, oxygen and a source of
ignition. Crewed spacecraft, by necessity, contain all three. In addition, spacecraft
frequently operate at an ambient oxygen mole fraction higher than that of air, have
limited options for escape, and have almost no tolerance for damage to critical life
support systems. As a result, NASA maintains a very disciplined safety culture with
respect to fire through strict material controls, rigid design standards for electronic
equipment (and all possible ignition sources), and mandatory suppression systems on
all spacecraft.
Although NASA has been vigilant in its approach to accidental fires, the approach
to fire safety aboard spacecraft was dominated by a general lack of knowledge about
how fire behaves in microgravity. This resulted in several critical misconceptions
about potential fires in spacecraft:
1. A steady fire cannot exist in a quiescent microgravity environment.
2. A fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off.
3. B ecause the reduced-gravity environment is inherently safer, terrestrial fire

Super-Critical Processes
Hydrothermal flames (e.g., Figure 20) are defined as regions where oxidation
reactions occur in a super-critical water medium with sufficient intensity and rates
as to produce luminous flames. They may be utilized to solve both of the major
issues impacting SCWO mentioned earlier; i.e., surface fouling and flow blockage
that is due to the precipitation of salts and corrosion of internal reactor surfaces.
This may be accomplished by confining the flame to the interior of the reactor
within a co-flowing region of sub-critical water. Any precipitated salts formed in
the super-critical flame region will dissolve in the sub-critical fluid and the acidity
is diluted, thereby eliminating both precipitate build-up on and corrosion of the
reactor walls.
