offs of existing research since they require relatively smaller resources and hence may
be faster to develop. New initiatives such as Cool Flames in CIR, NASA Flammability
Test Campaign and Schlieren Diagnostic in MSG may fall into this category.
Cool Flames would be an example of how one of the unprecedented findings of CIR-
FLEX studies can set the stage for a new research direction on combustion utilizing
existing hardware available on the ISS. Cool Flames objectives include: (i) use a range
of fuel types and environmental conditions (e.g., pressure, diluent concentrations,
etc.) in order to determine the necessary pre-conditions for hot-flame/cool-flame
transitions, cool flame stability and spontaneous re-ignition and (ii) development
of a robust numerical modeling capability with detailed che

ine the necessary pre-conditions for hot-flame/cool-flame
transitions, cool flame stability and spontaneous re-ignition and (ii) development
of a robust numerical modeling capability with detailed chemistry to complement
analytical development of Cool Flame Theory. The initiative has great relevance to
the next-generation engine designs such as Homogeneous Charged Compression
Ignition and Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition since these engines rely on
low-temperature combustion processes, such as Cool Flames, to control emissions
and reduce fuel consumption. This research also has significant impact on spacecraft
fire safety concerns; reduced-gravity environments have been shown to be particularly
conducive to a low-temperature combustion regime marked by very weak but

persistent flames, invisible to the unaided eye, that will spontaneously re-ignite
long after the visible flame has been extinguished. The necessary pre-conditions, the
combustion chemistry, and the mechanisms for spontaneous re-ignition are poorly
understood. The Cool Flames development effort would utilize existing FLEX-2 CIR/
MDCA hardware augmented with some additional diagnostic capabilities.

Acceleration Measurement and Environment Characterization
The terms microgravity, reduced gravity, low gravity, zero gravity and weightlessness
are often used interchangeably to describe an environment where the gravitational
body force is significantly less than that on Earth. This ambiguous description
points to a question of how to measure and characterize a reduced-gravity
environment and any disturbances. Disturbances in a microgravity environment
are created by crew activities such as exercising, push-offs and landings, and simply
opening and closing drawers and doors in addition to equipment operation, vehicle
docking and undocking, thruster firings, and other movements. These disturbances
must be measured to understand their impact on the data from scientific and
engineering experiments.
The Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) and the Microgravity
Acceleration Measurement System (MAMS) provide continuous measurement of
the ISS vibratory and quasi-steady acceleration environment, respectively. SAMS
sensors measure acceleration levels using tri-axis accelerometers. SAMS flew on
Mir from 1994 to 1998, continued on 20 shuttle missions

Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
The CIR was designed to test experiments that focus on fire prevention, detection
and suppression of fires in space. The hardware was delivered on STS-126
(November 2008) to the ISS and installed in the U.S. Laboratory. The CIR

provides a 100-liter chamber with eight optical windows with easily reconfigurable
diagnostics, digital cameras and lighting with large data storage capability, gas
distribution/cleanup, passive vibration isolation, and vacuum resources to support a
wide range of gravity-dependent gaseous, liquid and solid combustion experiments.
The current research program on gaseous fuels includes five experiments planned for
the CIR on the ISS. These experiments are part of the ACME project where each
will be conducted using a single modular set of hardware. The ACME experiments
are focused on soot processes, flame stability and extinction, materials flammability
and electric-field effects. In alphabetical order, the experiments, described in more
detail above, include BRE, CLD Flame, E-FIELD Flames, Flame Design and
Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame). The ACME set of
experiments are expected to begin operating in 2016. As with their predecessors,
the ACME experiments are all laminar diffusion flames. Two experiments take
advantage of the microgravity environment by using a one-dimensional, spherical
flame enveloping a porous spherical burner. Another experiment uses

The SoFIE flight hardware (Figure 10), involving combustion research on solid
fuels, is currently under development as a CIR insert and planned for launch in
2019. The SoFIE project is in the Science Definition phase to serve up to five
separate investigations. These investigations all support the overall objective of the
SoFIE project, which is to study and characterize ignition and flammability of solid
spacecraft materials in practical geometries and realistic atmospheric conditions.
The SoFIE insert in the CIR could continue to be used by additional NRA-selected
private investigators who wish to study solid fuel flammability and flame spread
with different geometry fuels in a variety of oxygen, pressure, flow and external heat
flux conditions.

Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
The MSG is a rack facility aboard the ISS in which fundamental and applied
scientific research is conducted. The MSG has been operating on the ISS since July
2002 and is located in the U.S. Laboratory. The unique design of the facility allows
it to accommodate science and technology investigations in a workbench-type
environment. The facility has an enclosed working volume that is held at a negative

pressure with respect to the ISS pressurized volume. This allows the facility to
provide two levels of containment for small parts, particulates, fluids and gases. This
containment approach protects the crew from possible hazardous operations that
take place inside the MSG work volume.
Research investigations operating inside the MSG are provided a large, 255-liter,
enclosed work space, 1,000 watts of dc power via a versatile supply interface (120,
28, + 12, and 5 Vdc), 1,000 watts of cooling capability, video and data recording
and real-time downlink, ground commanding capabilities, access to ISS Vacuum
Exhaust and Vacuum Resource Systems, and gaseous nitrogen supply. These
capabilities make the MSG one of the most utilized science facilities on ISS. In
fact, the MSG has been used for over 10,000 hours of scientific payload operations.
MSG investigations involve research in cryogenic fluid management, fluid
physics, spacecraft fire safety, materials science, combustion, plant growth, human
health and life support technologies. The MSG facility is ideal for advancing our
understanding of the role of gravity upon science investigations and research and to

Telescience Support Center
The Telescience Support Center (TSC) was established in 1993 to provide ground
support for shuttle experiments. With the development of the ISS in 2001,
additional capabilities were needed to support new ISS experiments. During this
time, the TSC was reconstructed and doubled in size. Currently, the TSC consists
of 33 workstations that provide real-time audio and video downlinks allowing
researchers to observe and control experimental operations aboard the ISS from
the ground. The ISS video downlink provides a real-time view of the astronauts
aboard the ISS interacting with the experiment. The TSC also allows researchers
to operate and control experiments remotely with little astronaut interaction after
the installation and setup of experimental hardware. The TSC supports projects 24
hours a day, seven days a week; and since 2001, the TSC has logged over 26,000
hours of continuous support of microgravity experiments aboard the ISS. The TSC
continues to provide ground support to the ISS experiments today.

Complexity of the experiment should be minimized if at all possible. Science
requirements that add complexity not only add additional cost to the development,
but often lengthen the development time, making turnover an issue for both the
project team and, in particular, for the principal investigator and his/her science
team when the experiment timeline extends beyond the typical tenure of a Ph.D.
student. It is strongly recommended to design the experiment to be flexible and
repairable. Unlike the space shuttle experiment days, the International Space Station
is very much like a laboratory on Earth and crew members gain good experimental
skills while operating a particular experiment over months rather than just a week
or so, and they can become quite adept at experiment repair if this capability is
designed into the experiment and clear straightforward procedures are provided.
Although experiments in microgravity offer enticing rewards to combustion
researchers, the harsh realities of experiments in reduced-gravity facilities present
significant hardware and diagnostic challenges to scientists and engineers. Drop
tower and space-based experiments have severe space, weight, volume

significant hardware and diagnostic challenges to scientists and engineers. Drop
tower and space-based experiments have severe space, weight, volume, safety,
and power limitations. The hidden benefit of these limitations have been the
developments of technology with applications far beyond the microgravity
combustion science program. Future capability needs for conducting combustion
science in space certainly include advanced diagnostics, and supporting such needs
requires more space and power.
One of the most severe limitations of future space-based combustion science
experiments is crew time. Astronaut availability is prioritized on the basis of many
factors and the realistic assumption should be that it will remain as limited as it has
been in the past. It is therefore extremely important that the space experiments be
built with a capability for autonomous start, operation, and finish, and with as little
maintenance as possible. The test matrices should be designed such that minimal
crew interaction is necessary for fuel and oxygen supplies, sample and holder
change-out, diagnostic adjustments, etc.

solicitations are facilitated through the web-based NASA Solicitation and Proposal

calls through the peer review and selection process.

What Is Microgravity?
Gravity is a force that governs motion
throughout the universe. It holds us to the
ground and keeps the Earth in orbit around the
Sun. Microgravity describes the environment
in orbital space flight, which has very weak
gravitational effects (one-millionth of what is
felt on Earth) and which is sometimes referred
to as a state of “weightlessness.” The condition
of microgravity occurs when an object is in
“free fall.” In free fall, an object falls faster and
faster, accelerating with exactly the speed of
attraction caused by gravity. Objects travelling
around the Earth in a state of continuous free
fall, or orbit, are essentially weightless even
though their mass remains the same.
Conducting research in a microgravity
environment gives researchers a unique oppor-
tunity to study the true nature of processes and
materials without having to consider the effects
of Earth’s gravity. Thus, physics theories can be
tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible
on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the
mystery of how gravity affects processes such
as combust

tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible
on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the
mystery of how gravity affects processes such
as combustion science and fluid physics. This
knowledge can then help to improve the way
we do things on Earth.

The term “microgravity” will become more com-
monplace when the International Space Station (ISS) is
fully operational. The ISS will be the largest orbiting space
structure and the largest international scientific and tech-
nological endeavor in history. Sixteen countries, including
the United States, are participating in this record-breaking
project. The ISS is a permanent laboratory in space where
studies can be performed without the effects of gravity.
The space station provides researchers with all the
laboratory space and equipment and electrical power
needed for safe, long-term research by human beings in
space. The ISS enables larger and longer experiments than
were possible on the typical 2-week space shuttle mission.
This gives scientists time for more detailed observation in
the microgravity environment.
The knowledge gained from ISS microgravity experi-
ments is benefiting research on Earth in many fields. Our
understanding of theories relevant to everything from high-
temperature superconductivity to weather prediction will
be advanced. New insights into areas such as human health

Combustion Science
Combustion, or burning, is a process in which a sub-
stance reacts with oxygen to give off heat and light. Com-
bustion meets almost 85 percent of the U.S. energy needs.
While it does a good job of powering how we live on Earth,
combustion is a major contributor to air pollution.
The cost of combustion energy is about $450 billion
each year in the United States. In any area of the economy
where a huge amount of money is spent, even the small-
est improvements in efficiency can mean savings of very
large amounts of money. A mere 1 percent increase in
fuel efficiency, like improving your gas mileage from 25
miles per gallon to 25.25 miles per gallon, would translate
into a savings to America of nearly 100 million barrels of
oil a year (roughly $5.5 million per day at today’s cost).

Although today combustion is vital to transportation, mate-
rials processing, hazardous waste disposal, and many other
areas, there is still only limited understanding of many of
its fundamental characteristics.
There are over 2500 fatalities and tens of billions of
dollars in property damage each year in accidental fires.
Combustion research in microgravity can lead to
advances in fire prevention, detection, and fighting. In addi-
tion, combustion research in microgravity can lead to more
efficient use of energy, reduced pollution, and improved
processes for making high-technology materials. Glenn
Research Center’s experience with jet engines provides a
solid background in combustion and Glenn scientists have
already begun to study combustion in space.
A simple example of microgravity’s effect in combus-
tion is the behavior of flames in space. On Earth, hot air
rises around a candle flame, which causes the flame to
flicker and take on an elongated shape. In microgravity,
however, no such distortion takes place. The

FCF allows researchers to study aspects of combustion,

Fluid Physics
Of the four states of matter—solid, liquid, gas, and
plasma—three are fluid, meaning they flow in response
to an applied force. An understanding of fluid physics is
not only vital to advancing aircraft and spacecraft applica-
tions, such as airflow and propellant management, but is
also essential to understanding the human body, aspects of
everyday life, and many industrial processes. In micrograv-
ity, fluid positioning and flow characteristics can be studied
from a new perspective.

Experiments by Remote Control
While the astronauts perform their roles in experiment
setup, operation, observation, evaluation, and feedback, the
FCF is teleoperated from the NASA Glenn Research Cen-
ter. Operation of experiments via remote control is coor-
dinated through the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at
Glenn. Telescience is the systematic monitoring, command,
and control of an experiment from a remote location and
has already been implemented successfully by NASA on
the shuttle/Spacelab and the Russian Mir Space Station. In
concert with the work performed by the astronauts in space
and the Cleveland-based operations team, the FCF principle
investigator’s (PI’s) experiment can remotely monitor and
control from the PI’s home site through Glenn’s TSC.
The concept of telescience offers several advantages.
Typically, the development of an experiment takes years
and involves a varied group of scientists, engineers, and
support personnel. Only a few of these people need to be on
the operations team that travels to a NASA cente

ment of an experiment takes years
and involves a varied group of scientists, engineers, and
support personnel. Only a few of these people need to be on
the operations team that travels to a NASA center to sup-
port actual mission operations. A major benefit of remote
operations is that the entire team that developed and built
the experiment can be connected to the operations team to
support data analysis, command decisions, anomaly resolu-
tion, and other real-time considerations. Also, some facili-
ties that are not physically located at NASA centers can be
included (e.g., colleges, universities, and industrial labs).
Additional benefits are reductions in travel requirements
and increases in the amount of science data acquired.

file: PSI-22_Presentations_Chien et al 2019 Ion Current and Flame Changes with Electric Fields.pdf
text:
Electric field, ions and flames Background and motivation
• Hydrocarbon flame’s inherent electrical
property was reported more than two
centuries ago.
• Most of the theories with regard to the
electrical charge carriers and ionization
process were not extensively elaborated
until after the 1950s.
• The book, written by Lawton and Weinberg,
on the electrical aspects of combustion
integrated the knowledge at the time (1969)
of a flame’s systematic ion generation as
well as electrical control of flames based on
laboratory tests and observations.
• Pederson and Brown (among others)
identified chemi-ionization mechanisms in
hydrocarbon flames in 1993.
Why microgravity?

Electric field, ions and flames
Background and motivation
• The dominant ion, H3O+,
from the hydrocarbon
flame zone is found
experimentally and
numerically.
• CHO+ + H2O à H3O+ + CO
• Chemi-ion driven wind is
the result of the ion drift.
• The ion transport is
dominated by the
electrokinetic drift while
the ion convection and
diffusion are relatively
small.
• Ion drift velocity: the
positive ion accelerates
between each collision with
neutral gas molecules.
• Induced drift velocity: each
collision transfers the newly
acquired kinetic energy to
the neutral gas.

F: body force

• Electric body force is around
1-10 times the buoyant
force on earth.

text:
Electric Field Effects
Ion reactions make up a small subset of
combustion kinetics.
Microscopic electric field effects:
• Charge separation
•Acceleration prevented by collisions
with neutrals
• ~100 m/s ion drift velocity
Macroscopic field effects:
• Ion-driven wind (~1 m/s)
• Reshaping of the reaction zone
• Change in flame luminosity
• Altered stability
• Forced extinction
Starik and Titova, 2002

influence of chemi-ionization on
combustion without buoyancy.

Conclusions and Future Work
• Flame oscillations are present for a variety of applied field strengths.
• Field driven oscillations can be arranged into two regimes:
• Those which cause visible flame movement (~10 - 20Hz)
• Luminous oscillations (~30 - 40Hz region)
• Lower coflow velocities are necessary to recognize the contribution of buoyancy to
ionization.

file: PSI-22_Presentations_Lopez-Camara et al 2015 Numerical simulation of a co-flow methane-air flame.pdf
text:
Summary
• No published model for non-premixed co-flow
methane/air flames that contains both chemi-ions and
excited species.

• 2D OpenFOAM® simulation showed promising results
explaining certain hypotheses from past studies for
gravity and microgravity environments. However, 1D
CHEMKIN® simulation showed that errors exist in the
reduced mechanisms as regards the prediction of ion
precursors.

• Inconsistencies in the reduced mechanism are more than
likely propagating into even larger errors in the
prediction of the chemi-ions.
Summary

text:
Main Flame characteristics
• Flame height was shown to not be affected by a change in gravity field.
• Flame width was affected by producing a thinner plume as it was expected.
• Detachment with the burner tip was observed numerically and it might be
attributed to the numerical challenge of these boundary conditions.
• The new combination of chemical kinetic model proposed containing excited
species and ions has shown to predict important characteristics of the non-
premixed methane laminar jet flame.
CH* chemiluminescence
• CH* profiles showed a brighter flame while going to higher gravity
environments (hypergravity conditions).
Ions
• High concentration of H3O+ produced and transported far away from the
flame.
• Higher concentration of naturally produced ions has been observed under
hypergravity conditions. The electric field effect could be increased under
strong gravity environments.
Summary
33rd ASGSR Annual meeting. Oct. 25-28, 2017. clopezca@uci.edu 14

text:
• The extruded burner geometry shows an I-V curve similar to the one obtained in the experiments in a 1g
environment. Changes in the boundary condition have to still be performed.
• The saturation point in the I-V curve obtained using the flush burner geometry simulation is aligning with
the one obtained experimentally. The peak of positive charges (H3O+) that reach the upper electrode (anode)
is displaced from the center, aligning with the experimental observations. However, simulations at sub-
saturation regimes show that higher e-fields are needed in the simulation in order to get the same ion
currents (z-direction) than the ones obtained experimentally. This might be caused by the interaction
between burner (positive electrode) and reaction zone. More investigation has to be performed in order to
clarify this phenomena.
Next steps:
• Define why sub-saturation flush burner geometry simulations show that higher electric fields are needed to
achieve the ion currents obtained experimentally.
• Proceed by simulating jet geometry burner flames at 1g.
• Proceed by simulating the three burner geometries at 0g.
ASGSR Annual meeting. Oct. 31- Nov 3, 2018. clopezca@uci.edu 11

Final remarks and future work
Final remarks
• We have built a chemical kinetic model that contains the minor species CH*, OH*, H3O+
and HCO+ and trust-worthily predicts non-premixed flame behavior at steady state.
Comparison between experimental and numerical results validated the reduced model.
• Speed up in the simulations without e-field in comparison with detailed model was
obtained (> x2).
• The size of the reduced model should be small enough to handle e-field 2D simulations.
Near-future goals
Validation of the model
• Change the burner geometry and repeat the simulation, comparing it to experiments.
• Check how the methane flame responds to an external applied e-field, comparing it to
experiments (at 1g and µg).
Others
• Repeat the mechanism reduction process with an C2H4 detailed model.

K. Swenson1, S. Karnani2, D. Dunn-Rankin2, F. Takahashi3, D. Stocker1, and

This paper describes measurements aimed at understanding the influence of electric fields on
flames where buoyancy has been removed. Given that buoyancy and an electric field can have a
similar influence on flames, buoyancy can obscure the contribution of an electric field in a normal
gravity (1g) environment. Experiments were performed in the microgravity conditions of NASA’s
2.2 Second Drop Tower on a simple jet diffusion flam e to isolate the influence of an electric field.
Results show similarities between the ion current response of a methane flame in an electric field
in both 1g

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Presentations_Swenson et al 2011 Electric field induced convection in microgravity combustion.pdf:1:1
file: PSI-22_Presentations_Swenson et al 2011 Electric field induced convection in microgravity combustion.pdf
text:
rop Tower on a simple jet diffusion flam e to isolate the influence of an electric field.
Results show similarities between the ion current response of a methane flame in an electric field
in both 1g and microgravity ( μg). Under some coflow velocities an d electric fields strengths, it is
possible to modify the flame shape so that it resembles a flame in 1g.
1. Introduction
When oxidized, hydrocarbon fuels produce a nu mber of intermediate species, a small
subset of which are charged. Hence, an electrosta tic field applied across the flame zone creates a
charge separation; opposites attr act and ions move to ward their respective opposite electrode.
Acceleration of the ions is limited as momentum is transferre d through collisi ons with neutral
molecules. These repeated co llisions induce a wind of comp anion neutral gas, which can
potentially affect flame stability [1, 2], induce convection [3], and simulate microgravity [4-6].
In a 1g environment, the plume of hot gases from a flame naturally induces, through mass
continuity, a convective flow to the neighboring cooler environmen t, giving rise to the flame’s
characteristic teardrop shape. In a microgravity environment, buoyant

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Presentations_Swenson et al 2011 Electric field induced convection in microgravity combustion.pdf:1:2
file: PSI-22_Presentations_Swenson et al 2011 Electric field induced convection in microgravity combustion.pdf
text:
naturally induces, through mass
continuity, a convective flow to the neighboring cooler environmen t, giving rise to the flame’s
characteristic teardrop shape. In a microgravity environment, buoyant convection, which in 1g is
responsible for the trans port of fresh oxidizer to a flame, is removed, leaving forced convection
to dominate the flow field while species transport is a function of both that and molecular
diffusion[7]. A number of experiments [8-10] have studied electric fields applied to flames in
microgravity environments to measure mobility, its influence on burning rate constants, and the
feasibility of inducing forced convection in a buoyancy free environment.
The comparable influence of buoyant c onvection makes studying ion wind effects on
flames in a 1g environment difficult. By re moving buoyancy, the ion wind becomes a dominant
force capable of creating similar flame shapes in a non-buoyant environment. This paper’s
objective is to explore the different ion current re gimes of a small diffusion flame when affected
by an electric field in 1g and μg using the NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.

2. Experimental
The experimental drop rig (Figure 1) includes a cylindrical test chamber (24.6 cm i.d., 53.3 cm
length), flow system, and data acquisition/control hardware. The burner is a stainless-steel fuel
tube (2.1 mm i.d., 2.4 mm o.d.), coaxially positioned inside the cylindrical test chamber. For
conditions requiring a coflowing annulus of gas, the stainless-steel fuel tube is coaxially
positioned inside a Pyrex® converging nozzle (27.3 mm exit i.d.), through which air flows. Gas
flow was controlled with a fixed orifice and upstream pressure. A hot-wire igniter (coiled 29-
gauge Kanthal, 11 cm length), which can be positioned over the burner by a rotary solenoid is
used to ignite the fuel (CH4, 99.97%). Data signals from thermocouples, pressure transducers,
radiometer (Dexter, ST150 Amplified), and a tri-axis accelerometer (Crossbow, CXL02TG3-S)
are digitized and recorded at 20 Hz. The flame is observed by a CCD color camera (Hitachi HV-
D30), transmitted through a tethered optical fiber, and recorded using a digital video recorder
placed atop the Drop Tower.

3. Results and Discussion
Flame response is presented in the following graphs by plotting the measured ion current as a
function of the applied field. It should be noted that the burner is always grounded and electrical
potentials are applied at the electrode. The polarity of the field is considered positive when the
mesh electrode has a positive potential with resp ect to the burner electrode. All data points,
except where noted, are averaged between t = 1.6 s to t = 2.1 s of the drop to avoid measuring the
flame’s transient response. Data points were only in cluded in the data set if a flame was present.
Error bars represent the standard deviation of the shunt voltage in this same time period.
Figure 3 shows the relationship between ion curr ent and electric field strength for a 24 cm/s

region characterized by a near quadratic increase in ion current with voltage and a saturation

4. Conclusion
The ion current response is nearly identical in μg and 1g environments, with the exception of the
positive saturation plateau. This is expected cons idering that ion production is a global measure
of flame behavior that is dependent on the flow field regardless of the driving mechanism. At
electric field strengths greater than 1.8 kV/cm in μg, the flame begins to oscillate and the ion
current jumps up significantly. At this point a fa int corona glow is observed from the nozzle tip.
At electric field strengths more negative than -1 .6 kV/cm, the flame is unable to adjust to the
abrupt change in flow conditions and extinguishes . Future research will include intermediate
voltage steps or a ramp for testing at higher fiel d strengths. Within the re spective uncertainties,
the surface area and flame base loca tion of the images presented in Figure 4 are equal; where a

Conclusions
1.Transient Effects due to Voltage Steps
IA wave is created in thermal plume. The wave is more apparent near
satuartion ﬁelds and for longer electrode spacings.
IAverage plume wave velocity was linear with average ﬁeld strength
I75hz oscillation appears in the ion current measurements when ﬁeld strength
surpasses 2kV/cm. This oscillation can clearly be seen in the schlieren
videos
2.Time-Scales
IUCI H.V. power supply produces electrode potential on the order of a 1kV in
2-3ms. The ACME H.V. power supply produces the same electrode potential
at a rate 0.1kV/ms
IBulk of ion current arrives downstream at⇡10-20ms
IPlume reaction time for a voltage step from the UCI power supply was

text:
Introduction
Chemi-ions:
Ions naturally produced within the combustion reaction of hydrocarbon
ﬂames.
How do external electric ﬁeld eﬀects produce observed ﬂame reactions?
Explanations:
1. Electronic thermal eﬀect
joule heating increasing ﬂame temperatures.
2. Electronic chemical eﬀect
highly energized electrons enhancing reaction rates.
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
mechanical drag on bulk gas by migrating ions.

text:
Introduction
1. Electronic thermal eﬀect
Jaggers and Engel (1971)
▶ combustion power - ∼104W
▶ electrical power - ∼1W
2. Electronic chemical eﬀect
▶ not well deﬁned
▶ Fialkov (1997)
comprehensive survey of literature concluded,
“a high-frequency electric ﬁeld aﬀects the propagating ﬂame velocity, but
shows little or no eﬀect on the burning velocity of the ﬂame on the burner.”
3. Ion wind eﬀect:
Majority of electric ﬁeld combustion community agree that ion wind
theory could almost completely account for the observed eﬀects.

Discussion
What is the source of the super-saturation ion currents?
Possible sources:

▶ global breakdown - unlikely
(since ﬁeld strengths ≪ 25kV/cm)

▶ enhancement to gas ﬂow dynamics enhancing local mixing leading to

ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56

15 Nov. 2018
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 55 and 56

ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project,
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).

Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information.

Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin, University of California, Irvine, CA
PI project scientist: Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, University of California, Irvine, CA
Lead collaborator: Prof. Sergey Minaev, Far Eastern Federal University, Vladivostok,
Russia
NASA Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:1:1
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
I. Introduction
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat,
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong
electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting
behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing
through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and
stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of
ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:1:2
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:2:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56

experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical
benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the
electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:2:1
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives:
A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as
functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert
(nitrogen) in the fuel.
B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion
current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene)
flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.
C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of
luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions
of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to
the fuel stream.
D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize
the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven
wind to stabilize or reattach these flames.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:2:2
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of
flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and
polarity are the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests are conducted with
methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-
producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They are conducted with both a
simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner is conducted with and without a
coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to
assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provides a different
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).
In a typical test, the mesh electrode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner),
where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is
measured. The field strength is

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:2:3
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
ode is energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner),
where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength is
measured. The field strength is changed in repeated steps or is instead smoothly ramped.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:2:4
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.
Microgravity flame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone. Length scales are
increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-
dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:3:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56

velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to
their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames
because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity
flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The
absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability
behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing
can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the
gravitational environment of the combustion application. Chemi-ion species, electronically
excited chemiluminescent species are are very low concentration in typical flames, making the
reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

II. Methods/Research Operations

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:3:1
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the
ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry
stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or
soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56, where the console commanding
during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog
ops video that the flame had extinguished.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:3:2
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.

Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
A total of 142 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment during Increments
55 and 56. The first round of testing occurred from March to May 2018, which was
followed by a second round, which began in September 2018 and was still underway at
the beginning of Increment 57. The first round of tests resulted in 120 ignited flames

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:4:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56

conducted with the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD
Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’s second round occurred between the two rounds
of the E-FIELD Flames expeirment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results
in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific
outcome.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:4:1

text:
E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests
are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.
Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane
(CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot
given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting
because of its carbon double bond. For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel
and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions. For limited cases, the fuel
and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch. ACME bottles were launched
with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on
a volume basis). Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%,
50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis). But the ACME
hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing
for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations. In all cases,
the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume bas

Pre-flight and post-flight activities are generally not addressed in this report.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies
1. Mission anomalies
The primary hard drive for the CIR’s IPSU-G Image Processing and Storage Unit - for
Gigabit Ethernet (GigE) cameras – failed to boot on April 27, 2018 (18117). For ACME
experiments, the IPSU-G is used for two key cameras, the ACME color digital ‘data’
camera (i.e., DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera,
which is used for CLD Flame with a narrow bandpass filter to image CH*
chemiluminesence. Use of the IPSU-G was recovered by astronaut Scott Tingle on
May 7 (18127) by the removal of that primary drive. The removed drive was
reinstalled on Aug. 14 (18226) by astronaut Ricky Arnold during the second round of
CLD Flame testing. Although the hard drive was installed in the secondary position,
the IPSU-G surprisingly again became unusable. Therefore, it was removed on Aug.
22 (18234) by astronaut Alex Gerst, returning it to use, albeit without the intended
storage capacity.

The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was
only intermittently operable in mid-Sept. 2018 and was not operable at the start of E-
FIELD Flames’ second round. Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD
Flames, where the illumination is significantly blocked by the mounting bracket for
the mesh electrode. Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269) and Oct. 1 (18274) were
conducted without HiBMs imaging or the CIR illumination. It was later determined to
be an issue with a cable connection, which was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on
Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other ACME tasks.

text:
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically abort (due to the controlling software
script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter. As a
result, there is little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. The aborts
normally occur because of communication issues with IPSU-1. These are infrequent,
but there are some days when tests abort repeatedly.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:6:2
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been
sufficiently primed. Ignition is sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of
the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH*
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH*
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible
spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to
false ignition detection.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:6:3

ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and
synthetic air (i.e., 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen, on a volume basis) have
unfortunately not always performed adequately. The fuel and especially nitrogen
flows sometimes oscillate. Furthermore, the MFC used for the ‘air’ coflow behaves as
if it is sticking in a few places, where the flow rate won’t linearly ramp when
commanded (as required for the CLD Flame experiment). It tends to stick in some
places and then abruptly overshoot where that has sometimes been seen to
extinguish the flame. As a result, mass flow controllers are tested - without flames -
after they are first installed. Adjustments are often then made to (1) the settings that
control when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID)
settings. This activity has involved significant testing, separate from flame tests, and
has taken place during CLD Flame operations on 17333, 17334, 17347, 17354, 18008,
18022, 18038, 18046, 18143, and 18241. In this regard, there are an assortment of
MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gases. While the MFC tuning

has been beneficial in some cases, it has not eliminated all gas flow problems. It was
seen that nitrogen oscillations tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow was
implemented so that the oscillations would typically end before the flame
measurements. That approach has been partially successful and was introduced
during E-FIELD Flames’ first round. Later, a procedure of re-zeroing the MFCs prior to
each test was also implemented during E-FIELD Flames’ second round. A replacement
MFC for the ‘air’ coflow is being prepared for spaceflight, where a limited third round
of CLD Flame testing is being planned to accomplish its extinction limit objective.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:7:1

text:
The final day of testing during E-FIELD Flame’s first round was conducted with highly
sooty ethylene flames and a positively charged mesh, which tends to push the flame
down toward the burner. A significant amount of soot deposited on the burner, both
on the inner tube from which the fuel issues as well as the honeycomb in the burner
annulus from which the air flows. The extent of the soot wasn’t appreciated until
flame testing for CLD Flame’s second round began on May 25 (18145). Additional
evaluation tests were performed on May 31 (18151), and the decision was made to
have the crew clean the soot from the burner because it was clear that the gas flow
from the burner was affected by the soot buildup. A cleaning procedure was
developed, approved, and carried out by astronaut Ricky Arnold on June 19 (18170).
The cleaned burner was imaged with the CIR cameras on June 21 (18172), but the
evaluation testing was deferred because of a cable mating issue. The cable mating
was corrected by Arnold on June 25 (18176) and the evaluation testing of the cleaned
burner was conducted on the following day, June 26 (18177). Regular flame testing
in CLD Flame’s second round finally commenced on July

old on June 25 (18176) and the evaluation testing of the cleaned
burner was conducted on the following day, June 26 (18177). Regular flame testing
in CLD Flame’s second round finally commenced on July 5 (18186), six weeks after the
soot accumulation was identified as an issue. However, useful scientific results were
obtained on the June 26 evaluation day, so the burner cleaning effectively led to a 1-

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:7:3

text:
C. Completeness/Quality of Data
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1)
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD),
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-
voltage power supply. Following the revision, a total of 74 E-FIELD Flames tests were
identified as required. In contrast, 120 flames were ignited in the experiment’s first
round, i.e., first half. In that round, roughly 200% more flames were ignited than had
been planned.

It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests. As
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination
package. Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:8:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56

Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be
managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing
within the project constraints.

Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually
become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing,
they are a degradation of the image quality.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:8:1
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). In this regard,
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).

Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has
been secured and E-FIELD Flames is considered to be highly successful.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:8:2
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
D. Status of Data Analysis
Data from the E-FIELD Flames experiments includes video recordings from the operations
camera for general flame behavior, the ACME data camera for high resolution images at
various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera
images and non-imaging data at 100 Hz. The non-imaging data is extracted using Matlab
scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to show trends of ion
current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters
(fuel, flowrate, burner type). Image data is processed using the OMA software (also
developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).

The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day, the data
has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine. At this stage,
with operations ongoing, the analysis is comparative and qualitative, just to show the
major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:8:3
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
E. Preliminary Research Findings
Results from the early E-FIELD Flame experiments have demonstrated clear differences
between normal-gravity and microgravity flame behaviors. A few examples include the
distinct maximum of ion current for co-flow burner flames in microgravity, where the 1-g
flames more smoothly reach a saturation condition. The results also show that the
electric body force can produce flame oscillations similar to those driven by buoyancy in
normal gravity, and microgravity flame shapes with an electric field can mimic normal-

gravity flames without electric fields. Burner type plays a role in the flame/field
interaction, and in particular, reversing the field polarity for the jet flame does not
produce an inverted result over the entire voltage range tested. Results also demonstrate
the interactions between electric fields and soot are more complex in microgravity. At
the same time, the preliminary findings suggest that some of the key expectations
generally hold (e.g., ion current scales approximately with flow rate for a fixed fuel and
burner).

The key measurement for the E-FIELD Flames experiments is the ion current as a function
of applied voltage, i.e., the voltage-current or V-I curve. This curve provides information
on the flames ability to produce chemi-ions based on its saturation ion current, and it
provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of
carbon influx into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process. More
compact, higher temperature flames produce more chemi-ions than do larger more
diffuse reaction zones of lower overall temperature for the same fuel flow. The first effect
(i.e., the relationship between carbon influx and peak ion current) can be seen in Figure
2, where the flow of 15 cm/s methane produces slightly above 2 microamps of ion current
at the peak (1.5 kV/cm) and the flow of 19 cm/s methane has a peak of 2.75 microamps.
While the ratio is not exact, the peak ion current is nearly proportional to the flow

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:10:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf

velocity. Another interesting feature of these curves is the peak value. Traditional
electrical aspects of flames studies look for a saturation ion current plateau, where the
ion current remains fixed despite an increase in applied electric field. For these
microgravity flames, there is a pronounced peak in the ion current at saturation and then
a gradual decrease to a global saturation plateau. This is a strikingly different behavior
than is seen in 1-g, and the behavior is even more pronounced for the case where there
is zero coflow.

Figure 2. Ion current as a function of the field strength and fuel velocity with a 3.1 cm/s
coflow. (a) 15 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:10:1

As can be seen in Figure 3, which is the same V-I curve result in microgravity for the case
where there is no coflowing air, and Figure 4 shows the flame images. These figures again
show a reasonably linear scaling of peak ion current with fuel flow velocity, but they
demonstrate a very pronounced peak ion current with a rapid drop to a global saturation
ion current plateau. Since these are diffusion flames, essentially all of the fuel is being
burned independent of the flame’s shape and the applied electric field, but it seems clear
that the electric field is affecting the chemi-ion production capability of the flame. As is
apparent from the flame images, the flame is most compact at the voltage consistent with
the peak ion current. With increasing voltage, the flame becomes less compact and the
ion current decreases. We presume that the flame remains at saturation throughout this
period (that is, the flame is producing as many ions as it can, and those ions are being
removed from the reaction zone as soon as they are created) so the decrease in ion
current results from a change in combustion intensity. We can explore this hypothesis
further using the PMT data collected in the exp

In all of the curves, the jagged features are spikes following a voltage step change that
are mostly associated with the transient capacitance of the system when rapid steps are
requested. These overshoots notwithstanding, the V-I curves follow smooth and
reproducible trajectories.

For comparison, the equivalent V-I curves for 1-g flames with the same burner
configuration with no coflow are shown in Figure 5. The results are too recent to allow a
detailed analysis and discussion of the differences, but some significant observations from
these results and the comparison follow.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:12:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56

(1) The ion current reaches a peak at approximately the same field strength for both
velocities in 1-g while in microgravity the ion current peak for a lower fuel velocity
occurs at a lower field strength. The field strength at the peak current seems to scale
linearly with the fuel velocity.

Figure 5. Ion current as a function of field strength and fuel velocity with no coflow in
normal gravity. (a) 16 cm/s methane. (b) 19 cm/s methane.

(2) In microgravity, the ion current does not smoothly increase to saturation nor does it
show a gentle peak with a mild decrease as is seen in the normal gravity results.
Instead, in microgravity there is a distinct peak in the ion current with a severe
decrease throughout the saturation condition, with a final saturation plateau
observed at voltages substantially above the voltage at peak ion current. That is, the
microgravity final saturation is not the maximum ion current observed. This
difference is more dramatic when there is no coflow, which suggests that entrainment
plays an important role whether caused by buoyancy or a forced coflow.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:12:1
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
(3) The peak ion current is higher for microgravity than comparison 1-g flames. The
reason is not obvious at this point but may result from a more focused upward flow
from the electric body force and ion-driven wind as compared to the combined effects
of the ion wind and buoyancy.

(4) The peak ion current is approximately proportional to fuel flow velocity, which, as
described in prior studies, reflects the relationship between ion production and the
carbon flux into the system. The peak ion current also increases with the coflow which
suggests that healthier oxidizer transport helps increase the ion production.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf:13:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2018 - E-FIELD Flames 30-day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 55 and 56 20181115.pdf
text:
30% ethylene with coflowing air at 3.1cm/s
The results from ethylene flames with coflow are shown in Figures 6 and 7, positive field
and negative field respectively. At 15 cm/s, the ion current reaches a peak around 2.7
microamps which is similar to the 19 cm/s 100% methane coflow air case but with only
0.4 of the volumetric carbon content. The results for 15 cm/s also presents a rapid
parabolic behavior after reaching the saturation peak. In the negative field case, the peak
ion current decreases to 0.56 of the positive field case at the same flow rate 19 cm/s (or
0.4 for 15 cm/s). Another aspect is that the ion current peaks sooner for the higher flow
rate/carbon content in the negative field configuration as compared to the positive field
experiments. These phenomena, particularly for the positive field strength have not yet
been measured in the laboratory at 1-g. The difference in behavior appears to be related
to the removal of the buoyancy force so that the momentum flow coupled with the ion
driven flow tends to resettle under the electric field body force. Detailed analysis is
underway.

1 June 2019
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 57 and 58

ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
E-FIELD Flames is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project,
which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels
in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The investigation was carried out in two rounds of
tests, where the first (with ACME’s coflow burner) occurred in Increment 55 and the second (with
a gas-jet burner) began in Increment 56 and ended in Increment 57. As a result, there is nothing
to be reported for Increment 58.

Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for E-FIELD Flames and ACME information.

file: PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf
text:
I. Introduction
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat,
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong
electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting
behavior of the flame. Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current
passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature,
soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the
analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the
development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf:2:0
file: PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58

An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames
experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the
electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical
benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions
with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the
electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic.
It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the
residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our
critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf:2:2

The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of
flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and
polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests were conducted
with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of
soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They were carried out with both
a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without
a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner
to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different
electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane).
In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the
burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field
strength was measured. The field str

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-

Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone. Length
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot
free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species,
electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames,
making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.

text:
II. Methods/Research Operations

A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the
ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.
The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry
stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or
soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console
commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed
in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished.

III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s
testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment
58. The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and
September-November 2018. The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited
flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was
developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD
Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames
experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned
years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies
1. Mission anomalies
The CIR’s IPSU-1 Image Processing and Storage Unit, which is used with the High Bit-
Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera and the collimated illumination package, was
only intermittently operable at the end of Increment 56 and was not operable at the
start of Increment 57. Those capabilities were not seen as critical for E-FIELD Flames,

electrode. Therefore, the tests on Sept. 26 (18269), Oct. 1 (18274), Oct. 9 (18282),
Oct. 12 (18285), and Oct. 17 (18290) were conducted without HiBMs imaging or the
CIR illumination. It was later determined to be an issue with a cable connection, which
was corrected by astronaut Alex Gerst on Oct. 22 (18295) when he carried out other
ACME tasks. As a result, the subsequent E-FIELD Flames tests were carried out using
the HiBMs camera and illumination package.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling
software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the
igniter. As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt.
The aborts normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1. These
are infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf:6:1
file: PSI-22_Reports_2019 - E-FIELD Flames 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 20190601.pdf
text:
Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of
the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been
sufficiently primed. Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the
automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of
the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter
is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite.
This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH*
chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH*
chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited
flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible
spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to
false ignition detection.

C. Completeness/Quality of Data
The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1)
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD),
using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner
to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the high-

identified as required. In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment, so nearly
three times as many flames were ignited than required.

It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests. As
discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round
of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination
package. Those are not critical for E-FIELD Flames, so tests continued without their use.

Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is
done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be
managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice
some image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.
This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing
within the project constraints.

Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually
become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing,
they are a degradation of the image quality.

D. Status of Data Analysis
Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings
from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the
ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame
luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz. The non-imaging
data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame
researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function
of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type). The PMT data
is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations. Image data is processed using
the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).
