Experimental Objectives
Understand flame ion production and use ions to control
diffusion flames by modifying local convection (via the ion
wind) and local species transport (via direct ion drift)
A) Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and
chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the
amount of inert in the fuel.
B) Obtain the time response of flame chemiluminescence, luminosity,
and ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of
total fuel flow rate and amount of inert added to the fuel stream.
C) Evaluate and control sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction
and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field
voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate
and amount of inert added to the fuel stream.
D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied
voltage to characterize and control the combustion behavior of
near-limit lifted flames in a coflow burner.

1. Introduction
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment to
facilitate its analysis. The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of
soot or the combustion gases. For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-
imaging measurements. Additional files such as camera metadata and operational logs provide
information that can support the analysis.

It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the E-FIELD Flames data begin by familiarizing
themselves with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the E-FIELD Flames
Final Report or the more comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation
document.

Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document. To interpret the non-imaging data,
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 18073A3_data.csv, which has
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The data
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D).

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

Additional documents that may be important include:
ACME-RPT-010 A Data Camera Characterization Report, Rev. A
ACME-RPT-011 Radiometer Characterization Report
ACME-RPT-013 PMT Characterization Report
However, the BRE Radiometer Characterization Report, ACME-RPT-012, is not relevant because the BRE
radiometer was developed specifically for ACME’s Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment. E-FIELD
Flames instead made use of the standard radiometers addressed in ACME-RPT-011.

2. E-FIELD Flames Overview
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report, which provides descriptions of the
science, preliminary results, and more. It is suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in analyzing
the E-FIELD Flames data.

The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is one of six
independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International
Space Station (ISS).

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:3:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin of the University of California,
Irvine (UC Irvine). Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, also of UC Irvine, served as the Project Scientist at the
university. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is NASA’s Project Scientist
(PS) for ACME including E-FIELD Flames and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop
testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy
Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde
and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:3:3
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
E-FIELD Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 55-57, which were
more specifically in March-May and September-November 2018. The break in testing (from May to
September) was intentional and planned years in advance to allow the research team to analyze early
results and use the insights obtained from the analysis to plan the second round so as to maximize its
scientific output.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:4:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

3. Tests Conducted
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/E-FIELD Flames – 30-Day Operation
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increments 57 and 58 (which is included in the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final
Report).

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:4:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77
respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58. Note that the investigation’s testing was
completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58. The first and
second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November
2018. The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and
gas-jet burners, respectively. The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion
Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two
rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was
intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail
and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:4:4
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for E-FIELD Flames; all of the ISS results were
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently planned
ACME experiments.

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

4. Data Interpretation
This key section provides (1) a general description of the raw experimental data and associated files and
(2) guidance on data conversions, e.g., to engineering units. Only limited guidance is provided for the
processing of image data, with the important exception of the conversion of the ACME DataCam images
from the raw Halcon object (HOBJ) format.

A. Non-Imaging Data
Data and files discussed in this section include the following:
Data Output File
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data

Some ACME experiments featured measurements made with the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph
Instrumentation Package (GCIP), but it was not used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment and a such
that data type is not addressed in this document.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:6:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
1. Data Output File
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D). The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and
test (a letter and single-digit number). As such, the example, 18073A3 is test A3 conducted
on the 73rd day of 2018. But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 74th) day because
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:6:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 18073A1, 18073A2, and 18073A3) are
normally similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or
repeat. Letters I and O are not used because of their similarity to 1 and 0. While initially used
in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient. As a related
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not
conducted at all. The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted
alphabetically. However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter.

The basic data is in a CSV format, i.e., with comma-separated values, which can be opened by
spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel. The first row is a header and provides a limited
summary of the hardware and operational conditions. The header is explained in Section 10.1
Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.

file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

Additional conversion is required for the measurements of the gas flow rates found in second
through fourth columns of the data file. By column (e.g., in Excel), the flow rates are for:
B MFCA1StaticMixerFlow oxidizer (or inert) gas
C MFCA2BypassFlow nitrogen
D MFCA3FuelFlow fuel

The ACME MFCs are Hastings HFC-D-302 with default standard temperature and pressures
(STP) of 0 Celsius and 760 torr for computations of volumetric flow or velocity. It is very
important to understand that slpm, i.e., standard liters per minute, is a measurement of the
mass (or alternatively molar) flow rate which is independent of the actual temperature or
pressure. This is discussed for example in the MFC manual, where chapter 9 (on page 39) is
“Volumetric vs. Mass Flow.”

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:8:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Conversions for the actual gases can be made with information provided in the manual on
subsequent pages and the spreadsheets GasDataTables.xls and Inside gas mix calculator.xls
which were both provided by the MFC manufacturer. First, open GasDataTables.xls and
enable content, and then open Inside gas mix calculator.xls and enable content. From this,
one should be able to enter mixtures and compute appropriate Gas Conversion Factors
(GCFs).

Alternatively, the conversions above can be made with spreadsheets prepared by the ACME
engineering team, where options include the following:
ACMEFlowCalculator.xlsx
ACMEFlowAndPressuresRawDataConversion.xlsx

Computation of gas velocities, for example for the gas-jet and coflow burners, depends on
burner dimensions. For the coflow burner, ACME mechanical design engineer Adrian Drake
indicated the following:

“The inner diameter of the inner tube is .085 inches. Its cross sectional area is .00567
in^2, or 3.66 x 10^-6 m^2.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:8:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
The flow of the outer tube is a little tricky to calculate, based on where and how you
measure. There’s an internal step in the outer tube that can’t be seen from outside, and
blocks the flow to the outer honeycombs. Because of this, when we calculated the cross-
sectional are of the outer tube, it measures from the inner step.

The outer tube’s outer diameter at that step is 0.984 inches. Its cross section area at that
diameter is .7605 in^2. From this we have to subtract the inner tube’s outer
diameter: .095 inch diameter, so area is .00709. Subtract from the Outer Diameter and
we get .7534 in^2, or .000486 m^2.”

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:9:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

The dimensions of the coflow burner’s inner tube are documented in greater detail in the
ACME Inspection Verification Report (ACME-VER-001 Rev. A, ACME-VER-001_A.pdf) on
pages 138-143 of the pdf file. From that section:

The 2.1-mm gas-jet burner used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment used the same tubing as
the coflow burner’s inner tube, where the tube dimensions are based on certification by the
tubing manufacturer rather than measurement. The tubing dimensions for this burner are
documented in greater detail in pages 102-104 of ACME-VER-001_A.pdf. From that section:

Of course, dimensions are also available from the burner drawings, but the dimensions are
often not found on the assembly drawings so the appropriate component drawings must
typically be consulted.

While the basic data file includes measurement of the gas flow rates, it may be helpful to
understand the intended flow rates, where that information is found in a separate file for
each test with a name like 18073A3_mfcSetpoints.csv. While it shares strong similarities to
the basic data file, the rows of data are not added at a continuous and consistent rate. The
file is briefly discussed in section 8.2 Mass Flow Controller Setpoint File on page 124 of ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D.

3. Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) data
Relevant pressure, temperature, etc. data from the CIR is not found in the data output file
discussed in section 4.A.1 of this document. Instead, it is found in 1-Hz files with names such
as 18073A3_ACME_CAM3_Exposures.txt which are again in a comma-separated values (CSV)
format despite the misleading txt suffix. As such, these files can be opened with standard
spreadsheet software.

Columns A and B (e.g., in Excel) both include timestamps, which can slightly differ (e.g., by a
second), where column A is from the Image Processing and Storage Unit for Gigabit ethernet
cameras (IPSU-G, which is also referred to as IPSU-5). The IPSU-G was used to record the
image data from the ACME Data Camera (DataCam) and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
intensified camera. Meanwhile, column B provides timestamps for the CIR’s FOMA Control
Unit (FCU), where the FOMA is the Fuel Oxizidizer Management Assembly. The headings for
the first two columns are therefore:
IPSU5 TimeStamp FCU TimeStamp

text:
4. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and
installing alignment guides) on each test day. However, the CIR was equipped with a 3-axis
SAMS sensor head. The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS).

The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn): In
addition to the documentation and links from the PIMS home page, we introduce a few ways
below to get started with exploring the CIR microgravity environment taking the perspective
of SAMS measurements from within the rack.

Roadmap Spectrograms
To get a high-level, spectral roadmap view within two days after measurement, you can:
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/roadmap

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:12:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

b. In the upper left pane, you can navigate by GMT date to see a list of plots (PDF files)
in the right pane for the GMT date of your choice. We refer to these PDFs as roadmap
plots. For SAMS, these are acceleration spectrograms, which for vibratory data are a
good way to look at patterns, structures and boundaries in both time and frequency
for long time spans -- nominally, 8 hours per plot. These spectrograms are mostly
qualitative and crudely quantitative three-dimensional plots in that a color scale
attempts to map power spectral density magnitude as a color for the 3rd dimension.
NOTE: Ticking the Navigation Filter for “es05” in the bottom pane will then only
highlight days in yellow in the upper left pane when the operations team powered on
the SAMS sensor in the CIR to take measurements.
c. You might want to navigate directly to a GMT day of interest for your science
operations or run, but you can also browse day-by-day too in order to get some
context comparing various 8-hour spans to get a feel for the environment under
various conditions.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:12:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Binary Data
To download actual SAMS measurement data for use with your models or to correlate
acceleration measurements with your science or support data, you can…
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad
b. Navigate by GMT date, for example you can follow year, month and day links to end
up at: https://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad/year2020/month06/day18/ where you see
a list of SAMS sensor directories. The sensor subdirectory of interest for CIR is
samses_accel_es05.
c. Once you click into that directory link, you will see data and header files listed for the
CIR sensor.
d. The instructions at the following link help you to read these data:
http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/plots/user/mohan/how2read_pad_binary_files.html

B. Image Files
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras:
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera
ACME Data Camera (DataCam)
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:12:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used
for E-FIELD Flames or most of the current ACME experiments. Thus far, the Structure and
Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) investigation is the only ACME study to use the
LLL-UV camera.

1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the
combustion chamber and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera. Its primary
purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as such is
also often referred to as the operations or ops camera.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:13:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps. It is not recorded on the space station
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media
Player which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/. That software
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making
measurements of flame dimensions.

2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam)
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench. It is equipped with a motorized lens with
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus. It has a filter barrel with a fused silica
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for
imaging CH* and HCHO (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:13:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of
the CH* concentration.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:13:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Soot temperatures can be determined from this camera’s images via techniques such as those
described in the following references:
a. S. De Iuliis, M. Barbini, S. Benecchi, F. Cignoli, and G. Zizak, Determination of the Soot
Volume Fraction in an Ethylene Diffusion Flame by Multiwavelength Analysis of Soot
Radiation, Combustion and Flame 115 (1998) 253–261.
b. B. Ma and M. B. Long, Combined Soot Optical Characterization Using 2-D Multi-Angle
Light Scattering and Spectrally Resolved Line-of-Sight Attenuation and Its Implication
on Soot Color-Ratio Pyrometry, Applied Physics B 117 (2014) 287–303.
c. B. Ma, S. Cao, D. Giassi, D. P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, B. A. V. Bennett, M. D. Smooke,
and M. B. Long, An Experimental and Computational Study of Soot Formation in a
Coflow Jet Flame under Microgravity and Normal Gravity, Proceedings of the
Combustion Institute 35 (2015) 839–846.
d. N. J. Kempema, B. Ma, and M. B. Long, Investigation of In-Flame Soot Optical
Properties in Laminar Coflow Diffusion Flames Using Thermophoretic Particle
Sampling and Spectral Light Extinction, Applied Physics B 122 (2016).
e. N. J. Kempema and M. B. Long, Effect of Soot Self-Absorption on Color-Ratio
Pyrometry

text:
Meanwhile, TFP measurements can be made using approaches such as those discussed in:
f. V. Vilimpoc and L. P. Goss, SiC-Based Thin-Filament Pyrometry: Theory and Thermal
Properties, Symposium (International) on Combustion 22 (1989) 1907–1914.
g. W. M. Pitts, Thin-Filament Pyrometry in Flickering Laminar Diffusion Flames,

Particularly when making quantitative measurements, implementation of an Abel transform
or similar is likely appropriate given the axisymmetry of the flames in the E-FIELD Flames
investigation. In fact, all six of the current ACME experiments feature axisymmetric or
spherically symmetric flames. Approaches are compared in this paper:
k. C. J. Dasch, One-Dimensional Tomography: A Comparison of Abel, Onion-
Peeling, and Filtered Backprojection Methods, Applied optics 31 (1992) 1146–
1152.

file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
The a-k references above were taken from the following conference paper on early ACME
results from the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment:
Jesse Tinajero, Davide Giassi, Dennis Stocker, and Marshall Long. “Experimental Study on
the Influence of Gravity on Highly Diluted and Sooting Coflow Flames,” 11th US National
Combustion Meeting of the Combustion Institute, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019.

Meanwhile, this paper on an ISS precursor to the CLD Flame experiment is an appropriate
reference for determination of CH* concentration.
D. Giassi, S. Cao, B.A. Bennett, D.P. Stocker, F. Takahashi, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long,
“Analysis of CH* Concentration and Flame Heat Release Rate in Laminar Coflow Diffusion
Flames under Microgravity and Normal Gravity,” Combustion and Flame, Vol. 167, pp.
198-206 (2016).

Images are normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images are often
downlinked during a test day. Regardless, the images are downloaded in a wrapped Halcon
object (HOBJ) format, which are not readily opened with typical image processing software.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:14:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Most ACME investigators are processing the HOBJ files using the OMA2 software developed
by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment. The OMA2
software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the latter can
be used with both PC and Linux operating systems.

The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten as a Python function by Dr. Jesse Tinajero
(Yale U.), where Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for
MacOS, Linux, and Windows operating systems. The Python script to open the HOBJ files can
be downloaded from https://github.com/mblong/hobjExample.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:15:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

The HOBJ files can also be readily viewed and processed using ImageJ or its preloaded Fiji
variant, where both can be freely downloaded. In either software package, the HOBJ files can
imported (rather than opened) as raw files with the following settings:
Image type 16-bit unsigned
Width 1360
Height 1024
Offset to first image 6244
However, imported DataCam images will be monochrome unless a Bayer filter (e.g., as
described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayer_filter) is subsequently implemented. It
should be possible to install a plug-in to accomplish that color conversion. As another option,
Python and Matlab both have image demosaicing functions.

NASA is also working (at the time of this writing) toward providing converted images from the
ACME DataCam, where the general priority is to support the ongoing ACME testing rather
than covert images for experiments like E-FIELD Flames which have already been completed.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:15:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
In order to use the ACME DataCam for quantitative measurements it is critical to avoid
saturation, for example by using a camera gain of zero. Another employed approach was to
not use the camera’s white balance which by default multiplies the red and blue by 1.41 and
1.68, respectively, because that could inadvertently lead to saturation. Such multiplication
can be done after the HOBJ file is converted and the colors demosaiced, where in OMA2 the
white balancing is accomplished with the commands:
*rgb 1.41 1 1.68
clip 4095
In summary, the white balance, if desired, needs to be done after the fact through software
because it was generally not done with the hardware to avoid the risk of saturation.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:15:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Note that the ACME images will be naturally dark because of the use of the 16-bit file format
with 12-bit image data. As such, adjustments to the image brightness will generally be
necessary even if the images are not demosaiced. Furthermore, cameras’ CCD arrays are
susceptible to radiation damage while in orbit. As a result, the images feature hot pixels which
increase in number over the months and years in space. As such, it will appear as if there is a
star field within the combustion chamber. Therefore, the images should ideally be processed
to remove the bright outlying pixels. The radiation damage is also obvious in the ops camera
imaging.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:15:3
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Although the DataCam was typically set for imaging at 30 fps, that is trumped by the exposure
settings which were often long because of the dim nature of the microgravity flames. As a
result, the framing rate was typically far less. Different exposures could have been selected
for different phases of the tests, e.g., prior to ignition and during the test, so the framing rate
may not be consistent. Bracketed imaging could also be employed, where a repeating
sequence of different exposure durations is used to enable appropriate photography under
uncertain or varying flame intensities. Bracketing is also used to simultaneously accomplish
multiple imaging objectives, e.g., to appropriately image both brightly glowing soot (or TFP
fibers) as well as the much dimmer blue portion of the flame.

In interpreting the image data, it may be helpful to check the ACME DataCam metadata file

file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf

The formatting of this file changed during early 2018 (between mid-March and early April),
when the first round of E-FIELD Flames tests (using the coflow burner) was being conducted
on the ISS. Therefore, examples of early and later versions are presented, where their suffixes
were respectively metadata and mdipsug. However, both are in a comma-delimited (CSV)
format and can be opened with spreadsheet software or alternately as a text file. Column
headings are found in the first row of such files.

Regardless of the version, it is very important to understand that the exposure time, in
microseconds, trumps the specified framing rate (in fps), i.e., where long exposures will lead
to a shorter actual framing rate. In this example case, the 0.1-s exposure time means that the
framing rate (at the test’s start) was nominally 10 fps rather than the 30 indicated by
FrameRate. It is furthermore important to understand that the exposure time (and thus
actual framing rate) was often varied during the test, where that could be seldom or often if
bracketing was employed, i.e., where a repeated sequence of images was taken at different
exposures.

For the DataCam, the exposures times, etc. can also be found in files with names like
18073A3_ACME_CAM3_Exposures.txt, where such files are discussed in section 4.A.3 of this
document because (despite the file naming) they primarily include pressures, flow rates, and
temperatures from the CIR’s Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA).

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:18:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
The parameter files, with names such as 18073A3_VoltageSweep.txt, control the DataCam
exposures and much more. However, these files were not always saved as intended and were
sometimes corrected after the fact. In contrast, the text-file logs, with names such as 2018-
10-17_12-26ACME.log, are a reliable source for the parameters which specified the imaging
settings and much more. There is a single file of this type for each test day (at least normally)
and the parameters are a small fraction of the automated log content, but one can search for
a test by its number. Log files like this are discussed in section 4.C.4 of this document.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:18:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
Due to the use of a turning mirror, the DataCam images should be flipped vertically if upright
images are desired, i.e., where the burner is at the bottom and the flame extends upward. In
this regard, note that the DataCam provides images in a ‘landscape’ format with the image’s
long dimension orthogonal to the burner and chamber axis. This is contrary to an ACME
science requirement specifying that the long dimension be aligned with the experimental axis
to provide images in a ‘portrait’ format. In this regard, the science requirements were not
always met, e.g., because of design tradeoffs, etc.

There is some variation in the ACME camera zoom, where its setting is not completely
reproducible. Therefore, the scaling of the image data should be established for each day of
testing, or each subset of tests if more than one zoom setting was used within a day. The
scaling can typically be carried out using images regularly taken of the ceramic fibers for Thin
Filament Pyrometry (TFP), where such imaging is normally made at two fiber array positions.
However, the fiber array was not used for the E-FIELD Flames experiment because of the

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:19:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

interference of the electric field and electrode mesh. Therefore, scaling must be carried out
using the burner or other visible hardware. Meanwhile, the other cameras had fixed lenses.

Note that files named for example 20180314_162445.789_ACME_18073A3.next are not
useful for data interpretation, where such text files simply indicate the next ACME image
number that would have been archived, i.e., until that test’s image archiving came to an end.

3. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera
This intensified camera was typically configured with a CH* bandpass filter and was generally
archived at 23 fps. The grayscale image files are in a Tagged Image File Format (TIFF) format
and can be opened readily, where brightness/contrast adjustment may again be required.

While it wasn’t an issue for E-FIELD Flames, this camera’s Field of View (FOV) is partially
blocked by the arms of the fiber array for Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) when it is moved to
position the fibers across the flame. But E-FIELD Flames didn’t use the fiber array because of
interference with the electrode mesh and the electric field itself.

that there are two version of this file relevant to the experiment. Although they are largely
similar, the latter has two additional parameters, BitShift and CameraSpeed, and some
additional changes, e.g., where some parameter names changed and where the parameter
order has changed. Therefore, detailed information on both versions will be presented where
the parameter descriptions and names of the corresponding camera parameters were
provided by ACME software engineer Jeffrey Eggers. Both versions are in a comma-delimited
(CSV) format and can be opened with spreadsheet software or alternately as a text file.

text:
Note that ‘next’ files named for example 20180314_162445.789_INTNS_18073A3.next are
not useful for data interpretation, where such text files simply indicate the next image
number that would have been archived, i.e., until that test’s image archiving came to an end.

4. High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package
The HiBMs camera was used in combination with an opposed backlight, i.e., the CIR’s
collimated illumination package. The resultant imaging was used in preceding droplet
combustion experiments for measuring droplet diameter, but it may also be useful for
determining the soot volume fraction via light extinction. However, the camera’s red filter,
corresponding to the red illumination, is broad enough to permit significant soot
incandescence to pass through the filter. As a result, this imaging is unlikely to be useful for
soot volume fraction measurements for all conditions. After post-processing on the ground,
the images were made available in the TIFF format and as such are readily opened. The
grayscale images were typically archived at 15 fps.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:24:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

It is important to understand that this camera’s images are notably of limited value for E-
FIELD Flames because the bracket for the electrode mesh significantly blocked the
illumination. ACME’s cameras and other optical instruments encircle the burner and made it
difficult to avoid optical interference in all circumstances, where design trade-offs were
necessary. However, the soot volume fraction can also be computed using images from the
ACME DataCam as discussed in that camera’s section.

In initial ACME testing with the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, the
monochrome camera was used without a filter, but that was abandoned because the camera
is nearly insensitive to blue. The red filter was used throughout E-FIELD Flames testing.

C. Test Parameters and Other Files
Files discussed in this section include the following:
Test parameter file
Notes
Test timing
Logs

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:24:1
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
1. Test parameter file
Each E-FIELD Flames test was controlled by a software script and corresponding parameter
file, named for example 18073A3_VoltageSweep.txt, specifying settings for imaging, ignition,
gas flow, and more. The parameter file and script are discussed extensively in the ACME/E-
FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure document, which should be referred to for information
on this file type. But note that the ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the as-run
test parameters, where the separate parameter files are unfortunately not completely
reliable. They were not always saved and as a result were sometimes recreated after the fact.

2. Notes
Notes of various types are available for test days, where not all types were collected or
necessarily prepared for each test day. It is important to understand that the notes, whether
handwritten or typed, may include mistakes. It is better to rely on automated logs, metadata
files, and parameter files or of course the measurements themselves when possible.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:24:2
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
The daily test point logs, with names such as ‘18087 daily test point log.pdf,’ chronologically
list the tests and the image data acquired which was to be downlinked. Typically, image data
was not downlinked without successful, i.e., sustained, ignition. As an example, image data
wasn’t downlinked if the test aborted prior to ignition. However, the reverse is not always
true. Image data was sometimes downlinked when ignition was unsuccessful and as a result
the test point log is only a clue as to what transpired. Furthermore, note that image data
from certain selected cameras, typically the HiBMs and/or CFI intensified camera(s), was
sometimes not downlinked due to the limit of how much data could be reasonably
downlinked in a subsequent two-shift day.

Notes with names such as ‘18087 efield & velocities traces.pdf’ include preliminary plots of
the electrode mesh voltage and flow rates (as seen on a console during testing), typically along
with additional information about the tests.

id: PSI-22:doc:PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf:25:0
file: PSI-22_Science Documents_E-FIELD Flames data interpretation document.pdf
text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

The test parameter notes, with names such as ‘18087 test parameter notes.pdf,’ show the
parameter values which were planned in advance of the test day and the changes made on
the test day.

The test sheets, with names such as ‘18087 test sheets.pdf,’ are summary notes about the
conduct of each tests conducted that day.

3. Test timing
Timing files with names such as 18073A3_TP.txt can be a convenient way to determine the
phases of the test in which the images were acquired. An example E-FIELD Flames file is
presented here:
Test Point: 18073A3

text:
ACME/E-FIELD Flames Data Interpretation 2 Oct. 2020

4. Logs
There are four primary types of automated logs of which two, with names like the following,
may be helpful.
2018-10-17_12-26ACME.log
2018-10-17_12-51_IPSUG.log
As a reminder, the IPSU-G is the processing and storage unit for the images from the ACME
DataCam and CFI intensified camera.

Meanwhile, the two logs of commands, with names like the following, are unlikely to be useful
for interpreting the E-FIELD Flames results.
2018-10-17_12-59ACMECommands.log
2018-10-17_12-51_IPSUGCommands.log

Each of the four log files are created for each day of testing, rather than for each test. They
are text files (despite the log suffix) and as such can be readily opened.

The ACME.log files should be the best way to verify the test parameters, where the separate
as-run parameter files are unfortunately not completely reliable. A portion of the log
corresponding to a single test, 18290F1, is presented here, where this can best be interpreted
after becoming familiar with the contents of the ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental
Procedure document. But the test parameters and timing of the test are obvious in the
excerpt.

Science Requirements Document
SRD Version 2.0
March 31, 2010
for

ELECTRIC FIELD CONTROL OF FLAMES
E-FIELD Flames Experiment

Principal Investigator:

Derek Dunn-Rankin
University of California
Irvine, California

Co-Investigators:

Felix Weinberg; Imperial College, London
Zeng-Guang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research (NCSER)

Project Scientist:

Dennis Stocker, NASA GRC

This project utilizes electric fields in microgravity combustion science to establish a fun-
damental understanding of chemi-ionization and ion-driven convection in flames. It also
uses this understanding to demonstrate electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and
stability limits in the absence of buoyancy. This work is based on prior foundation stud-
ies that included simulating zero-g combustion of small gas jet diffusion flames in an
earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics. The cur-
rent SRD proposes to use the extended-duration microgravity environment to further de-
velop an understanding of electric fields in combustion processes and their potential ap-
plications.
The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created
through chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in
microgravity environments. For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric
fields have demonstrated powerful influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning
velocity, extinction, and stability. The source of these influences resides in ion wind ef-
fects. In microgravity, where t

e demonstrated powerful influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning
velocity, extinction, and stability. The source of these influences resides in ion wind ef-
fects. In microgravity, where there are no density-driven buoyant effects to contend with,
ion winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to
manipulate combustion systems. This project includes both academic study of electric
field effects and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion proc-
esses.
Our prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be
used to produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in
order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because
flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be critical at near-limit conditions;
(b) creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front – this proc-
ess can provide a local actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to
affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are
shared chemical pathways and because s

ocal actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to
affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are
shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions; and
(d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there is a relationship between
flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it can produce at satu-
ration.
In 1-g, the above-mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interactions
that cannot be unraveled. Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following
experimental objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the
relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel
flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of
the flame’s chemiluminescence and ion current to rapid changes in electric fields; (C)
determine sooting behavior in relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate
the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields.
The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a co-

n relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate
the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields.
The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a co-flow burner.
The basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nominally non-
sooting and sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame
strength. The co-flow or environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21%
O2 and 79% N2. The experimental concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber

and to install an electrically active planar mesh electrode downstream of the burner
mouth. The potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a
steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine
the flame’s steady state response and time response. The data to be recorded include the
applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband luminosity, the CH* luminosity,
flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric
potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field. In addition, a
desired measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field
as a function of the electric field conditions.
The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of
flame ion production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electri-
cally control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits
and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a
lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor
poin

xtinction limits
and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a
lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor
point. Therefore, electric fields acting on near-limit flames can exert a large influence
because they can affect the local mixing behavior. The role of electric fields on soot
formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven wind has a large influ-
ence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical effects are found im-
portant) in sooting flames.
Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those
driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth grav-
ity. In addition, raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the
response to an electric field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy ef-
fect, making it difficult, on earth, to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy.
In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and
develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric field

from those due to buoyancy.
In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and
develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under
all conditions. Extended run times are crucial for all of the studies because the timescales
of flame property changes (which includes chemi-ionization) are dominated by convec-
tion (length scale/velocity) and past studies have shown that soot studies require high
quality zero gravity timescales longer than is available in aircraft and drop towers. In ad-
dition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames requires ex-
periments lasting tens of seconds.
Overall, the goal of this zero-gravity study is to understand chemi-ionization behavior
and the resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames
can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct
chemical or local convective influences). Electric field effects on flames have been
documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influ-
ences that affect ion generation behavior. For flames near transitions

Electric field effects on flames have been
documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influ-
ences that affect ion generation behavior. For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant
influences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using
electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames. The proposed study removes this
confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric
field effects on jet diffusion and co-flow flames.

Figure 1. 1. Principal pathways of hydrocarbon flame
ion chemistry
1 INTRODUCTION

The first subsection provides the fundamentals that link chemi-ionization in flames with
convective flows created when electric fields act on the ions generated. Later subsections
describe the variety of 1-g laboratory experiments exemplifying the scientific data we
have found valuable in linking flames to their electrical properties. For the purposes of
this SRD, the details of this introductory section are less important than the examples of
our preliminary results which inform our proposed selection of objectives and science
data end products. To focus on the proposed flight experiment, it is possible to skip di-
rectly to Section 1.4 and then refer to background information as needed.

1.1 Background and Overview of Ion Driven Winds in Flames

In addition to being a major liberator of chemical energy, hydrocarbon flames naturally
produce charged intermediate species (ions and electrons) during the chemical-to-thermal
energy conversion. Generally speaking, chemi-ions and their associated species in hy-
drocarbon flames do not participate substantially in the major heat release reaction path-
ways. Hence, the chemical kinetics of ion species in hydrocarbon flames has not been
studied as extensively as for those species or reaction mechanisms associated with igni-
tion/extinction phenomena and pollutant formation. Nevertheless, many of the chemical
kinetic pathways are fairly well
articulated. Figure 1.1 shows the
chemi-ion pathways from Starik
and Titova [1] and Pederson and
Brown [2]. The major ions are
formed through reactions which
involve CH molecules. The CH
molecules are formed either from
acetylene and other C2 molecules,
or via the oxidation of CH3.
Green and Sugden [3] proposed
that CH is produced in a meth-
ane/air stoichiometric mixture
primarily via the oxidation of
CH3 through CH3+O 
CH+H2O. Peeters et al. [4] have
used this reaction successfully in their computations, and Jones et al. [5] examined modi-
fyin

toichiometric mixture
primarily via the oxidation of
CH3 through CH3+O 
CH+H2O. Peeters et al. [4] have
used this reaction successfully in their computations, and Jones et al. [5] examined modi-
fying the rate constant of this reaction to result in a better correlation with experimental
observations. Pederson and Brown [2] used a 13-step reaction scheme for the determina-
tion of the ion profiles. Their results indicate that for a stoichiometric mixture, H3O+ is
the most important ion; its maximum concentration is more than two orders of magnitude
higher than that of C2H3O+ and C3H3 +, and three orders of magnitude higher than that of
HCO+. The latter ion is, however, an important component for the production of H3O+.
Prager, et al. examined ion chemistry more recently and found H3O+ to be dominant in
lean flames [6]. They also identified several areas of uncertainty, primarily the anion
(negative ion) chemistry. Despite these uncertainties, there is general agreement in the

literature that the weak plasma nature of flames is relatively unimportant for the heat re-
lease reactions. For example, the most populous cations (positive ions) are present in
peak concentrations on the order of 1010/cc, or with mole fractions in the range of 10 ppb.

The concentration of electrons (which
make up the majority of the negative
charge carriers) is even lower than the
concentration of positive ions because
electron mobility is very high so that
relatively few electrons are needed to
balance the charge flux carried by the
more massive and more populous
positive charge carriers. Nevertheless,
the free charges in the flame make the
reaction zone a very good conductor
(similar to that of a conductive metal).
More importantly, if an electric field is
applied across the flame, the charges
can be separated into unipolar regions, as shown in Figure 1.2. In the case where the an-
ode (higher potential electrode) is close to the flame, the electrons can then easily exit the
gas phase system, leaving the positive ions to collide with neutral molecules as they mi-
grate through the unipolar space between the flame and the cathode (lower potential elec-
trode). During this migration process, the ions impart momentum to the neutral gas
equivalent to the acceleration they have achieved in the electric field between mean-free-
path collisions. The collisions are so frequent, that the ions quickly establish a drift ve-
locity governed by their mobil

the acceleration they have achieved in the electric field between mean-free-
path collisions. The collisions are so frequent, that the ions quickly establish a drift ve-
locity governed by their mobility. The collisions thereby link the ionization processes to
the neutral gas flow. This phenomenon is referred to as a Chattock wind, an ion-wind, or
more accurately an ion-driven wind, and is described in some detail by Lawton and
Weinberg [7].

In all of the applications involving electrical generation of convection, a unidirectional
gas flow is induced by using a large electric field to act on the charges of a unipolar ion
cloud in the region between the ion source and a second, usually earthed, electrode, or set
of electrodes. In these cases, the body force on a unit volume of the gas is equal to that

The above equations show that an electric field applied to the flame can create a direct
body force, or force per unit volume, on the system just as buoyancy does in a gravita-
tional field. Because buoyancy can be a dominant characteristic of terrestrial combustion
processes, it may seem less than obvious why physics regards gravity as a “weak force.”
However, if we consider a small magnet picking up a metal object with the entire earth
pulling in the opposite direction, it becomes obvious how much stronger the electromag-
netic forces are. It is hardly surprising, therefore, that electrical forces acting on charge
carriers can effectively substitute for gravitational influences or, more generally, provide
for vigorous combustion control in its absence (i.e., in microgravity). It is the opportu-
nity for exploiting the electric force in flames that motivates this research activity. Al-
ready, electric fields have demonstrated powerful influences on combustion processes
that include flame shape [12,13], sooting behavior [14-16], burning velocity [17,18], ex-
tinction [11,19], and stability [20,21]. The foundation of many of these results, as dis-

ame shape [12,13], sooting behavior [14-16], burning velocity [17,18], ex-
tinction [11,19], and stability [20,21]. The foundation of many of these results, as dis-
cussed in Lawton and Weinberg [7], reside in ion wind effects. In microgravity, where
there are no density driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion winds represent an im-
portant (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to manipulate combustion
systems. Hence, the zero gravity environment provides a unique opportunity to probe
and exploit the electrical aspects of flames [22].

1.2 Opportunities in Microgravity for Understanding Electric Field Effects on Flames

There are at least four ways that detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames
in microgravity can be used to improve our understanding of flame electrochemistry and
to potentially improve combustion performance:

(1) Extracting flame ions in order to change flame chemistry – we have already described
that ion radicals are not considered a large contributor to combustion heat release.
However, in the situations of weak flames, as can be represented by diluted diffusion
flames in zero gravity and terrestrial flames near extinction limits, their role is likely
to be more important. In addition, in near-limit flames, ion manipulation may be used
to extend stability behavior.

(2) Creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one
of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a
localized actuator. A one dimensional estimate of the equation for the forces avail-
able shows that the typical values for a flame can produce ion winds with flow veloc-
ity on the order of 1 m/s and forces on the order of one or two times the buoyant force.
Although this sounds like a fairly modest wind, it has been shown to be capable of
substantial effects, including flame extinction [11,19]. The effect of the wind has
been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity [12]
and in a spherical cage drop tower [13], but there has been no systematic study of the
ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal
influence of buoyancy. The actuation of the flame can be used to control flame per-
formance despite external fluctuations.

(3) Using electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely
linked because there are shared chemical pathways [23] and because soot particles are
charged by the flame ion attachment or electron ejection. It is possible, therefore, to
modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By
adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxi-
dation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in
different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change
the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.

(4) Using the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable rela-
tionship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at
saturation [24]. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization de-
tector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hy-
drogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct
flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect
the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom con-
centration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected
by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is pos-
sible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
There are also many opportunities identified for ion sensors as part of a combustion

control scheme, where input variables can be tuned to optimal performance as meas-
ured by ion current. HCCI engines, for example, would benefit from an in-cylinder
diagnostic to determine the combustion quality [6,25].

Examples of the kinds of methods and phenomena described above are provided in the
next subsection.

1.4 Summary of Findings and Open
Questions

The above earth gravity experiments
have resolved many questions regarding
ion driven winds in small diffusion
flames, and all of the important experi-
mental conditions and procedures have
been established. The ion pathlines and
the link between ion driven winds and
the flame shape and behavior for small
diffusion flames have been identified.
Modeling of the electrokinetics along
with the fluid dynamics has been successful, thereby providing an analytical tool for un-
derstanding the ion wind/flow coupling. The open questions regard the relationship be-
tween flame character (e.g., level of partial premixing) and the electric response. In addi-
tion, uncertainty remains regarding the chemical versus physical role of ions, and the po-
tential for dynamic manipulation of flames using electric fields.

The 1-g studies to date did not involve any quantitative analysis of soot because carbon
particles complicate the interpretation of electrical properties, but this component of
combustion is important to include because electric fields can modify soot formation and
burnout [14,40,41]. There is no question that flame soot is electrically charged, as
shown in Figure 1.18, but there is a long-standing debate in the combustion community
regarding the role of ions in the formation of soot. Essentially, there are the more numer-
ous adherents to the mechanism of soot growth by the addition of neutral hydrocarbon
that is exemplified in the work of [42,43] versus those that believe that the addition of ion
radical hydrocarbon species are important, as discussed in [23,44,45]. Although recent
numerical work has focused primarily on the neutral species approach, there continues to
be strong interest in the possible role of ions because there has been no satisfactory ex-

The ultimate objective of this experiment is to develop an understanding of the mecha-
nisms of chemi-ionization in flames and to describe the interplay between convective
flows driven by those flame ions and their generation rate. With this information it will
then be possible to detect and control flame behavior electrically. In 1-g, laminar diffu-
sion flames are often controlled to a large extent by natural convection, and particularly
by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence,
the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local convection. As described in
Section 1, an electric field acting on flame ions produces a body force and convection
(analogous to buoyancy) which affects the combustion process. The change in the com-
bustion process can in turn affect the ion production rate, which is responsible for the
body force. This coupled interaction is very difficult to measure, study, and understand
in 1-g because buoyant forces (of approximately equal magnitude) interfere. In micro-
gravity, there is no such complication and the body force in the flame is associated en-
tirely with the ion-driven wind. 1-g experiments have

To accomplish this scientific goal, there are four fundamental experimental objectives, in
priority order, using a jet diffusion flame burner and a co-flow diffusion flame burner.
The jet flame is the more critical configuration because it has a large 1-g data foundation
and it can be more easily modeled as an ion and thermal source. In zero-g, however, it
will be primarily driven by ion wind convection (no buoyant contribution and at its low

which may limit its operating range. The co-flow flame allows a forced convection com-

reproducible lifted flame for stability and soot behavior studies:

The interaction between soot and electric fields is very complex because it combines the
direct influence of electric fields on the chemistry, the ion wind effects on residence time
and mixing, and the electric forces on the charged soot particles themselves. The zero-
gravity environment, using the combination of the jet diffusion flame and the co-flow
flame provides a wide range of conditions where these different influences can be al-

co-flow burner will minimize the influence of the axial ion-driven wind, which helps to
distinguish the direct electrical effects on ion chemistry in soot formation. In addition to
demonstrating the direct control of soot behavior by electric fields, separating the influ-
ences can help distinguish between neutral molecule addition mechanisms of soot forma-
tion and those that presume the importance of ionic species. For example, changing the
strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors,
and electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history. In addition,

Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame
strength, its measure (both average and fluctuating properties) with low electric field
voltage can be used to detect flames approaching their limit condition. By adjusting the
electric field, 1-g studies indicate that an ion driven wind can be used to reduce the lift-

ing, analysis, and control.

diffusion flames, particularly with regards to stability and extinction limits and soot for-

Total flow rate of fuel (including inert) – the total fuel flow rate sets the exit jet velocity
and thereby the relative importance between jet momentum and ion driven convection.
The electrical effects will dominate under conditions of low ejection momentum. How-
ever, in the co-flow burner, even when the exit jet velocity is fairly high the momentum
match between the fuel stream and the co-flow sheath means that the cross flow momen-
tum can be low, so radial electrical influences may still be important. This total flow rate
parameter also controls the liftoff height of the flame.

Dilution with inert (nitrogen) of fuel – ion production mechanisms predict higher concen-
trations of chemi-ions under conditions that create higher concentrations of oxygen radi-
cal. In a premixed flame, this variable can be manipulated by adjusting the equivalence
ratio and reducing the flame temperature. In a simple non-premixed flame, however, the
reaction zone coincides with the stoichiometric condition and so dilution of the fuel with
an inert can serve this purpose. In addition, dilution with an inert can weaken the flame
by reducing the heat release rate per unit of fuel inlet flow mass. At their limit, these
flames are most susceptible to the forcing flows and entrainment that can be driven by
flame ions.

Voltage (V), polarity, and distance between electrodes – as shown in Section 1, the ion
wind body force is a direct function of electric field strength and ion concentration. The
electric field strength is a function of voltage and distance between the electrodes, as well
as any space charge effects. Switching the polarity of the voltage source is important for
changing the role of charge carriers during electric field forcing of flames. The direction
of the ion driven wind does not always change dramatically with electric field polarity
because the wind generally flows in the direction of the most distant electrode. This in-
teresting uni-directionality occurs because the active ion polarity switches to accommo-
date the change in field. That is, the ion wind is driven either by negative ions produced
by electron attachment to neutrals beyond the flame or H3O+ ions surviving beyond the
flame. Because their distance to the electrode is generally short, the oppositely charged
ions or electrons do not create a significant opposing wind. This behavior may not hold
when the flame is lifted a substantial distance from the burner surface. Even if the wind
direction does not change, howev

ectrons do not create a significant opposing wind. This behavior may not hold
when the flame is lifted a substantial distance from the burner surface. Even if the wind
direction does not change, however, its strength changes substantially because of the rela-
tive concentration and mobility differences between the ion species responsible. In addi-
tion, direct effects on charged species within the reaction zone will be different for differ-
ent polarities. We have observed clear indications of these directional wind changes in
microgravity from our recent results obtained in the 2.2 s drop tower.

2.3.2 Dependent Variables

Chemi-ion current (I) – the ion current is a primary indicator of chemi-ionization in the
flame, and varies depending on flame character, reaction zone size, and combustion in-
tensity (heat release rate). This is a global measurement of current flowing through the
shunt resistor. A current measurement without the flame present provides the baseline
leak current and ensures that there is no corona discharge or conducting pathway contrib-
uting to the measured current. Our 1-g studies show that the experimental configuration

described previously has essentially zero leakage current. Excessive leakage current with
no flame may indicate significant soot buildup and be an indicator of cleaning required.

Flame shape and size – in order to determine the effects of ion wind on the reaction zone,
images of the flame are needed. Images of the flame reveal the flame area, provide evi-
dence of combustion intensity, identify locations of soot formation, and show how the ion
wind (local convection) changes the flame shape for the various input flame parameters
and electric field strength. These line-of-sight integrated images will be Abel-inverted to
provide the true reaction interface size and location. Color video images provide infor-
mation regarding the location of luminous soot and the visible reaction zone interface.
UV images with a filter for OH* provide a sharp determination of the reaction zone. The
images of CH* chemiluminescence (desired) can be related to the local rate of heat re-
lease, which also correlates to chemi-ion production. This last measurement is “desired”
because the combination of the visible images and the OH* images are expected to pro-
vide approximately equivalent information.

Soot volume fraction – quantitative evaluation of the effects of electric fields on soot
formation, transport, and burnout require this information over the flame zone. We ex-
pect this measurement to be made by extinction followed by Abel deconvolution. Soot
volume fraction is also needed to estimate mean soot particle size from the Dushman
equation as described at the end of Section 1.

Spatially integrated luminosity – Broad spectrum flame luminosity, which includes the
chemiluminescence and soot radiation collected over a large solid angle (not imaging)
provides a rapid global response variable of how the flame reacts to changes in the elec-
tric field. Laboratory studies (see, for example, Figure 1.5 and 1.19) have shown that this
luminosity signal can be correlated to flame appearance and ion current.

Spatially integrated chemiluminescence (CH*) – CH* chemiluminescence can be related
to heat release rate and its collection over a broad solid angle (not imaging) provides a
rapid response variable of how the flame reacts to changes in the electric field. Normal
gravity studies have shown that this chemiluminescence signal can be correlated to flame
appearance and ion current and can be used as a sensor in controlling and monitoring
combustion [30].

Burner temperature (desired) – The temperature of the burner surface, provides the inlet
thermal boundary condition of the flow. This temperature is important to show how
much the flame interacts thermally with the burner. The burner/flame interaction has
been shown to affect flame stability for very small jet flames [48] and it can also change
the inlet conditions for coflow flames when the lift-off height is very small. This meas-
urement is desired because it is likely that the burner temperature effect is much more
significant in 1-g where a rising buoyant plume from off the burner can interact at the
flame base. In zero-g, this will not occur and so the effect involves only thermal aspects.

Gas temperature in and near the flame (desired) -- Measuring the temperature field be-
tween the flame and the electrode shows the shape and structure of the thermal plume. In

the jet diffusion flame, 1-g experiments show that this boundary coincides with that of
the ion-driven wind region. Schlieren imaging (e.g., as in Figure 1.5) provides an indica-
tion of the boundary and distributed temperatures (such as would be provided by shadow
deconvolution and soot pyrometry in sooting regions). Unfortunately, laboratory studies
have shown that silicon-carbide thin filaments in the flame change the electrical behavior
substantially, so we cannot use thin filament pyrometry in soot free regions. The thermal
information is valuable however, as it allows the current density, the ion mobility, and
thereby the electric body force, to be calculated most accurately. In laboratory studies,
for example, we have seen evidence of substantial differences in ion mobility and ion
wind depending on the thermal field the ions traverse. In the case of the co-flow flame,
the thermal plume is governed by a combination of the ion driven wind and the forced
convective flow. Comparison between the temperature fields with and without the elec-
tric field can be used to estimate the ion driven wind contribution in this case, which
helps resolve the controversy alluded to earlier reg

2.3.4. SDEP (Objective B) – time response of flames to electric forcing

Time resolved measurements after step changes in voltage are necessary to determine the
temporal response of flames to electric forcing. In particular, the time resolved ion cur-
rent, as shown in Figure 1.20, provides the ion flux timescale given by any time delay
beyond that of the natural capacitive decay time for the experimental apparatus. In 1-g
studies, the system electrical response is dominated by the slow capacitive timescale,
which may also be the case in microgravity. Time resolved measurements of spatially
integrated luminosity (including soot) and CH* filtered light from the flame in concert
with the ion current measurement monitor changes in the flame behavior for comparison
with the capacitive timescale. As shown in Figure 1.19, the steady-state flame luminosity
changes with electric field. The timescale of this change is a combination of any rapid
chemi-ion transport effects and the slower convective timescale effects arising from
changes in the ion driven wind. Computational and experimental studies show that at 1-g,
the convective effects can require hundreds of milliseconds to first influence the flame
and a longer time to reach quasi-steady state (e.g., [52]).

showing substantial changes with electric field will be identified from the data obtained
in Objective A and B. A comparison between the results in the gas jet diffusion flame
and the co-flow flame can distinguish the relative roles of ion-driven convection versus

2.3.6. SDEP (Objective D) – electric field sensing and control of near-limit flames

There are two main elements to this objective. One is to use the ion current as a sensor
for identifying the incipient extinguishment of lifted flames and the other is to increase
the flame’s resistance to blowoff. Diffusion flames near their blowoff limit in 1-g gener-
ally exhibit an unstable fluctuation just before extinguishing. The fluctuation appears in
the chemiluminescence, in the location of the flame base (liftoff height), and in the
chemi-ion current. The data products are, therefore, the mean and RMS ion current at
low voltages as functions of fuel flow rate and inert dilution in the fuel. Near limit
flames are identified from data in Objective A where the fuel flow rate and the inert con-
centration are increased to flame extinguishment. Extended time at microgravity is nec-
essary for these experiments because the blowoff process is stochastic and can involve
long periods of fluctuation.

The second element of this objective is open-loop control, using the ion driven wind to
restabilize near-limit co-flow flames. This phenomenon has been observed by Won, et al.
[46,47] as manifested by a resistance to flame lifting. They find, for example, that a
higher velocity is needed to maintain a fixed liftoff height when the flame is under the
influence of an electric field. There is a question, however, whether the effect is simply
due to an additive ion wind to the jet flow or if there is a more subtle influence of local

mixing that changes the flame propagation velocity. By measuring the liftoff height, the
fuel flow rate, and the ion current, it is possible to distinguish these influences. For ex-
ample, a substantial change in liftoff height accompanied by a modest ion wind (deter-
mined from the ion current and flame surface area) relative to the flow rate would suggest
a local mixing effect whereas when a larger ion wind is involved we would likely identify
a broader mean flowfield influence. Extended microgravity conditions are necessary to
establish the relationship between electric fields and liftoff height behavior because the
flame’s liftoff height can oscillate slowly for several cycles before it either blows off or
reattaches [54].
