2.4 Knowledge to be Gained

As is detailed more completely above, the knowledge expectation is to develop a chemi-
cal and physical understanding of flame ion production and the potential to then use this
information to control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinc-
tion limits and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. Hence,
we begin by mapping the electrical response of a wide range of flames and then concen-
trate on particular conditions of interest, particularly those near limit and transition condi-
tions in diffusion flames. For example, the saturated ion current is a characteristic of the
carbon flux into the flame so long as the flame character does not change. As the ion
driven wind begins to influence the reaction zone, the saturation current can change dra-
matically. We are interested in the flame condition near this transition. Similarly, a lifted
diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor point.
Electric fields acting on such flames can exert large influence because they can affect the
local mixing behavior. We are interested, therefore, in these near-limit flame conditions.
Finally, the role of

ctric fields acting on such flames can exert large influence because they can affect the
local mixing behavior. We are interested, therefore, in these near-limit flame conditions.
Finally, the role of electric fields on soot formation will be most dramatic under condi-
tions where the ion driven wind has the largest influence on flow residence time (or on
ion residence time, if chemical effects are found important) in sooting flames.

The explanation of the knowledge gaps associated with electric field effects in diffusion
flames have been described in the foregoing sections. It is worth making some general
statements in this regard, however, to summarize. The goal of this zero-gravity study is

to understand chemi-ionization behavior and the resulting ion driven winds sufficiently
well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion
current) and control them (via direct chemical or local convective influences). Electric
field effects on flames have been documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in
1-g all include buoyancy influences. For flames near transitions and limits, buoyant in-
fluences always confound any understanding of the role of ion driven winds in using
electric fields to characterize and manipulate flames. The proposed study removes this
confounding influence and allows definitive measurement and analysis of the electric
field effects on sooting, saturation current, and dilution on coflow and jet diffusion
flames.

Understanding the electric field effects on soot is another area that requires high quality
zero gravity timescales longer than is available in drop towers. A variety of zero gravity
diffusion flame experience has shown that quasi-steady soot formation requires many
seconds [22,56,57]. The long duration is necessary since we are exploring the relative
importance of residence time modification of these processes in these flames. In addi-
tion, as mentioned above, instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames gener-
ally have a stochastic character so that relatively long observation times are needed to
quantify electric field effects. For example, lifted flames in electric fields can exhibit an
oscillatory behavior where they alternately approach and recede from the burner exit until
they finally reattach. Tens of seconds for this process is not unusual. Extended micro-
gravity conditions will clarify the role of electric fields (via ion winds) on stability limits
of flames.

3. EXPERIMENT REQUIREMENTS

3.1 Requirements Discussion

This section does not include any requirements, but instead describes their importance in
achieving the experiment objectives. The requirements have been incorporated into the
ACME-SRD-001 Integrated Science Requirements.

3.1.1 Ambient Environment

The experiments are to be conducted in the chamber described in the combined ACME
science requirements. The gas fill for the gas jet tests and the coflow gas for the coflow
burner tests is nominally nitrogen (79%) and oxygen (21%) by volume. For the coflow
burner tests, the fill gas is as specified in the CLD Flame experiment SRD (as is the com-
position of the co-flow gas). Oxygen composition should not fall below 19% during the
tests. Oxygen makeup gas can be added as it is consumed to maintain an appropriate
overall oxygen concentration. The makeup oxygen is based on the assumption of com-
plete combustion of the fuel flowing into the system. Because there is no direct oxygen
concentration measurement, we expect that the chamber will be flushed and refilled ap-
proximately every 7-8 tests based on how much uncertainty has developed regarding the
ambient oxygen concentration. We want to ensure that the oxygen level does not leave
the window between 19 and 21%.

3.1.2 Burner Material

The gas-jet and coflow burners shall be electrically conductive and able to withstand a
constant temperature of 1000 ºC. The burner temperature requirements reflect the maxi-
mum temperature observed at the burner tips in past laboratory 1-g experiments. The
burner material requirement stems from the necessity of the burners to serve as electrodes
in the high voltage circuit. Figure 2.4 illustrates how the burners complete the electrical
pathway for measuring the flame’s ion current by forcing electric current into a shunt re-
sistor for measurement. The magnitude of the current is simply determined with Ohm’s
law and dividing the voltage drop across the resistor by the known value of the resistor.

3.1.3 Burners

Two different burner types are to be used. One is the simple gas jet burner. The second
type is the coflow burner as specified in the CLD Flame experiment SRD. Two different
nozzle diameters are included (one required and one desired) for the gas-jet burner to
vary the exit velocity of the fuel mixture without altering the flow rates specified in each
experimental test series and to match prior 1-g studies. The precise dimensions of all
burner nozzles must be known to ensure accurate velocity computations and conditions
for later numerical simulations by others if desired.

3.1.4 Electric Field

The electric field shall be produced between a copper mesh electrode and the burner.
Copper mesh is an ideal electrode because its open surface area allows combustion gases
to flow through preventing interaction with the flame. The range of mesh screen densities
in the ACME science requirements have been used successfully in past experiments.

Another desired capability is to place the mesh electrode at a range of axial positions to
achieve a desirable charge distribution in the electric field while preventing contact be-
tween the flame and the mesh. If the flame and mesh come into contact while the electric
field is active, a short circuit will result, and the flame will allow electric current to flow
between the burner and mesh electrode. Because the flame height and lift-off heights will
vary across the two burners and the vast experimental conditions, variable positioning is
highly desirable. A preliminary estimate of coflow burner lift-off heights suggests that
the mesh be placed approximately 5 cm away from the burner nozzle, preferably at two
different heights no less than 1 cm apart. The mesh diameter should be no less than 8 cm
to collect sufficient ion current from the flame based on our electrokinetic calculations of
ion flow. The electric field potential should be controllable in 50V or smaller increments
and should be able to reach 10kV across the electrode space for both polarities.

3.1.5 Ion Current Measurement

The proposed method of ion current measurement involves measuring the voltage across
a shunt resistor connected between the burner and the high voltage ground. Based on our
past experiments, the resistor and data acquisition system should have a resolution better
than 0.05 microamperes with an expected maximum current of 25 microamperes. For
example, we suggest that the shunt resistor value shall be 100 kΩ, and will measure cur-
rents on the order of microamperes. The resulting voltage will be on the order of 0.1 Volt
with an expected range of ± 4 Volts to be read by a 12-bit A/D converter. The resistor
tolerance should better than or equal to ± 0.1%, and have the lowest possible temperature
coefficient for precise measurements. The resistor should also be placed sufficiently far
from the burners to prevent changes in the resistance value due to heat conduction
through the connecting wire.

To ensure that the total ion current is measured at the shunt resistor, it is required that the
mesh electrode and burner be electrically isolated to prevent current leakage. Current
leakage should be less than 25 nanoamps at maximum voltage. The mesh electrode
should withstand +/- 20kV without breaking down. In addition, it is suggested that a cop-
per ring with a cross-sectional diameter of 2-3 mm be soldered to the perimeter of the
mesh to reduce the likelihood of break down at the tips of the mesh wires at high voltages.

3.1.6 Flame Imaging and Chemiluminescence Measurements

Color images of the flame will reveal the flame area, provide evidence of combustion in-
tensity, identify locations of soot formation, and show how the ion wind (local convec-
tion) changes the flame shape for the various input flame parameters and electric field
strength. UV images with a filter for OH* are required to provide a sharp determination
of the reaction zone. Images of CH* chemiluminescence are desired for observing spatial
changes in heat release rate due to electric field actuation, and may also be used as a sen-
sor for quantifying the electric field control effect. Density imaging is highly desired as
this provides a secondary indication of the reaction zone location but more importantly
shows the path of the convected hot gases driven by the ion wind for comparison with our
electrokinetic modeling. It is also possible to extract temperature from density images in
the soot-free regions of the flame, which is valuable for ascertaining electrical mobility.
Density images should be at no less than 15 Hz.

3.1.7 Soot Measurements

Soot volume fraction and soot temperature are needed to show the effects of electric
fields on the location, mean size, and amount of soot in the flames. Soot temperature
provides information regarding the thermal field in highly sooting regions of the flame.
The mean size of the soot is to be determined from assessing the presumed thermionic
current from the soot. The ion current is related to soot surface area and so the mean size
can be determined from the ratio of soot volume to soot area.

3.2 Operational Sequence

As described in Section 2, the E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objectives correspond-
ing to 4 series of tests using 2 different diffusion flame burner configurations. The first
three test series provide the key fundamental information regarding the electrical charac-
ter of diffusion flames and the influence of electric fields on soot formation; the final se-
ries focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames.

General Operations -- preparatory actions -- before any of the electric field experiments,
the high voltage mesh should be installed (or moved into position). Leak current should
be measured by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV with no flame pre-
sent. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and sets the
upper limit on the potential. The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep
with no flame to provide a point-by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep
should be completed following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. The leak
current allows a baseline for higher precision in the flame ion current determination. In
addition, excessive leak current at relatively low voltage may indicate electron emission
from carbon buildup on the gas jet flame tip. If the leak current exceeds 10% of the flame
ion current, cleaning of the gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual wiping
or possibly burning off the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be
a rare request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-
situ monitor. We assume that the chamber

3.3 Test Matrix

quired) and 2.1 mm diameter (required), and (b) a co-flow burner (same as in the CLD

the latter size matches the inner fuel tube of the co-flow burner. Some of the conditions

3.4 Success Criteria

Minimum Success:
• Obtain V-I curve in quasi-steady conditions for undiluted methane fuel on either
diameter of the gas jet burner or the co-flow burner
• Simultaneously capture color images of flame responding to electric field during
V-I sweep

Complete Success:
All of the above plus:
• Obtain V-I curve in quasi-steady conditions for both fuels (methane and ethylene)
on one gas jet burner and the co-flow burner with a range of inert dilution of fuel
• Simultaneously capture flame images during voltage sweeps to allow measure-
ment of liftoff height has a function of applied voltage
• Measure soot luminosity (radiometer measurement) as a function of applied volt-
age during VI sweeps and step changes
• Capture color images and soot luminosity (radiometer measurement) as a function
of coflow velocity during Electric Field Effects on Soot experiment.

Superior Success:
All of the above plus:
• Demonstrate open loop control of flame near sooting and stability limits using ion
current and luminosity as sensors by determining the decrease (or increase) in
soot luminosity and by evaluating the extent to which stability limits can be ex-
tended using an electric field
• (Desired) Obtain thermal field information for the gas jet or coflow flame to visu-
alize ion driven wind

The post-flight data analysis will use many of the tools and follow many of the proce-
dures established in our 1-g experiments, as shown in Section 1. In particular, we will
employ electrokinetic modeling based on measured flame shapes and total ion currents,
along with established relationships between flame area and ion flux to evaluate the links
between flame behavior and chemi-ionization. Analysis of test results will be conducted
both concurrently and at the conclusion of the flight experiment. Concurrent analysis is
required at key points in the E-FIELD Flames test matrix to determine the specific test
conditions and parameters necessary for a following set of related tests. Specifically, an
analysis of ion current saturation, luminosity, and blowout will be conducted at the con-
clusion of the voltage sweep test sets (described in Section 3.2) to determine the best flow
rate and nominal voltage range for soot effect tests and open-loop control tests. An analy-
sis of step response experiments is also required to determine time constants for modeling
the flame and designing the control parameters for open-loop experiments. Finally, an
analysis of the near-limit test results

nse experiments is also required to determine time constants for modeling
the flame and designing the control parameters for open-loop experiments. Finally, an
analysis of the near-limit test results in the E-FIELD Flames test matrix (and, desirably,
the results of CLD Flame near-limit experiments) is required to determine the flow rate
and mixtures that are most suitable for the stability experiments. It is important to note
that while tentative conditions for soot effects and control tests have already been identi-
fied in the test matrix, the ability to select conditions based on analysis of previous tests
will enhance the probability of success, and will ultimately maximize the value of the
science product.

The final analysis of all experimental data will be conducted at the conclusion of the
flight experiment until each objective (listed in Section 2.1) is achieved. Video, imagery
(luminosity), thermal field information, and ion current data will be analyzed together to
evaluate the ion wind strength, ion flux, ion production rate per unit carbon, and effects
of electric fields on soot—completing Objectives A and C. Ion concentration will be de-
termined from the saturation ion current: the point where ion collection and production
are equal. The mobility can be determined from numerical methods previously discussed
in Section 1 (see, for example, Figure 1.9) and in reference [52]. Once mobility is deter-
mined, we can ascertain the convective effects on the flame due to electricity.

One feature of the co-flow burner which makes this test unique is that axial convection
on the flame is dominated by the forced flow (buoyant convection is removed). Hence,
by reducing exit flow velocity and adjusting the magnitude of the electric potential at the
mesh, it is possible to create an equivalent local flow velocity with different electrical
effects. Adjustable flow configurations such as these would enable us to determine
whether the electrical effects on soot are residence time based or chemical in nature.

Open loop control measurements allow us to understand the dominant factor in flame re-
attachment and extended blowout limits: is it the mean ion wind or mixing effects at the
base? Analysis of the variation in ion current and luminosity time response in the step
voltage experiments will be conducted to distinguish chemical effects of the electric field

from diffusion and ion wind since their timescales are sufficiently well separated. This
analysis will fulfill Objective B. Objective D will be achieved by analyzing the effective-
ness of the electric field to vary soot luminosity, vary lift-off heights, and delay extinction
of a near-limit flame. All analyses completed during and after the flight experiment will
be documented in anticipation for future disclosure.

Impacts, Benefits, and Products
This text is the ‘Impacts, Benefits, and Products’ section from the 2019 version of the final report.

The impact of this work is, as the original objectives identified, the delivery of a unique data set of chemi-
ion behavior in flames under sufficiently stable and symmetric conditions that models and theories can
be evaluated against the results. As an example, the very distinctive shape of the V-I curve in microgravity,
when matched in models, will give a very good indication that the feedback between ion driven wind and
changes in flame shape and burning behavior that then further change the ion current is captured
accurately.

These results have already garnered the interest of other groups working on electric field effects on
flames.

The use of electric field effects on flames can be as sensor (variations of ion current as associated with
combustion behavior) or actuator (ion-driven wind changes the flame shape and characteristics). This
work, as was originally planned, provides quantitative evaluation of the sensing and response potential of
electric fields in combustion. The applications can include the control of flames.

Patents
Thus far, no patents have resulted from the E-FIELD Flames research.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Experimental Procedure 23 July 2020

1. Introduction
The narrative description of the experimental procedure is from the ‘Methods / Experimental’ section of
the following conference paper:
Y.-C. Chien, J. Tinajero, D. Stocker, U. Hegde, and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Electric Field Effects on Flames in
Microgravity on the International Space Station,” 2018 Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States
Section of The Combustion Institute, Minneapolis, MN, 20-22 May 2018.
This description also appears in Section 4.B Overview of Experiment Test Operations of the E-FIELD Flames
Final Report. Note that the referenced Figure 4 (showing the coflow burner geometry) is not included in
this document.

The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in near real
time but doesn’t allow for commanding. In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements were made so that
the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the research team to participate
in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s planned parameters. That team does not
see the telemetry during the testing, but is in communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA
research partners at the GRC ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). While there are many preparatory
steps, the tests are ultimately conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files. In
advance of the test day, the UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep
script and specifies other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.

It is also possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry. For example, the electric field potential can be
adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit.

Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, the low
rate results from several unavoidable factors. After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-imaging data is
downlinked for immediate review by the science team. A small sample of images are often downlinked
to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for those images are typically
selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples. The review helps to verify parameters
or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the voltage range after determining where the
ion current saturates for the given flame conditions. After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber
atmosphere after which the chamber is vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.
Midway through a day’s E-FIELD Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter
cartridge filled with molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion
products, e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products. The tests are only
conducted when both Ku and S band communication is available

Another constraint is the available time in a day, where the console personnel and ISS resources, such as
the video downlink, are planned for a limited number of hours. When necessary for the research, NASA
does have continuous 24-hour/day operations for some non-CIR experiments. But as discussed, the ACME
tests are typically two minutes or less in duration, so the testing is almost always limited to the planned
durations.

Data limits are yet another constraint, where the on-orbit hardware can store a limited amount of data.
More importantly, 127,000 MB is the most that can be reasonably managed in a two-shift transfer and
downlink day. Therefore, tests days are limited to this amount of data, where image data from select
cameras is often archived at reduced rates to mitigate this challenge. Nonetheless, the limit sometimes
forces decisions to abandon recorded images.

2. Test Sequences and ParametersAll E-FIELD Flames tests conducted on the ISS
were carried out using automated software which had its roots in ACME’s Integrated Science
Requirements Documents (ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) and Science Operations Requirements
Documents (SORD, Rev. A). The E-FIELD Flames Science Requirements Document (SRD) is of course
pertinent but only that which was incorporated in the ISRD and SORD was used by the engineering
team in developing the control software.

Multiple software scripts and corresponding parameter files were prepared to address the various
objectives explained in this excerpt from section 4.2 of the ACME ISRD. The section is fully included with
the important exception of the tables detailing the envisioned operational sequences. Given that they
were conceptual, they were left out to reduce the chance of a confused understanding of the engineering
implementation. For example, excessive electromagnetic interference (EMI) led to a change in the design
of the electric field system limiting the voltage to a single polarity on a given test day. As a result, the step
response procedure could not be carried out as detailed in Table 4.2.2 of the ISRD.

The E-FIELD experiment consists of 4 objectives corresponding to 4 series of tests using 2 different
diffusion flame burner configurations. The first three test series provide the key fundamental
information regarding the electrical character of diffusion flames and the influence of electric fields on
soot formation; the final series focuses on electric field sensing and control of flames.

General Operations
Before any of the electric field experiments, the high voltage mesh should be installed (or moved into
position). Leak current should be measured by sweeping the voltage from 0 to 10kV and 0 to -10kV
with no flame present. A steep rise in current under these conditions indicates corona discharge and
sets the upper limit on the potential. The test sequence involves a complete repeat voltage sweep
with no flame to provide a point-by-point current leak measurement. A similar sweep should be
completed following flame extinguishment at the end of a test set. Only ion current would need to be
measured during the no-flame sweep. In addition, excessive leak current at relatively low voltage may
indicate electron emission from carbon buildup on the gas jet flame tip. If the leak current exceeds
10% of the flame ion current, cleaning of the gas jet tip is requested. Cleaning consists of a manual
wiping or possibly burning off the carbon with a modified flame condition. We expect this to be a rare
request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We
assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 t

ct this to be a rare
request, but the continuous monitor of flameless ion current provides a reliable in-situ monitor. We
assume that the chamber will be emptied and refilled approximately every 7-8 tests to minimize the
oxygen concentration uncertainty in the test chamber. The exact times for settling and voltage steps
may vary (they should be reconfigurable from the ground), but a nominal expected operational

(B) Step Response—This test will involve the rapid change of voltage from a base level to a much
higher (or lower) level, while the ion current (and flame luminosity and shape) is monitored in time
as it settles to its new steady value. The key measurable is the ion current as a function of time through
the voltage step change and the flame’s subsequent settling. As in test set (A), video, luminosity, and
chemiluminescence will record flame behaviors in response to an instantaneous change in the electric
field. A typical experiment sequence might comprise a 15 second ignition and stabilization, step
changes on the order of hundreds of volts, and recording ion current for 2 seconds between step
changes (where steps will not be limited to a single polarity). Settling time for these step changes in
zero gravity (particularly, for soot related phenomena) may need to be adjusted via uplink; the test
procedures shown are based on a nominal settling time observed in preliminary testing at 1g and the
2.2 Second Drop Tower. The range of times between voltage steps may vary between 0-100 seconds.

(C) Electric Field Effects on Soot – The following tests will demonstrate the effects of electric fields on
soot (measured by broadband emission from the flame and soot volume fraction) by slowly increasing
the coflow air velocity, comparing the flame structure at each step to a flame affected purely by
electric forcing. Conditions will be uplinked and derived from experiments (A) and (B). Timing will
depend on the burner, but each test will be allowed at least 100 seconds. Also, note that the step
time between one coflow velocitity and the next shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of
0-10 seconds. Broad solid angle collection luminosity, flame images along with soot volume fraction
and soot pyrometry will be collected.

(D) Open Loop Sensing and Control – The experiments associated with control will be uplinked, based
on the results of the above baseline mapping experiments (A) and (B) above. Timing will depend on
the condition, but each test will be allowed at least 70 seconds. The procedure is a series of voltage
ramps (or small steps with continuous data collection). Ion current and luminosity (broadband and
CH*) fluctuations will be collected as well as flame images. The time between voltage changes for
flame adjustment and data collection shall be adjustable via uplink between the values of 0-10
seconds.

Although four types of E-FIELD Flames tests are discussed above, it was determined by 2017 that three
types of tests could be used to address the four experimental objectives, where a separate script to
investigate effects on the soot was not needed.

While scripts were developed for the three remaining sequences, it was later determined that the open
loop objectives could be accomplished by proper selection of parameter values with the voltage sweep
script, e.g., limiting the voltage range. Furthermore, the step response script was ultimately not employed
because of the slow response time of the high-voltage power supply. As such, all of the experiment’s
flame tests were conducted with the voltage sweep script. Therefore, that procedure is the only one to
be further discussed in this document.

More specifically, the script was updated between testing on April 16 (GMT 18106) and April 23 (18113)
with the addition of the parameter nitrogenPrimingDurationSec. The parameter was added because it
was observed that unwanted oscillations in the nitrogen flow often diminished with time. Therefore, an
early start of the nitrogen flow could reduce or eliminate oscillations while the flame was burning. This
feature can be seen in a simplified graphic of the test sequence (with constant flow rates) in Figure 2. At
the same time, four bracketing parameters were updated to enable the bracketed exposures to increase
via multiplication by a specified constant rather than via addition of a constant time. The revised set of
parameters was retained through the second round of testing with the gas-jet burner that was carried out
in Sept. to Nov. 2018.

4. Test Matrices
For all ACME experiments, including E-FIELD Flames, the test planning is refined in multiple steps as
described in this section. Despite refinement, the experiments are always expected to address the science
objectives approved in the ACME ISRD.

A. Test Matrices: Years in Advance
The test matrices found in section 5 of the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document
(ISRD, RDR version, Rev. B) were the basis for planning the equipment and resources, such as gas
bottles, needed to carry out each of the NASA-selected ACME experiments. For E-FIELD Flames,
the test matrices are found in section 5.2. The investigators were each directed to define matrices
with required testing which included at most one burner configuration and no more than
nominally 50 flames ignited. Regarding these constraints specified by Project Scientist Dennis
Stocker, the intent was to conduct focused rather than comprehensive research given the
considerable resources required for testing on the International Space Station. Meanwhile, there
were no limits put on desired or highly desired tests because of NASA’s plan to only carry out tests
designated as required.

However, in the case of E-FIELD Flames, the science loss associated with the slow response time
of the developed electric field system led to the decision to allow a second burner type and an
increased number of required tests. Specifically, the matrix was expanded to 74 flames rather
than the planned 58, where it must be understood that voltage sweep tests as defined in the ISRD
require 2 flames, where the voltage is increased in one test and decreased in the other. As a result
of this allowance, E-FIELD Flames was carried out with both the coflow burner (developed for the
CLD Flame experiment) and a gas-jet burner with the same tube size as the coflow burner’s inner
tube. This enabled testing with and without the coflow and in the absence of the outer tube (i.e.,
with the gas-jet burner) in order to assess latter’s coupled effect on the electric field distribution
and oxidizer entrainment.

NASA Glenn’s ISS Control Board later decided to limit ACME testing to nominally 4 months of ISS
testing per experiment which with preparatory operations, minor delays, repeat testing due to
science loss, etc. were expected to typically occur in a total of 5 months. This decision was made
with the expectation that the required testing, e.g., as specified in the ISRD, could at least mostly
be accomplished in that time period assuming the availability of crew and other needed
resources.

As part of his planning, Stocker instigated an alternating sequence of experiment testing, wherein
investigators would get a break in their testing in order to analyze early results in depth and with
that knowledge achieve higher science outcomes in their second round of testing. As a result,
each experiment was expected to get 2 months of testing per round, which meant nominally 8
test days per round of testing. Within that time constraint and available resources, experiments
were ultimately permitted to plan for and conduct more tests than had been specified as required
in the ISRD, despite the initial planning which ignored desired and highly desired testing.

B. Test Matrices: Months in Advance
At least a few months in advance of testing, ACME investigators are directed to submit a refined
test matrix for the upcoming round corresponding to available hardware, gas bottles, and the
agreed number of test days. The refinement can be based on what is learned from experimental,

analytical, or computational efforts subsequent to the 2013 ISRD. Generally, this planning has
been done in detail comparable to that found in the ISRD, with the important exception that it
must furthermore establish the required hardware, including the specific mass flow controllers
(and thus specification of the flow ranges) and gas bottles so that overall experiment operations,
including crew activity, can be adequately planned. In this regard, it must establish operational
plans for the chamber atmosphere on each day of testing including filling, scrubbing (via
circulation through the adsorber cartridge), venting (whether partial or complete), and
measurements, if any, with the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). However,
GCIP measurements were not made during the E-FIELD Flames or CLD Flame experiments.

includes all of test parameters within the script and additional ones which are outside of the script
Most of the latter deal with camera settings which don’t change during a test, for example the

intensified camera. Outside of the script, the investigators must again specify the chamber

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

16 Dec. 2020
30-day Operational Accomplishments Report
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increment 63

ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
s-Flame Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
The s-Flame investigation is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME
project, which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning
gaseous fuels in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The first round of s-Flame tests was
conducted during Increments 60 and 61, while the second round was conducted fully within
Increment 63. There were no tests conducted in Increment 62 because of limited crew availability.

Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for s-Flame and ACME information.

Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. C.K. (Ed) Law, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Stephen D. Tse, Rutgers University, Piscataway, NJ
Lead collaborator: Dr. Vladimir V. Gubernov, P.N. Lebedev Physical Institute of the
Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia
NASA Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH

I. Introduction
Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment were
conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The purpose of s-Flame
is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and
instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames. The results may contribute to the development
of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth.

The spherical flames are ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally
towards steady-state or extinction. Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the
fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere. The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures
for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames. One experimental objective is to identify the
extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame
extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out,” respectively. Another objective is to
determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically
predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives:
A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species
distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame
structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different
C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system
Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system
Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and
different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
A. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da),
and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically
predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that
are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions.

As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion
flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still
oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity. The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates
data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation.

The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the
motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction
because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss. The study is focused on the thermal
radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in
computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the
extinction boundaries. (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition,
the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame
spread, extinction, and instability.

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

II. Methods/Research Operations

A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
The s-Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not
conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc.
for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME
chamber insert.

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload
Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. As expected, no s-Flame tests
were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry
stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception
of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature
has reached a critical value.

Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.

Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
A total of 276 flames were ignited for the s-Flame experiment, with 29, 116, and 131
respectively ignited during Increments 60, 61, and 63. These numbers neglect some
flames which quenched promptly after ignition. In this regard, science testing began at
the end of Increment 60 and the first round of tests were completed during Increment
61. No tests were conducted in Increment 62 due to a lack of crew time, where the
second round of tests were fully conducted during Increment 63.

The tests were conducted in two rounds, where the first was conducted in increments 60
and 61 featured 145 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen (i.e., in the chamber
atmosphere) were diluted with nitrogen. The second round conducted in increment 63
featured 131 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen were instead diluted with
helium.

The s-Flame experiment does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but
the tests are independently conducted with various gaseous fuels, including hydrogen,

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

methane, hydrogen/methane blends, and ethylene. These are simple hydrocarbon gases
for which the chemistry is relatively well understood.

No samples (e.g., of soot) were collected for s-Flame; all of the ISS results were
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently
planned ACME experiments.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies
1. Mission anomalies
While there were certainly issues with testing discussed in the next section, there
were no significant anomalies during s-Flame’s Increment 63 testing. However,
anomalies did occur during Increment 60 and 61 which led to corrective actions
and/or make-up testing.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this
increment. All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber
atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in
Increments 60 and 61. The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making
comparison testing very desirable for manifestation of different phenomena.
Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen,
so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames. The power
level was slowly increased from test to test until ignition was finally achieved on the
ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11
(20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63. The cautious approach was taken
because of concerns that the igniter tip might fail (i.e., burn out) if too much power
was applied. An igniter failure would have likely halted testing for weeks given the
need to schedule the commander’s time to replace the igniter tip.

After that first test day, the decision was made to have the igniter replaced with a coil
rather than loop design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker
wire. Furthermore, the igniter tip had not been replaced in months, and the tips do
degrade with time, especially when they are not quickly retracted from the ignited
flames. The coil igniter was used successfully but still with caution, where flames were
not always ignited successfully. Subsequently, some tests were conducted in
atmosphere with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%. As one
would expect, that proved to be helpful for achieving ignition. But the end result was
that some tests were conducted with 21% oxygen, some at 30%, and some at both
nominal concentrations. Fortuitously, this mixture of conditions may provide deeper
insight into the mechanisms of flame dynamics and response.

Tests are also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite, where that occurred, for
example, during Increment 61 in tests 19304A4, 19304A6, 19308C1, and 20006A1.
That can be corrected by adjusting various test parameters and other settings. In this
case, adjustments were subsequently made to the ignition position (e.g., after
19304A4 and 19304A6), the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation (e.g.,
after 19308C1), and the duration of the igniter activation (e.g., after 20006A1). As
another example, failed ignition can result from false ignition detection and
deactivation resulting from the combination of settings for ignition and detection,
e.g., the gain for the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module measuring the OH*
chemiluminescence. The latter, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and
visible spectrum.

Testing on June 3 (20155) was cut short due to a combination of issues. The final test
was aborted due to an error with an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU).
Consoles needed to be reset for the new increment, and there was an issue with the
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) Control Unit, i.e. the FCU. Rebooting
the FCU inadvertently set the valve safety timers to zero, which cannot be reset
without venting and refilling the combustion chamber with the intended atmosphere.
Those issues combined with an extended loss of commanding prevented further
science operations on that day. Therefore, an additional test day (July 8, i.e., 20190)
was added to make up for lost science, e.g., where only one test was successfully
conducted at ~21% oxygen on June 3. The FCU was off nominal because of a high
carrier gas pressure in the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).
Imaging of the hydrogen flames was often an issue, where they were not apparent or hardly
visible to the operations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera
for ACME testing. The testing with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted
on Dec. 18 (19352), Jan. 24 (20024),

erations camera and ACME DataCam, where the latter is the primary camera
for ACME testing. The testing with the extremely dim flames was limited to that conducted
on Dec. 18 (19352), Jan. 24 (20024), June 3 (20155), and July 8 (20190). This shortcoming
unfortunately inhibits assessment of the three-dimensional flame symmetry as the two
intensified cameras were opposite of each other.

The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a
challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative
extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints.

At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While
nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing
offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the
supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the
supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the
flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the
flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even
parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube.

When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC)
performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow
rate differed from that desired. However, this was not a surprise to those familiar
with the hardware.

Flow perturbations have been noticed in some s-Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs
used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always
performed satisfactorily. In tests conducted using the 1-slpm fuel MFC (where the
flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has been seen to overshoot and
undershoot when first opening. Small flow irregularities have been most apparent

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

through their effect on the Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) measurements, e.g., of OH*
and CH* chemiluminescence. A momentary increase in fuel flow, as has occurred in
some s-Flame tests, naturally leads to increased light from the flame. The MFCs are
tested - without flames - after they are first installed. Adjustments are typically made
to (1) the setting that controls when the valves open and (2) the Proportional-Integral-
Derivative (PID) settings. This ACME activity has involved significant testing, where
there is an assortment of MFCs with different flow ranges for each of the three gas
types. While the MFC adjustments have been beneficial, they have not eliminated all
gas flow problems. It was seen in prior ACME testing that nitrogen oscillations (if any)
tend to damp with time, so a nitrogen pre-flow can be used so that such oscillations
might end before the flame is ignited. As another measure, the MFCs are re-zeroed
prior to each test, where that was another measure adopted in earlier ACME testing.

As mentioned previously, s-Flame tests have sometimes automatically aborted
(because of the controlling software script), where that is normally prior to gas flow
and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME experiments. As a
result, there was little lost other than the available experimental time in the failed test
attempt. ACME aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an IPSU,
which for example happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20024N1, and
20024J1. A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified
outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included for
example 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013C2. ACME aborts are infrequent, but there
are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here.

During Increments 60 and 61, nine days of tests were conducted during which 145 flames
were ignited for the first round of testing. In contrast, only 29 tests were specified as
required or highly desired in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document
(ISRD) for that round. Therefore, a wealth of data was obtained for this round of testing
which featured gaseous fuels diluted by nitrogen.

However, there was a significant loss of data. Most importantly, the first fuel bottle
appeared to leak on installation (in Increment 60) and later on-orbit testing (in Increment

those test days were nominally repeated on Jan. 29 (20029) and Jan. 24 (20024),
respectively (i.e., in a reversed order). For these reasons, a simple comparison of the total

the first round of testing is somewhat misleading.

DataCam. Neglecting that factor, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels

gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in
image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality.

It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available

D. Status of Data Analysis [provided by Prof. Stephen Tse, Rutgers U.]
Image files are currently being processed. Radial positions of maximum CH*
chemiluminescence is being plotted against time. Different radii are being considered
and plotted together, as some flames are not completely symmetric. MFC and PMT data
are being compared with video images to assess and confirm experimental settings.
Radiometer data is being reviewed. Analyses of the fiber pyrometry data are ongoing.
MATLAB code is used to isolate fiber images, which are then color assessed for
temperature.

Computational simulations with detailed chemistry and transport of the test cases are
underway. Time-dependent simulations will be compared with the time-dependent
experimental data, where tracking of the flamefront location is based on
chemiluminescent emission. Steady-state simulations will produce the Isola curves
mapping flame response versus system Damkhöler number for given fuel mixtures. The
experimental cases will then be pin-pointed on the computational mappings to assess
whether the experimental conditions are in quasi-steady state or near extinction limits,
either kinetic or radiative. Oscillation behavior will be correlated to possible pulsating
oscillations found in the simulations.

E. Preliminary Research Findings [provided by Prof. Tse and lightly edited by Stocker]
The s-Flame experiment utilizes spherically-symmetric diffusion flames and their
dynamics and responses to investigate fundamental processes, such as extinction,
instability, and soot formation.

The tests conducted on 19254 (near the end of Increment 60) revealed that a quasi-steady
flame could be attained for extended duration at low flow rate, i.e., 3 cc/s for 20%
C2H4/80% N2 (on a volume basis). The flame was shut down by the automated system
because the burner reached a cut-off temperature of 250°C. Although the flame
oscillated near the end of the test, it was likely due to influence of the burner tube.
Comparisons with computation simulations will help to clarify the involved processes. For
higher flow rates, e.g., 5-10 cc/s, with the same mixture, radiative extinctions were
observed. Generally, the flames showed unstable behavior near the burner tube prior to
extinction, likely because of lack of fuel mixture and heat loss in that region. Other
mixtures, e.g., 25% C2H4/75% N2 and 30% C2H4/70% N2, also showed radiative extinctions
at higher flow rates. For some cases, the pyrometry fiber interacted with the flame,
allowing determination of temperature in on-going analyses. Soot was observed only

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63

during ignition, which went away as the flame established itself. To assess whether these
nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures
were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents
(e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher
ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4). The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no
sooting was observed. Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow
rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our ground-
based studies, given the limited microgravity durations. Radiative reabsorption extends
flame size at extinction. In ISS testing, radiative extinction has been found to be a
common event, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for
our flame conditions.

The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction. Similar to
the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe
kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp
down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit. High flow rate
cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively
extinguished. Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established
before ramp down in flow rate. The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain
a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down. However, for stronger mixtures, i.e.,
20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were
observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. Radiative extinctions for ramp up
cases were also examined. Similarly, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice
flames were established at 3 cc/s; and radiative extinctions were observed during ramp
up before reaching 8 cc/s.

Testing on 19304 investigated 45% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into an air atmosphere.
The results indicated that the flow rates specified by the fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) were in the
regime of kinetic extinction. Quasi-steady flames could not be established. Furthermore,
larger flow rates could not be provided by the MFC, so observations of radiative extinction
could not be achieved. Even with a larger capacity MFC, characteristically larger flames
would be expected to be asymmetric. As such, nitrogen-diluted methane flames were
planned to be reexamined in increased oxygen atmosphere, i.e., 30% O2/70% N2.

Consequently, the 19308 tests investigated nitrogen-diluted methane flames in 30%
O2/70% N2 atmosphere. Various methane concentrations from 45% down to 15% were
examined. For 45% CH4/55% N2, relatively long duration flames of ~15 s and ~10 s were
established at flow rates of 2 cc/s and 3 cc/s, respectively. At larger flow rates of 5 and
9.4 cc/s, the flames expanded to large radii and then extinguished. These flames
appeared to demonstrate radiative extinction. Reduction of flow rate from 2 cc/s to 1
cc/s resulted in extinction during ramp down, indicating kinetic extinction. For 30%
CH4/70% N2, flow rates of 3, 5, and 10 cc/s produced flames that expanded to extinction
(assumed radiatively); while reduction of flow rate from 3 to 1 cc/s resulted in presumably
kinetic extinction during ramp down. For 25% CH4/75% N2, flow rates of 5 and 10 cc/s

yielded flames that expanded to extinction. For 20% CH4/80% N2, constant flow rate of
10 cc/s created a flame that expanded until extinction (assumed radiatively); while
reduction of flow rate from 10 cc/s to 1 cc/s resulted in wavering extinction during ramp
down, suggesting kinetic extinction. For 15% CH4/85% N2, flames were ignited, but
extinguished very quickly. These tests of 19308 suggest that they could manifest both
radiative and kinetic extinction for the conditions specified.

The 19352 tests examined various concentrations of H2 (45%-70%) diluted with N2 issuing
into air. The installed fuel MFC had a maximum output of 0.1 slpm, which unfortunately
provided a less-than-sufficient flow range where its use may have precluded the study of

flames was a challenge, especially since the hobj image files from the ACME DataCam
were mis-formatted. Furthermore, little could be seen in the analog ops imaging, e.g.,
where it, like the DataCam and Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera, cannot
image the ultraviolet OH* flame emission (at 310 nm). Analysis of images from the Low

expect, little could be seen with the CFI intensified camera using its broadband CH2O filter.
Quasi-steady flames seem to be present at low flow rates (e.g., 2.4 cc/s for 70% H2), as
inferred from PMT, pyrometry fiber emission, and burner temperature observations.
Kinetic extinction seems to occur as the flow rate is ramped down. There were various
problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H

Kinetic extinction seems to occur as the flow rate is ramped down. There were various
problems with the IPSU and some tests aborted. Using the 100% H2 bottle with a higher
flow rate MFC was later performed for tests of 20024 (see below), which was a make-up

The tests conducted on 20006, using the 44.4% H2/55.6% CH4 bottle, examined 20%
H2/25% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Flames extinguished, some with wavy
oscillating behavior prior to extinction. However, it seems that even for very small flow
rates, e.g., 2 cc/s, extinction was by the radiative mechanism during flame
expansion. There was too little parameter room in terms of flow rate and burner size to
identify conclusively kinetic extinction during ramp down for these mixtures. In short,
radiative extinction (with local flame extinction and re-ignition seemed to occur prior to
ultimate extinguishment) during flame expansion after ignition was observed. However,
it is unclear whether ramping down the flow rate resulted in kinetic extinction. Detailed
analyses of the data are needed. The various cameras seemed to capture the tests well.

The 20013 tests, which used the 66.7% H2/33.3% CH4 bottle, mainly investigated 30%
H2/15% CH4/55% N2 mixtures issuing into air. Radiative extinction was difficult to identify

with patchy extinction areas, until time out. Larger flow rates could not be examined

The 20024 tests using the 100% H2 bottle repeated and augmented conditions for those
of 19352 where the 0.1-slpm fuel MFC range was too low to examine radiative extinction
and the analog and intensified cameras did not pick up the flame images at all or well.
Here, the 0.5-slpm fuel MFC was used and only a fused silica filter was used for the Cool
Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera. 45%-15% H2/N2 balance mixtures were
investigated. The flames at high flow rates, e.g., 10 cc/s, did not extinguish, appearing
quasi-steady until time out. The pyrometry fibers glowed, perhaps making good flame-
structure measurements, which will be evaluated subsequently. The flames seemed to
extinguish during ramp down, but further analysis is needed to assess kinetic extinction.

The tests conducted on 20029 used 50% C2H4/50% N2 and repeated and augmented
conditions of 19256, when the images were not good. Again, the results indicated both
kinetic and radiative extinction phenomena under corresponding conditions. However,
no sooting flames were established, necessitating 100% C2H4 and an enriched oxygen
atmosphere to facilitate sooting behavior in possible future tests.

The 20132 tests kicked off a round of tests with helium-diluted fuel and oxidizer. The
ambient was 21% O2 and 79% He. The fuel was composed of 25% H2, 20% CH4, and 55%
He. Using He as inert made igniting the mixture much more difficult compared to that for
the N2 inert cases of Round 1, using the same ignition parameters. The reason is believed
to be due to the 6X higher value in thermal conductivity of He versus that of N2. As a
result, ignition parameters were varied, e.g., with a longer preheat time and higher
power, to achieve ignition for the He-diluted mixtures and ambient. The tests produced
flames at 3, 5, 7, and 10 cc/s that expanded outwardly quickly and extinguished. For 5, 7,
and 10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're-ignite' with a "flash" before final
extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon. Moreover, the
radiation mechanism is not conclusive, as it appears different than for the N2-diluted
cases. We did not have a chance to examine lowering of flow rates to assess kinetic
extinction.

The 20136 tests examined 20% H2/25% CH4/55% He issuing into 21% O2/He. For 5 cc/s
and 7 cc/s, the mixture ignites but immediately extinguishes, with almost no observable
flame-front expansion. For 10, 13, 15, and 17.5 cc/s, the mixtures ignite, expand quickly,
and extinguish. We believe that the extinction mechanism is radiative and will compare
with computational simulations. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the flames
seemed to extinguish before ramp down. Thus, we were not able to assess purely kinetic
extinction. Ignition parameters were varied to investigate thresholds for igniting the
mixture for different flow rates. Only flow rates above 7 cc/s showed flame-front
expansion leading to extinction, with 17.5 cc/s showing a flash or wavering of the flame
before final extinction.

The tests conducted on 20142 investigated 30% H2/15% CH4/55% He issuing into 30%
O2/He. Elevated oxygen was approved for study, since ignition and extinction limits in
previous testing were affected by the high thermal conductivity of He. For 5, 7, 10, 15,

Testing on 20160 investigated 45% CH4/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He.
Without H2 in the mixture, even larger energy and power were needed to ignite the

More analysis is needed. Tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere needed even more energy and

The 20164 tests began study of ethylene-based flames, where 20% C2H4/80% He issued
into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He atmospheres. For 5 cc/s, the flame expanded and
remained quasi-steady until the burner limit temperature (250°C) was reached. At 6, 7,
10, and 15 cc/s, the flames expanded to extinction, with the higher flow rates (i.e., 10 and
15 cc/s) exhibiting sooty ignition. Fuel flow of 5.5 cc/s seemed to correspond to a
condition where the onset of oscillating extinction was simultaneous with the burner
reaching the 250°C temperature limit. For the cases with a ramp down in flow rate, the

The tests performed on20170 investigated 25% C2H4/75% He issuing into 30% O2/He and
21% O2/He. At 5 and 5.5 cc/s, nice blue chemiluminescent flames were ignited, but
eventually were cut off because of the burner temperature limit being reached. At 6 cc/s,
a nice blue flame was ignited which expanded slowly to extinction. At 7, 10, and 15 cc/s,
sooty ignition occurred, but as the flames expanded, the soot went away, eventually
resulting in radiative extinction. By ramping the flow rates up, starting at 5 cc/s, soot at
ignition was minimized, and the flames could expand to extinction. Ramp down of the
flow rate resulted in almost immediate extinction. For tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere,
cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that expanded quickly to extinction. Less
soot was present at ignition compared with that for the 30% O2/He atmosphere cases.
Consistent ignition was not always achieved for the same conditions, which is puzzling.

Testing on 20176 explored 30% C2H4/70% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. At
5 cc/s, a long duration flame was established that eventually reached the burner
temperature limit. At 6, 7, 10, and 15 cc/s, the flames were sooty at ignition, but the soot
dissipated; and they expanded to extinction. Ramping up the flow rates, starting at 5 cc/s,
minimized soot at ignition and resulted in flames that slowly expanded to extinction. For
tests at 21% O2/He atmosphere, cases at 5, 10, and 15 cc/s resulted in flames that
expanded to extinction. At 4 cc/s, the flame lasted a while before eventual extinction.
The 3 cc/s case did not ignite. Ramp down of the flow rate seemed to result in flames
that extinguished quickly before the protocol could ramp down the flow rate.

The last testing of Round 2, which was a makeup of 20155, occurred on 20190, with 45%
H2/55% He issuing into 30% O2/He and 21% O2/He. For both oxygen concentration

off by automated protocol before self-extinction when the burner temperature limit was
reached. As for cases where the flow rates were ramped down, extinction detection was
observed for both oxygen concentration environments. We are currently analyzing the
data to determine if extinction was kinetic or due to heat loss to the burner. A last set of
tests were conducted with a reduced oxygen concentration atmosphere, i.e., 17.5%
O2/82.5% He. Some cases indicated that radiative and kinetic extinction were possibly
observed.

o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames and in air seemed to
indicate kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow
rates. As previously mentioned above (and in our report for the preceding
increment pair), such phenomena were not observed in our ground-based
research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons
with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction
behavior.
o Cases run for nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to show kinetic extinction
at ramp down. However, for the mass flow rates that could be accommodated,
radiative extinction was not observed.

1. Overview
The Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment is one of six independent
experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for
which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station
(ISS).

The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Chung K. Law of Princeton University. The experiment
has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), namely Prof. Stephen D. Tse of Rutgers University and Dr. Kurt R.
Sacksteder of the NASA Glenn Research Center. While Sacksteder was actively engaged in defining the
experiment, he had transitioned to other NASA work long before the spaceflight operations limiting his
overall contributions.

Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME
including s-Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Vedha Nayagam and Uday G. Hegde
who are also with CWRU.

The s-Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 60-63, where there
was no testing during Increment 62 due to limited crew availability. More specifically, the first round of
testing was conducted from Sept. 2019 to Jan. 2020, while the second-round testing – featuring helium
rather than nitrogen dilution - occurred from May to July 2020.

2. Science Overview
A. Background
This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document
(SRD) of Jan. 2010.

Recognizing that most combustion engines and devices operate on the basis of diffusion flames,
the proposed program aims to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and
dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well-defined flow fields such that the phenomena of
interest can be studied without being unduly complicated and compromised by complex and
sometimes non-quantifiable flow field effects. The basic flame configuration adopted for the
investigation is the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from
a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing ambience in microgravity. The one-
dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational
simulation.

The primary goals of the program are two-fold and strongly interdependent. The first objective
is to interrogate the fidelity of the chemical kinetic mechanisms and transport submodels used in
the simulation of aerothermochemical phenomena, and consequently identify possible
modifications. The second objective is to characterize and gain predictive capability on spherical
diffusion flames.

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021

The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the
movement of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition from a non-steady-state condition
and their extinction boundaries due to direct finite-rate chemistry and indirect radiative heat loss.
The emphases are on the relative importance of radiative emission and re-absorption, the
examination of the adequacy of the detailed chemical kinetics mechanism and transport sub-
models used, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction
boundaries. Results of the study are of relevance to the development of lean-burn engines for
improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions. (2) Studies of the response of
characteristically sooty flames to a non-steady-state initial condition with respect to the aspects
given in (1). The studies will include characterizing soot onset as a function of residence time for
expanding flames, as well as soot radiation and transport contributions in spreading, extinction,
and instability.

The project involves microgravity experimentation, computational simulation, and, where
appropriate, theoretical analysis. Interpretation of all phenomena will emphasize the
simultaneous and coupled influence of chemistry and transport.

B. Rationale for Microgravity
This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity Environment’ section (2.5) of the
experiment’s SRD from Jan. 2010. See the SRD itself for the references, etc. which are not included
in this report.

2.5.1 Limitations of Terrestrial (1g laboratory) Testing
We seek to make observations of truly one-dimensional flames whose structure can be studied
without complications due to uncertainties in the flow pattern caused by buoyancy. Such
fundamental study of flame structure and dynamics is best served via the elimination of buoyancy
through the reduction of gravity.

The minimum sizes of these flames imply that buoyancy would be significant if the experiments
were conducted in normal gravity. Previous experimentation on earth has amply demonstrated
this influence. Although studies of spherical diffusion flames were conducted in normal gravity
using the low-pressure, inverse-flame arrangement (see §1), the conditions are limited for small
flames, low pressures, low molecular weight fuels. Indeed, only the hydrogen flame can be
considered to be nearly buoyancy free. With such constraints, normal-pressure, micro-gravity,
hydrocarbon-based experiments are requisite.

One-dimensional spherical flames allow for the unambiguous study of such fundamental flame
phenomena as the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames (including the mechanisms of
flame front unsteadiness), soot suppression/formation, and flame front instabilities, without
gravity-induced baroclinicity and buoyancy, on the flame responses.

2.5.2 Limitations of Drop Towers and Aircraft
Extensive experimentation has been conducted in the 2.2-s drop tower, 5-s drop tower, and
parabolic aircraft, as reviewed previously in §1.3. Although experimental data of good quality
were obtained on the transient response of spherical diffusion flames in the 2.2-s drop tower
facility, the duration was insufficient to observe radiative extinction. The numerical simulations
indicate that, for the characteristic flames under study, more than 2.5s of microgravity time is
needed. Subsequent parabolic aircraft experimentation afforded the additional low-gravity

2.5.3 Justification for Space-Flight Facility
As explained above, extended microgravity duration, of high quality, is needed to make all
necessary flame structure measurements, allowing for the study of transient phenomena (such
as flame oscillations and fuel vapor accumulation) and extinction processes. Moreover, at
present, the advanced diagnostics found on the space-flight facility cannot be utilized in the drop
tower facilities. Numerical simulations indicate that about 25s of microgravity is needed for non-
extinguishing flames to reach 80% of their steady-state radius, for the fuel mixtures and flow rates
examined. It is expected that within this duration, the aforementioned phenomenon can be duly
investigated. The total experimental duration for a single case would be 25s. This duration is
within the 25s bound imposed by constant volume combustion within the specified CIR
dimensions (see §Appendix 5.1) regarding oxygen depletion for a “penetration depth” of 20cm.

C. Science Objectives
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.1) of the
experiment’s SRD from Jan. 2010.

Current experimental and theoretical capabilities make detailed, quantitative descriptions of
laminar flames situated in well-defined flow fields conceivable provided that comprehensive

ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021) 29 July 2021

chemical-kinetic and transport mechanisms are available. The comprehensiveness of these
mechanisms has been extensively tested for premixed but not diffusion flames, especially in
simple, well-defined flow fields not complicated by buoyant flows. A burner-generated spherical
diffusion flame provides a simple, one-dimensional flame geometry that permits a rigorous
comparison between detailed theory and experimental verification. Existing theory and limited
low-gravity experimental results suggest that quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames can exist
with some combinations of fuel mixture supply rates and quiescent ambient oxidizers. With
respect to the steady flame conditions, altering fuel supply rates to limit flame residence time
induces a convective-kinetic extinction limit. Alternatively, very large residence times allow
radiative heat losses and diffusive transport mechanisms to quench the flame. Near these dual
flammability boundaries of quasi-steady flames, flame-front instabilities may appear before the
flame is quenched.

We seek to investigate and improve the fidelity and comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic
mechanisms and transport submodels used in the simulation of aerothermochemical
phenomena, and consequently identify possible modifications, by characterizing important unit
combustion processes, including: (1) the dynamics and extinction of diffusion flames, with
emphases on fuel vapor accumulation, radiation heat transfer, flame pulsation, and flame
kinetics; and (2) the structure and response of characteristically sooty flames, with emphases on
flame front stability and soot formation. Comprehensive predictive capability can be achieved by
employing the simple flames of Process (1) to interrogate and suggest modifications of the kinetic
and transport data bases, and then validate their adequacy in the chemically and aerodynamically
more complex situation of Process (2).

A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and
sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties
and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence):

Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species
distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for
mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty),
for different flow rates.

Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low
system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system
Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different
C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).

Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function
Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted
to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical
Lewis number.

The success criteria is from the s-Flame’ portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME
