c. Dates of Operation
CFI experiments were conducted onboard the ISS from January 2017 through September 2017.

3. Science Overview
a. Background
Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental
importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day,
which averages out to an amazing 2.5 gallons per day per person. The primary reason for such high reliance
on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but in the rest of the
world, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability, compared to many other forms of
energy sources. With the emergence of newer technologies for internal combustion engines and the
increasing use of renewable bio-fuels, such as the Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engine
and bio-diesel, that promise cleaner more efficient and sustainable utilization of hydrocarbon fuels, the
need to understand the fundamental chemical and physical aspects of liquid-fuel combustion is bound to
increase.

Commercially available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many
hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes being major components. The combustion
characteristics of these alkanes are quite complex and follow branched-chain reaction pathways involving
many intermediate radicals. The chemical pathways vary, depending on temperature and, to a lesser extent,
on pressure. In general it is possible to identify a low-temperature reaction mechanism and a high-
temperature mechanism, with a transition region between them. Many hydrocarbons exhibit a unique
feature in this transition region, namely that the reaction rate decreases with increasing temperature,

leading it to be called the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) region. There area a number of models
available in the literature, simplified chemical-kinetic model involving hundreds of reactions as well as
detailed mechanisms involving thousands of reactions.

Droplet-combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) conducted onboard the International Space Station, as part
of the Flame Extinguishment Experiments, have revealed for the first time that large n-alkane droplets can
continue to burn quasi-steadily in the NTC region (see, Fig 1). NTC behavior of the heat-release rate is
necessary for low-temperature quasi-steady droplet burning to be stable. It was observed that the second-
stage combustion of the droplet controlled by low-temperature NTC chemistry, referred to as ``cool-flame
combustion" here for the sake of simplicity, abruptly ends at a finite droplet diameter, leaving the unburned
droplet to vaporize in the hot atmosphere. A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the
partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.

Figure 1. Three representative examples of radiative extinction and subsequent cool flame combustion of n-
heptane droplets in air. Inset shows the visible flame, backlit droplet images and the vapor cloud formation.

Furthermore, the second-stage flame is shown to lie closer to the droplet surface where the rates of heat
generation by the NTC chemistry is dynamically balanced by the heat loss rate. Unlike the hot-flame
combustion where the overall process is controlled by equilibrium thermodynamic properties of the fuel,
the cool-flame combustion depends on the chemical-kinetic details of the NTC region. These experimental
and numerical studies provide a new tool to further explore the NTC chemistry of liquid fuels in an entirely
new way. The experimental cool-flame droplet burning rates provide measures of the heat-release rates
and stoichiometry, the flame-diameter evolution provides insight into hot-flame diffusive and convective
heat-loss effects, and the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic
characteristic times.

The objectives of the CFI experiments is to further explore the cool flame phenomenon using pure fuels, and
fuel mixtures over a range of pressures and helium dilution.

b. Rational for Microgravity (if unusual)

Rationale for microgravity remains the same for all the droplet combustion experiments conducted onboard
the ISS. In microgravity the droplets burn in a spherically symmetric form, and therefore it is possible to
model the processes with complex chemical kinetic mechanisms involving thousands of reactions leading to
a better understanding of the chemistry. Moreover, the cool flames need much longer residence times and
cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.
c. NRA the Investigation was Selected Under
This project was initiated by NASA through a Science Definition Team (SDT) which formulated the overall
objectives. It was peer reviewed by an independent panel of scientists and approved by NASA HQ as a
follow-up experiments to FLEX, and FLEX-2 in the CIR using additional fuels and gases needed to complete
the test matrix. The experimental hardware is same as that of the FLEX experiments with few minor
modifications in the data acquisition systems.
d. Final Experiment Objectives
Examine the cool flame combustion behavior of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane fuel mixtures, and
farnesane fuels over a rage of pressure from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
4. Operation

Experiment Objectives
Examine the cool flame combustion behavior of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane fuel mixtures, and
farnesane fuels over a rage of pressure from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
4. Operations
a. Procedures
The operational procedure used in the CFI tests is the same as for the FLEX experiments. Once the ISS crew
installs the required fuel syringe, and the gas bottles containing the gas mixtures in the MDCA and CIR
facilities, all the actual experimental operations are conducted from the ground at the Telescience Support
Center (TSC) located at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Prior to each test the combustion chamber is filled
with the specified gas mixture at the required pressure, and the hot-wire igniters are positioned close to the
droplet deployment site. Subsequently, a droplet of desired size is dispensed between the hypodermic
needles and freely deployed, and ignited. The igniter is withdrawn from the FOV once ignition is detected.
When required a 40 micron silicon-carbide fiber is used to tether the droplet at one place and stop it from
drifting off from the field of view.

The combustion process is recorded using a backlit, black-and-white camera ( 5 cm X 5 cm FOV) to obtain
droplet size as a function of time, a UV-sensitive camera is used to image the OH* emission from the flame
which provides the flame size data. A color camera which is had a live downlink to the TSC is used to
perform and monitor the overall process. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers are used to measure
the radiation emission from the flame. Details of the experimental hardware and the data reduction
procedures can be found in Dietrich et al. (2014)

b. On-Orbit Testing
Over two hundred tests were carried out during the CFI experimental campaign. The initial droplet size was
kept around 4 mm so that radiative extinction and the subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed.
The list of experiments performed are as follows:

• Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3, and 5 atm.
• N-dodecane/Iso-dodecane mixtures: 75/25% and 60/40% by mass at pressures from 0.5 to 5 atm
• Helium dilution by 29% and 59% with O2 mole fraction at 0.21
• Farnesane: from 0.75 to 3 atm

c. Anomalies That Effect Science Surprises/New Discovery
No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient
pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame
extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed
by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed. This
behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments. Furthermore, the soot-shell

which surrounds the droplet and lies between the droplet surface and the flame, became unstable and ill-
defined at higher pressures, a phenomenon which is not fully understood.
d. Organization of Data in PSI
The organization od the data posted in the PSI website is as follows:

• Pure n-dodecane data: FLEX-1206 to FLEX-1284
• N-dodecane/Iso-dodecane ( 75%-25% & 60%-40%) mixture data: FLEX-1285 to FLEX-1387)
• Farnesane data: FLEX-1388 to FLEX-1431

5. Results
a. Findings
All the CFI data is yet to be fully analyzed and interpreted using theoretical and numerical models. A brief
overview of general observations made during preliminary data analysis prior to posting on the PSI website is
presented below. Interested researchers are welcome to propose to NASA for further analysis and
interpretation of CFI data.

5.1 Cool flames:
Cool flames were observed during n-dodecanol combustion as well as n-dodecanol/iso-dodecanol mixture cases.
The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol. Figure 1 shows a
typical case of cool-flame behavior for n-dodecanol.

Figure 1. FLEX-1223: N-dodecane at 1.25 atm pressure in air.

5.2 Warm flames:
Warm flames are a consequence of changing in chemical pathway during n-alkane oxidation. Figure 2 shows
(Westbrook, 2010) the various chemical pathways: cool flames occur when low-temperature branching is
dominant, when intermediate temperatures become more active warm flames are established. During warm
flames the heat release rate dynamically balance the heat loss rate. Addition of helium seems to enhance this
balance within the NTC region.

Figure 2. Chemical kinetic pathways for n-alkane oxidation (Westbrook, 2010).

Figure 3: FLEX-1268 – N-dodecane at 3 atm burning in 12%O2 – 50% N2 – 29% Helium. Reignition and warm
flame formation are shown.

Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not
visible in the color camera. Subsequently, a hot flame is ignited which quickly extinguishes to form a cool flame.

5.3 Cool flame extinction:

Cool flame extinction is controlled primarily by chemical kinetics. As the droplet size decreases, the residence
time in the reaction zone of the gas-phase diffusion flame is reduced to a value corresponding to which the cool
flame becomes statically unstable, and this leads to cool flame extinction. Figure 4 shows the cool flame
extinction diameter as function of ambient pressure for both free-floated and fiber-supported droplets for pure
n-dodecane burning in air. As mentioned earlier, as the pressure is increased above approximately 2 atm,
reignitions were commonly observed, eventually leading to complete combustion of the fuel droplet. It is
interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter.

Figure 4. Cool flame extinction diameters as a function of ambient pressure for n-dodecane droplets
burning in air.

Since the cool flame extinction is an instability phenomenon where the dynamic balance between heat release
and heat loss from the flame is lost at the lower turning point in the NTC region, one would expect addition of
helium to have a substantial influence on the process. Figure 5 illustrates the effect of helium dilution on the
extinction diameter for n-dodecane. Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger
extinction diameter.

Figure 5. Effect of helium dilution on cool flame extinction during n-dodecane droplet combustion.

5.4 Sooting behavior as function of ambient pressure:
The effects and the process of soot formation during cool flame combustion remains largely unexplored. The
shoot shell that forms during hot flame is stabilized by the balance of force between fluid mechanical drag
and the thermophoretic force. At low pressures a stable spherical soot-shell is formed. However, as the
pressure increase the soot-shell becomes diffuse and undefined. The reasons for this phenomenon is still
not well understood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not
formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet
surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot
flame extinction. The mechanisms behind this process has not been fully understood, and further analysis
and research is needed.

Figure 6. Backlit images of the droplet during hot and cool flame burning at atmospheric pressures of
approximately 380, 570, 760, 1520, 2280 and 3800 mmHg. The hot flame images are approximately 4 sec
after igniter withdraw and the cool flame images are approximately 5 sec after hot flame extinction. The
droplet in the cool flame image at 1520 mmHg was close to the edge of the FOV. The red circles during hot
flame burning at the two highest pressures show the approximate location of the droplet surface.

5.5 Summary of findings:
CFI experiments has provided cool flame burning data for pure n-dodecane, and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane
mixtures. Farnesane, a commercially available renewable fuel characteristics were also studied. The effect
of pressure and helium dilution were studied for these fuels. Data for droplet regression rate, hot and cool
flame diameters, extinction conditions, and radiant emission, both broad band and narrow band, are
obtained and posted to the PSI website.

b. Benefits
Low temperature chemistry is of fundamental importance in the combustion of many practical fuels. Low
temperature chemistry controls the autoignition of fuels when injected into a combustion chamber, and in
homogeneous mixtures of fuel and oxygen. New internal combustion engines, such as the HCCI engines,
operate at low temperatures reducing the pollution formation and increasing overall efficiencies. The CFI
experimental measurements provide a useful way to validate the complex chemical kinetic mechanisms that
are being developed. The cool flame combustion process itself maybe of use in fuel reformulation
technologies to produce hydrogen in fuel cell applications.

and systematically study hot flame ignition and
extinction in microgravity
• A new phenomenon where a hot flame extinction
leads to a low-temperature, “cool-flame” burning
in microgravity observed for the first time
• Cool flames are prevalent in FLEX experiments
o Strong function of ambient pressure
o Strong function of ambient environment –
ambient oxygen mole fraction and diluent
o Function of fuel composition
• No systematic study of cool flames and their
presence inferred and not observed

Experiment Objectives – Cool Combustion, CFI
1. Further understanding of the combustion characteristics of normal alkanes,
particularly in the low temperature region by conducting droplet combustion
experiments in low gravity with fuels that supports cool flame burning and
extinction.
2.  Investigate the low temperature burning behavior of droplets consisting of pure
fuels and bio-fuel constituents (and mixtures of them), as well as surrogate
reference fuels to determine the relationship between the cool flame burning
characteristics in microgravity droplet combustion and the octane/cetane
behavior of the fuel.
3.  Explore the low temperature chemistry of alkanes further by mixing additives to
the fuel that disrupt the low temperature chemical pathways. [Ground-based
only]

• Proposed experiments involve:

4. Cool-flame burning (5 – 60 seconds)
5. Cool-flame extinction
• Long-duration microgravity facilities are required for detailed parametric study

Requirements – Ambient Environment
• Pressure
o Strongly influences cool flame burning and extinction – both hypo- and
hyper-baric pressures
o 0.5 – 3.0 atm required, up to 5 atm desired (hardware limit)
• Oxygen Mole Fraction
o 0.10 – 0.40, similar to the range in FLEX experiments
• Ambient Diluent
o Primarily nitrogen (Objective 1 and 2)
o Helium and xenon (Objective 1)
Ø Strongly influence cool flame burning and extinction
• Misc. Ambient Requirements
o Similar to FLEX requirements
o Ambient humidity less than 10% (FLEX had lower requirement for
methanol)
o g-levels ≤ 10-5g0

Requirements – Droplet Imaging
• Measure droplet size and shape, droplet dynamics, soot volume fraction, etc. as
functions of time
• No change to camera or backlight for new experiment necessary
• Increase FOV from 30 mm (FLEX) to 50 mm (CFI)
o Increases success rate by allowing for greater free deployment droplet drift
o FLEX requires drift less than 1 mm/sec to stay in FOV
o Reduces spatial resolution (30 µm to 50 µm)

Requirements – Hot Flame Imaging
• Currently measure either OH* or CH chemiluminescence using intensified
black and white camera
o OH* (310 nm) images very dim, required pixel binning (2x2) to get good
images, but reduced spatial resolution
o CH (430 nm) images have improved contrast and reduced noise – possible
to eliminate binning (increases data storage/downlink requirements)
• Increase FOV from 50 mm (FLEX) to 80 mm (CFI)
o Increases success rate by allowing for greater droplet drift
• Current camera configuration acceptable for hot-flame imaging
o Unlikely to be able to perform chemiluminescence of both the hot-flame
and cool flame with current camera configuration
• Require the capability to image the hot-flame
o Either OH* or CH (preferred) chemiluminescence
o 100 µm spatial resolution
o 30 fps
o Adjustable gain required (almost impossible to know appropriate gain
based on ground-based testing)

Requirements – Cool Flame Imaging
• Currently have no way to image cool flames on CIR/MDCA
o Removing/changing filter and/or increasing gain on LLUV possible, no
way to shield the camera from ignition or hot flame
• Cool flame expected to be approximately ½ size of hot flame
o FOV, spatial resolution and framing rate requirements similar to hot flame
o Can use the same camera for both hot and cool flame imaging, but spectral
ranges are different and required gain is much different
• Based on literature search and FLEX radiometer data, cool flames are expected
to be very dim

Requirements – Flame Radiometer
• Original FLEX radiometers not sensitive enough to adequately
detect dim (hot) flames and had unacceptably low SNR
• Starting in 2011, FLEX testing used replacement radiometers
o Broadband: 0.6 – 10.0 µm sensitivity, images hot flame
o Narrowband: 5.0 – 6.5 µm ( H2O ), sensitive to cool flame
o 10 Hz frequency response, sampled at 100 Hz
o Fixed gain, not sensitive to both hot and cool flames
• Require flame radiometric measurements for CFI
o Same wavelength bands as current radiometer package
o Require auto-gain so each radiometer can capture both hot
and cool flame
Ø ~ 0.1 – 100 W flame radiance range
Ø May not be able to capture flame radiance during re-
ignition
• Require at least 10 Hz sampling (same as FLEX)
• Same FOV as FLEX radiometers

1 Introduction
Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and funda-
mental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid
fuels per day which averages out to an astonishing 2.5 gallons per day per person (Reitz, 2013). The
primary reasons for such a high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy
source, not only in the US but globally, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability
compared to many other forms of energy. With the emergence of newer internal combustion engine
technologies such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Reactivity-Controlled
Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines, understanding the autoignition and heat release chemistry
and kinetics of hydrocarbon fuels is more important that ever. These new technologies coupled
with the emergence of major sources of renewable fuels for both gasoline and diesel applications,
including butanols and heavier alcohols, bio-diesel, farnesane and high carbon number synthetics,
further emphasize the need to understand the kinetic eﬀects of blending renewables with petroleum
derived fuels.

Commercially available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised
of many hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes being the major compo-
nents. The combustion characteristics of these alkanes are quite complex and follow branched chain
reaction pathways involving many (hundreds) intermediate radicals. The chemical pathways vary
depending on temperature and to a lesser extent on pressure. Researchers typically identify a low
temperature reaction mechanism and a high temperature mechanism, as well as a region of tran-
sition between the two (intermediate or transition). Many hydrocarbons exhibit a unique feature
in the transition region where the reaction rate ﬁrst decreases with increasing temperature (the
negative temperature coeﬃcient, NTC region). The NTC region precedes a region in which the re-
action auto-accelerates to the high temperature region. Cool ﬂames and the associated multi-stage
ignition phenomenon occur as a result o

action auto-accelerates to the high temperature region. Cool ﬂames and the associated multi-stage
ignition phenomenon occur as a result of the low, NTC, and hot ignition behavior of the fuels. In
spark ignition engines, these chemistries are responsible for engine knock. The resistance of the fuel
to knock is frequently characterized by the fuel’s octane Number (ON); the higher the ON the less
prone the engine is to knock.
The same low temperature chemistry controls the autoignition process in Compression Ignition
(e.g., diesel) engines. The two stage autoignition process deﬁnes when combustion occurs and is
typically characterized by a fuel’s cetane number (CN); the more prone the fuel to autoignite, the
higher the CN.

netic mechanisms that result in cool ﬂame phenomena and thus control a fuel’s ON/CN. These
facilities include stirred reactors, ﬂow reactors, shock tubes, rapid compression machines, and
burner-stabilized two stage laminar ﬂames. All these studies primarily involve premixed gases and

2 Background
2.1 Low Temperature Chemical Kinetics
Traditionally cool ﬂames are associated with premixed combustion that lead to multi-stage ignition
of some fuels under certain pressure and temperature conditions. Though the existence of cool
ﬂames has been known since the days of Sir Humphry Davy (1817), Perkin (1882) was the ﬁrst to
conduct systematic studies and classiﬁed a range of organic compounds including alcohol, aldehydes,
acids, oils, and waxes that can support cool ﬂames. The study of cool ﬂames, however, remained
more of a scientiﬁc curiosity, because of its unusual oscillatory characteristics in a homogeneous
medium, rather than of any practical interest. Researchers proposed non-linear theoretical models
based on “isothermal” kinetics to explain the periodic cool ﬂame oscillations; including the one by
Frank-Kamenetskii and Thon (1955) based on the Lotka-Volterra equation. Salnikoﬀ was the ﬁrst
to propose a “thermo-kinetic” theory where thermal feedback played a role in intermediate species
production rate with a simple scheme:

Modern studies of hydrocarbon oxidation involve developing detailed multi-step chemical kinetic
schemes based on large number of elementary reactions that vary with pressure and temperature.
The rate parameters associated with these elementary reactions are either from experiments or cal-
culated from fundamental quantum mechanical theories such as transition state theory. Obtaining
accurate rate parameters, however, is often diﬃcult as they can contain large uncertainties. Over

have developed techniques to systematically reduce the number of reaction steps and species needed
from the detailed mechanisms to capture the salient features of the combustion processes both in

2.2 Microgravity Droplet Combustion
For over 50 years, scientists have been studying droplet combustion in microgravity, beginning with
the modest one-second drop-tower experiments by (Kumagai, 1956) and including space experi-
ments conducted onboard the NASA’s Space Shuttle (Dietrich et al., 1996; Nayagam et al., 1998).
Researchers exploit the spherica

d drop-tower experiments by (Kumagai, 1956) and including space experi-
ments conducted onboard the NASA’s Space Shuttle (Dietrich et al., 1996; Nayagam et al., 1998).
Researchers exploit the spherically symmetric, one-dimensional burning of liquid fuel droplets in
microgravity as a means to study the combustion characteristics of liquid fuels in a controlled fash-
ion that is amenable to detailed numerical modeling and theoretical analyses. Past studies include
many aspects of liquid fuel combustion including burning rates, ﬂame dynamics, soot formation,
multi-component eﬀects, and ignition and extinction characteristics under various ambient condi-
tions using microgravity droplet combustion experiments (e.g., Faeth, 1977; Law, 1982; Sirignano,
1983; Choi and Dryer, 2001)).
The conventional wisdom until recently has been that small hydrocarbon fuel droplets, once
ignited, either burn to completion, extinguish in a ﬂash as consequence of impurity or product
accumulation, or extinguish diﬀusively (Law, 1975) at a ﬁnite droplet diameter. This diﬀusive ex-

tinction occurs when the diﬀusion time, which decreases with decreasing droplet diameter, becomes
less than the chemical time required to complete the heat release in the gas phase. In microgravity
where the buoyancy-induced ﬂow is absent, larger droplets can extinguish as a result of the ex-
cessive radiant heat loss from the ﬂame zone (Chao et al., 1991). This radiative extinction occurs
because as the droplet diameter increases, the rate of radiant loss (proportional to the ﬂame vol-
ume) increases faster than the rate of heat release (proportional to the droplet diameter). Following
either one of these two modes of extinction, the droplet simply evaporates in the hot environment,
without any chemical heat release in the gas phase. Theoretical models (e.g., Chao et al., 1991;
Card and Williams, 1992b,a) and numerical simulations (e.g., Marchese et al., 1999a) with detailed
high temperature chemical kinetics support this understanding.

The ISS provides almost limitless microgravity time for combustion science research. The Flame
Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) is the ﬁrst experiment in the multi-purpose combustion facility
developed at the NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
provides the combustion chamber, most of the diagnostics, gas mixing system and the primary
interface between the ISS and the ground controllers at NASA GRC. The Multi-User Droplet
Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), inserted into the CIR, is the hardware that deploys and ignites
the liquid fuel droplets. It communicates through the CIR to ground controllers at NASA GRC.
The CIR facility, occupying a large rack in the Destiny module of the ISS and described in
detail elsewhere (Banu, 2008), consists of a 90 l combustion chamber that is capable of operating
pressures of approximately 0 - 9 atm. The maximum pressure for a given experiment is frequently
much less than 9 atm depending on a rigorous (and very conservative) safety analysis. For the
FLEX experiments, this analysis reduced the maximum working pressures to approximately 3 atm.

2.4 Summary of FLEX Cool Flame Experiments to Date
The original objectives of the FLEX experiments were to examine ﬂammability limits of isolated
pure fuel droplets (heptane and methanol) and inert gas ﬁre suppressant eﬃcacy. The follow-on
FLEX-2 investigation was more fundamental investigating the burning of single droplets of a range
of fuels, fuel mixtures and even binary arrays of droplets. The focus in both experiments was on the
hot ﬂame burning and extinction; the cool ﬂame regime a serendipitous discovery. The experimental
data in Figures 3, 4 and 5 represent ideal tests, free droplets that exhibited minimal drift and stayed
in the imaging systems ﬁelds of view, prolonged cool ﬂame burning and an identiﬁable cool ﬂame

2.4.1 Cool ﬂames are prevalent
The cool ﬂame phenomena is not limited to a single fuel or narrow range of ambient conditions.
They occur with all of the normal alkane fuels over a wide range of pressure, ambient oxygen
mole fraction and ambient gas composition. They occur almost exclusively as a result of radiative

ﬂame. These tests are likely ones in which the heat release from combustion and delivered ignition
energy were only suﬃcient to produce the low temperature kinetic activity driving the combustion
into the negative temperature coeﬃcient kinetic regime, but not through hot ignition. Outside
of these few tests, however, cool ﬂames only occur after radiative extinction of the hot ﬂame.

cially under the application of strong ignition energy conditions.. To achieve radiative extinction
requires test times greater than that typically available in drop towers2 primarily because droplets
of suﬃcient diameter to achieve radiative extinction cannot be produced in the available test time..

3 Experiment Objectives
As described in the previous section, cool ﬂame phenomena are inﬂuenced by a number of factors,
including the fuel molecular structure (for pure fuel cases), the ambient environment (pressure,
temperature, oxygen and diluent concentrations), and the fuel composition (the mixture of fuel
structures and perhaps fuel additives such as those used to change octane or cetane behavior).
The overall goal of the proposed experiments is to improve our understanding of low temperature
chemistry by studying the cool ﬂame burning and, most importantly, cool ﬂame extinction of droplet
burning with spherical symmetry in a long-duration microgravity environment. The experiments
to date show that prolonged cool ﬂame burning (in some cases up to 60 seconds) is possible. The
quasi-steady cool ﬂame burning regime abruptly ends at cool ﬂame extinction at a ﬁnite droplet
size, something easily identiﬁed in the proposed experiments. By varying the fuels and ambient
conditions, the experiments to date show that we can eﬀectively, and over a wide range, vary the
cool ﬂame extinction diameter which allows for the varying the characteristic time scales of the
cool ﬂame chemistry. This

eriments to date show that we can eﬀectively, and over a wide range, vary the
cool ﬂame extinction diameter which allows for the varying the characteristic time scales of the
cool ﬂame chemistry. This in turn will provide experimental data that can be used to both validate
and improve simpliﬁed and detailed low temperature chemical kinetic models.
3.1 Objectives of the proposed eﬀort
The primary objectives of the proposed experiments are as follows:
1. Further understanding of the combustion characteristics of normal alkanes, particularly in
the low temperature region by conducting droplet combustion experiments in low gravity with
fuels that supports cool ﬂame burning and extinction.
2. Investigate the low temperature burning behavior of droplets consisting of pure fuels and bio-
fuel constituents (and mixtures of them), as well as surrogate reference fuels to determine the
relationship between the cool ﬂame burning characteristics in microgravity droplet combustion
and the octane/cetane behavior of the fuel.
3. Explore the low temperature chemistry of alkanes further by mixing additives to the fuel that
disrupt the low temperature chemical pathways.

3.2 Fuel
3.2.1 Baseline Fuel
The molecular composition of a fuel has a profound eﬀect on the relative importance of low,
negative temperature coeﬃcient (NTC), intermediate, and high temperature kinetic behavior. The
low temperature, NTC and hot ignition kinetic behavior and associated heat release are key features
relating to premixed cool ﬂames and microgravity droplet combustion cool ﬂame behavior as well
as engine knock and compression ignition phenomena. Ground based kinetic experiments with C7
through C16 n-alkanes show increasingly more low and NTC behavior up to about C12. FLEX
experiments to date have also shown that cool ﬂame behavior will occur with n-heptane, n-octane,
and n-decane. And it is expected that n-dodecane will be even further active than these species.
Therefore in this study we propose to extend normal alkane experiments to include pure n-
dodecane. The molecular weight of n-dodecane is near the average of that found for petroleum jet
fuels and somewhat less than what is found for diesel fue

normal alkane experiments to include pure n-
dodecane. The molecular weight of n-dodecane is near the average of that found for petroleum jet
fuels and somewhat less than what is found for diesel fuels. The study of larger n-alkanes is not
necessary as it was noted above that carbon chain length, the production of ketohydroperoxides
and the resulting degenerate chain branching is no longer limited by the statistical probability

of O2QOOH isomerization through ﬁve and six membered ring formation. Though considerable
ground based work has recently been produced on n-dodecane combustion kinetics, cool droplet
burning research will add to improving our understanding of its low temperature and NTC behavior.
3.2.2 Isomeric Fuels and Surrogate Fuel Blends
Alkane isomeric structure can signiﬁcantly reduce low temperature and negative temperature kinetic
behavior of a pure alkane relative to an n-alkane of equal carbon number. The reduced activity
is caused by reducing the probabilities of ﬁve and six member ring formation. For example, two
recently produced renewable fuel components, farnesane (2,6,10 trimethyldodecane), and 2,2,4,6,6
pentamethylheptane of carbon number similar to n-dodecane have derived cetane numbers of 58 and
15 in comparison to n-dodecane and its derived cetane number of 78 (the higher the cetane number,
the more active low temperature and NTC chemical behavior. We propose to study these two new
alternate fuels in pure form to compare both their high temperature and cool droplet burning
behavior in relationship to n-dodecane. Mixtures of n-dodecane with each of these renewable
alternative fue

alternate fuels in pure form to compare both their high temperature and cool droplet burning
behavior in relationship to n-dodecane. Mixtures of n-dodecane with each of these renewable
alternative fuels are also proposed to be studied, in order to understand the interactive inﬂuence
of their chemistries on cool droplet burning behavior.
Finally, the blending of two or more molecular structures can also be used as a means of varying
low temperature and NTC kinetic behavior. The Primary Reference Fuel (PRF) mixtures of n-
heptane and 2,2,4 trimethylpentane (iso-octane) are used to emulate the behavior of real gasolines
and deﬁne the Octane number of a gasoline. Another mixture used for this purpose are termed
Toluene Reference Fuel (TRF) mixtures. We propose to study PRF and TRF mixtures that produce
octane values of 50, 70, and 90.
Moreover, experiments on gas turbine fuels in drop towers and in other ground based facilities
have been studying surrogate fuel mixtures of n-dodecane, iso-octane, n-propyl benzene, and 1,3,5
trimethyl benzene to emulate real gas turbine fuel behaviors, which also manifest cool ﬂame kinetic
phenomena. We propose to utilize one speciﬁc mixture that has be

trimethyl benzene to emulate real gas turbine fuel behaviors, which also manifest cool ﬂame kinetic

All of the above investigations contribute signiﬁcant, new fundamental science that has strong

3.2.3 Fuel Additive
Certain additives such as nitrates and peroxides when mixed with fuels alter their combustion
chemistry and reaction pathways by disrupting the availability of radicals in the oxidation chain
reactions. In some cases they are known to improve performance of diesel and other bio-fuel ﬁred
engines. In this study we choose di-tertiary-butyl-peroxide (C8H18O2) as an additive to be blended
with n-dodecane. Earlier studies in rapid compression machines has shown substantial reduction
in ignition delay times when small amounts of DTBP is added to the fuel Tanaka et al. (2003).

3.3 Ambient Conditions
The ambient gas in the proposed study is a mixture of oxygen and nitrogen. The oxygen mole
fraction will be varied in the range 0.18 to 0.35. The total pressure of the combustion chamber
will be varied in the range 0.5 to 5.0 atm. The initial combustion chamber temperature will be

Helium dilution studies will provide us with the ability to control cool ﬂame extinction diameters
over a larger range than simply using oxygen/nitrogen mixtures. The FLEX tests to date show

that large variations in cool ﬂame extinction diameter can be aﬀected by relatively small changes
in the ambient helium concentration.
The FLEX experiments show that xenon dilution will lead to long cool ﬂame burning and
burning at lower ambient oxygen mole fractions than in with either nitrogen or helium dilution.
This will greatly change the characteristic time and length scales and provide a wide parameter
space with which to compare against theory/modeling.

Typically the droplet life-time (τl) can be estimated from the initial droplet size (D0) and the
average burning rate constant (k) as τl = D2 0 k . The values of τl for n-heptane, and methanol droplets

droplets in drop towers. Dietrich et al. (2005) used the Japan Microgravity Center 10 s drop tower,

wide parameter space is the microgravity environment available in extended-duration microgravity
facilities (i.e. the ISS).

6 Test Matrix and Experiment Procedure
6.1 Flight Experiment Test Procedures
The proposed CFI experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively
large droplets. The experiments seek to observe the ignition, hot-ﬂame burning and ﬂame extinc-
tion, cool ﬂame initiation and burning and ﬁnally, cool ﬂame extinction of primarily free-ﬂoated
fuel droplets in q quiescent ambient envrionment. The Science Deﬁnition Team will work with
the engineering team to determine the optimal order for the experiments. The order is based
partially on experiment priority (e.g., it may be important to perform some tests ﬁrst), hardware
considerations (e.g., the fuel system operates better if the tests run in increasing ambient pressure)
and resource optimization. Based on the experience with the FLEX experiments, the experiment
sequence on a given test day proceeds as follows:
1. Select the ambient environment for the tests. This will be done several months before testing
and changes can be made up to 72 hours before the test day (changes to diluent may require
additional lead time for on-orbit bottle change-outs).
2. Perform the Fuel-Oxidizer Mixing Apparatus (FOMA) operations

s can be made up to 72 hours before the test day (changes to diluent may require
additional lead time for on-orbit bottle change-outs).
2. Perform the Fuel-Oxidizer Mixing Apparatus (FOMA) operations to set the test ambient.
This will be done immediately prior to testing.
3. Perform a droplet combustion test by completing the following operations in approximate
order.
(a) Position the igniters, ﬁber and needles and prepare the diagnostics for data acquisition.
(b) Open the fuel valve and begin dispensing fuel.
(c) Dispense the appropriate fuel volume for a given droplet size (this can be changed in
near real-time) using the downlink video view to guide the test.
(d) Zoom the downlink video view out to observe droplet combustion test.
(e) Run the automated sequence which consists of the following steps.
i. Turn the chamber lights oﬀ.
ii. Start data recording on all cameras and radiometers.
iii. Rapidly retract the needles to deploy the droplet.
iv. Power the igniters (they will turn oﬀ and retract after a preset period of time).
v. Observe the droplet burning on the real-time video (recording locally at the Tele-
science Support Center, TSC) until the test is complete and on-orbit v

and retract after a preset period of time).
v. Observe the droplet burning on the real-time video (recording locally at the Tele-
science Support Center, TSC) until the test is complete and on-orbit video recording
stops after a preset period of time.
vi. Run the circulation fan for approximately 15 seconds to mix the contents of the
chamber.
4. Determine the success of the test and whether to save the on-orbit video ﬁles. On-orbit
storage is limited and unsuccessful tests (e.g., no ignition) need to be deleted to save storage
space.
5. Repeat step 3 TBD times (typically 5 - 10) for a range of droplet sizes.
After completing the tests on a given test day, the on-orbit will be downlinked to the ground
and transferred to the TSC. There the data is de-compressed and provided to the SDT for detailed
analysis. This process typically takes 3 to 7 days. This process is then repeated for each desired
test atmosphere.

droplet size as a function of time, the initial and extinction droplet sizes, droplet shape (for ﬁber

8.2 Flame Shape and Structure
Two cameras provide ﬂame images as a function of time, the OH∗/CH and CH2O images and the
view from a color CCD camera. There is a large amount of data derived from these views including,
but not limited to ﬂame size and shape as a function of time, radial OH∗ proﬁles (Marchese et al.,
1996), ﬂame luminosity and color (qualitative measures of soot formation/destruction) as functions
of time, and the time of ﬂame extinction. Accurate measurements require that the ﬂame be in focus
and that appropriate scale factors are available. The archived data will include the raw images from
all of the cameras along with all of the camera settings and calibrations, and scale factors.

8.3 Flame Radiation
Data obtained from both the wide and narrow band radiometers will be used to measure the non-
luminous ﬂame radiation. Accurate measurements require calibrated radiometers with well-deﬁned
spectral characteristics. In order to be useful in extracting extinction information and obtain ratios
of radiative heat loss to combustion heat release, the data must be accurately time stamped and
correlated with the ﬂame, droplet and soot image data. The archived data will include the raw
radiometer data, the calibration factors and view factor information (geometry of the radiometer
relative to the droplet). Analyzed data will include, at a minimum, the ﬂame radiance as a function
of time (time-stamped to the video data).

The Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) is a risk mitigation experiment to evaluate the performance of the TSI P-Trak, a commercially available Condensation Nuclei Counter (CNC), in a microgravity environment.
The P-Trak is capable of counting individual particles as small as 20 nm diameter in an aerosol stream
The P-Trak is a key diagnostic for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) being developed for operation in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
DAFT Investigation Goals and Objectives
Low-gravity performance of the P-Trak can only be assessed in long-duration microgravity aboard the ISS
An added benefit is that DAFT can provide air quality measurements in the ISS cabin
The objective of SAME is to quantify the particle size distribution of smoke particulate to allow the rational design of smoke detectors for exploration vehicles and habitats
Experiments on STS-75 indicated that particles were larger in 0-g than in 1-g
Detection limits for existing smoke detectors may not be optimized for particles formed in low-gravity
Commercial P-Trak
Condensation Nuclei Counter

Operation of the P-Trak relies on the proper internal flow and recirculation of isopropyl alcohol
The required flow may not function properly in microgravity
P-Trak Operation
Aerosol-containing inlet flow passes through a mildly heated environment of saturated isopropyl alcohol vapor
The aerosol passes into a condenser section where the particulate serve as nucleation sites for the condensing alcohol vapor
Droplet grow large enough to be counted using standard optical methods
In the standard P-Trak, the condenser section depends on gravity to return alcohol to the saturator
The condenser was modified to so that capillary forces will induce the flow of liquid alcohol back towards the saturator1

he Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was
designed to ensure that a modiﬁed P-Trak®—a key component
of the forthcoming NASA Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment
(SAME)—will perform properly in the unique enviroment of micro-
gravity. If the P-Trak® performs as expected, the device will be used
in SAME to provide data that will help scientists design better ﬁre
detectors for future, long-duration, manned missions.
The Challenge The P-Trak® is a commercial device that counts ultra-
ﬁne particles (it can recognize particles as small as 0.02 micrometer in
diameter). It works by passing particulate-laden air through a heated
chamber of vaporous isopropyl alcohol. The individual particles serve
as “seeds” around which the alcohol condenses when cooled, forming
droplets large enough to be detected and counted as they scatter light
from a laser beam (see the schematic on the other side).
The P-Trak® must be tested in microgravity prior to its use in SAME
because its alcohol condenser was redesigned to work properly in mi-
crogravity. (The original smooth-walled P-Trak® condenser—meant
for Earth-based use—depends on gravity.) NASA scientists modiﬁed
the unit’s condenser

Research Procedure During the ISS tests conducted in 2005,
astronauts performed several steps:
Turned on the P-Trak® and the DustTrak®
Attached High Efﬁciency Particulate Air (HEPA) ﬁlters to the inlets
to “zero” the particle counters (since the HEPA ﬁlter removes all
airborne particles, if the particle counters don’t read “0” something
is amiss)
Connected the devices to a common sampling hose
Recorded the ISS environment for several minutes
Reconnected the HEPA ﬁlters to “zero” the particle counters
Turned off the P-Trak® and the DustTrak®
The tests were conducted in the US laboratory module Destiny in front
of EXPRESS Rack 4; in the modules’s aft end and port side; and in
Node 1. (The EXPRESS Rack is a standardized payload rack system that
transports, stores, and supports experiments aboard the ISS; Node 1 is a
hub to which various modules are attached.) Three of the tests sampled
undisturbed cabin air; the other test validated the instruments at high
particulate levels by having an astronaut create airborne debris at the P-
Trak® and DustTrak® inlets by separating pieces of Velcro®.

Results So Far The three tests that sampled the undisturbed
environment in the ISS showed very low levels of airborne
particulates, averaging fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 from the DustTrak®
and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 from the P-Trak® (these are typical
readings at the baseline). These numbers are dramatically lower than
the values recorded in the Space Shuttle in an earlier experiment (~
.050 mg/m3). Lower levels are to be expected because the ISS US
Lab has HEPA ﬁltration for the cabin air as compared to merely a ﬁne
screen on the shuttle air handler. Furthermore, the typical shuttle crew
of seven astronauts generates more airborne particulate than an ISS
crew of two astronauts.

I. Introduction
A. Abstract
In the wake of the Columbia disaster, NASA Headquarters put out a call for small experiments, designed to be launched aboard the Russian Progress, to be made available for launch within a six month period from the date of the request (March, 2003).
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME, formerly known as “Smoke”) required the utilization of a particulate counter that is designed to use gravity to facilitate its operation, and carried the question of its effectiveness in microgravity as a major risk.
The Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was designed as a risk mitigation experiment to test the improved the design of the TSI P-Trak, a COTS condensate nuclei counter, flight harden it and test its functionality in a microgravity environment. The experiment on-orbit operations were spread over 2 Increments (10 and 13).

e TSI P-Trak, a COTS condensate nuclei counter, flight harden it and test its functionality in a microgravity environment. The experiment on-orbit operations were spread over 2 Increments (10 and 13). The Increment 10 operations were performed by Leroy Chiao and consisted of the DAFT 1 and & 2 implementations which gave a preliminary look at the P-Trak functionality but did not provide full validation. These tests did however provide the first measurement of the particulate air quality on the space station. The Increment 13 operations were conducted by Jeff Williams and utilized the full DAFT 3 & 4 implementation. In all, 3 sample bags were tested. The results of both test sequences demonstrated the overall functionality of the modified Ptrak in a low-gravity environment, successfully mitigating the risk of the SAME experiment.
B. Hypothesis
Given the gravitational sensitivity of the P-Trak, two failure modes were identified for the device: 1) that the particulate counting system, containing a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or become obscured by the working fluid (isopropanol) and 2) that the internal dynamics of the optics chamber of the device would cause a

aining a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or become obscured by the working fluid (isopropanol) and 2) that the internal dynamics of the optics chamber of the device would cause an over counting of the particulates and give unreliable (high) readings. To mitigate the condensate control problems, the condensing section was re-designed to mitigate the detrimental gravitational effects. C. Objectives of Investigation
The objective of DAFT was to minimize the risks of its parent experiment, SAME, by demonstrating that the modified TSI P-Trak functioned effectively and predictably on orbit.
Background
The Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) is a risk mitigation experiment, created by its parent experiment, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The purpose of SAME is to create and measure the smokes of typical spacecraft materials when created in a microgravity environment, with the expressed goal of providing the data required for the development of the next generation of spacecraft smoke and fire detectors.
The design of the smoke detectors currently in use aboard the ISS and the NASA Space Shuttle are based on test results from the measurement of the smoke particulate created i

smoke and fire detectors.
The design of the smoke detectors currently in use aboard the ISS and the NASA Space Shuttle are based on test results from the measurement of the smoke particulate created in a 1-g environment. Previous experimental evidence, acquired by the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment on board the Space Shuttle, showed that there can be an appreciable difference in the quality of the smokes created in microgravity versus those created on earth. Although it was highly successful, CSD was not designed to have the ability to thoroughly characterize the aerosols created on orbit. SAME does have this ability.
SAME relies on a COTS device, the TSI P-Trak (a Condensate Nuclei Counter), to quantify the count of the number concentration of the smoke aerosol, a critical measurement for the success of the SAME experiment. The P-Trak, as designed by the manufacturer, relies on gravity to aid in the recycling of the isopropyl alcohol used as a condensate; hence the concern that it may not function properly on orbit. This concern is the driving factor behind the development of the DAFT experiment. The SAME project team developed a modification to the condenser of the

ern that it may not function properly on orbit. This concern is the driving factor behind the development of the DAFT experiment. The SAME project team developed a modification to the condenser of the P-Trak that should alleviate the problem but it could only be tested in a long-term low-gravity environment.
The original concept for DAFT contained a P-Trak (which included the modification to aid in the alcohol recycling), a DustTrak (a laser scattering aerosol measurement device, also manufactured by TSI, to be used as a comparator), an aerosol generation system and an unmodified P-Trak. Due to constraints with regard to the allowable upmass, DAFT was divided into four ‘increments’ (DAFT-1 through -4, respectively) that could be launched separately.
II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
In order to prepare the P-Trak for operation in microgravity, an analysis of its operation was performed. The P-Trak uses a small pump to draw the sample aerosol through a chamber saturated with alcohol vapor by means of a wick. That vapor/aerosol mix then passes through a condenser tube that allows the alcohol to condense on the particles in the aerosol, making droplets t

mber saturated with alcohol vapor by means of a wick. That vapor/aerosol mix then passes through a condenser tube that allows the alcohol to condense on the particles in the aerosol, making droplets that are large enough to count with a focused laser/photo cell combination. The condenser in the COTS device slopes down, enabling the alcohol from the droplets that adhere to the tube wall to be recycled back to the evaporator.
In conjunction with the Microgravity Fluids Branch at the NASA Glenn Research Center, a modification to the condenser tube was developed that effectively moves liquid alcohol from the tip of the tube back upstream to the evaporator using capillary forces. This was the major modification made to the device. Other alterations involved the removal of the mercury switch (for gravitational orientation), flight hardening and covering the device with foil tape for flammability concerns.
The TSI DustTrak, a laser scattering device based on Mie scattering and included as a measurement standard, was hardened in a similar fashion, but did not include a mercury switch.
After some consideration, it was decided to use a 15 liter Mylar bag for the containment of the aerosol. S

easurement standard, was hardened in a similar fashion, but did not include a mercury switch.
After some consideration, it was decided to use a 15 liter Mylar bag for the containment of the aerosol. Several issues, including safety and the atomizing of the particulates (and the fluid that contained them), precluded the use of commercially available mono-dispersed particles. Therefore, Arizona Road Dust (ARD) (fine), a NIST standard, was selected due to its known constitution and ease of dispersion into a pressurized gas stream.
A flight design was created, the parameters tested and determined, and flight-like hardware was created and tested with the measurement instruments to develop the correlation curves discussed in the results section.
One problem that exists with the ARD sample material is that it contains a substantial number of particles in sizes above 2.5 microns, which is above the measurement limit of the P-Trak. To mitigate this factor, the hardware included the DAFT Impactor which was developed by the project team based on particle impaction theory. The DAFT Impactor is a particle separator for large particles (only) that was designed specifically for the given flow rat

r which was developed by the project team based on particle impaction theory. The DAFT Impactor is a particle separator for large particles (only) that was designed specifically for the given flow rate of the combined test devices.
The P-Trak gives a number count of the particles in an aerosol, in readings of particles/cm3. DustTrak gives measurements of the total mass, in mg/m3. Since the distribution of the particulates in the aerosol is known to a certain confidence level, and the units had been correlated in testing on the ground, the experiment was conceived to create a similar aerosol on orbit and determine the device correlation in a microgravity environment to quantify the P-Trak’s measurement effectiveness.

For these reasons, the SAME (DAFT) project team feels that the DAFT experiment has been a complete success, and that it has confidence

e a good basis for acceptance within the bounds of that analysis.
For these reasons, the SAME (DAFT) project team feels that the DAFT experiment has been a complete success, and that it has confidence that the P-Traks as designed and manufactured for SAME will perform as accurately and effectively on-orbit as they have in the labs.
G. Conclusion
The DAFT experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified Ptrak as operated in low-gravity. This retired a significant risk that was being carried by the SAME project. It should be added at this point that SAME flew successfully in Increment 15 with flawless operation of the PTraks over the entire test matrix.

I. Introduction
A. Abstract
In the wake of the Columbia disaster, NASA Headquarters put out a call for small experiments, designed to be launched aboard the Russian Progress, to be made available for launch within a six month period from the date of the request (March, 2003).
The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME, formerly known as “Smoke”) required the utilization of a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) TSI P-Trak particulate counter that is designed to use gravity to facilitate its operation, and carried the question of its effectiveness in microgravity as a major risk.
The Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was designed as a risk mitigation experiment to test the functionality of a modified and flight-hardened P-Trak, in a microgravity environment. The experiment

osol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was designed as a risk mitigation experiment to test the functionality of a modified and flight-hardened P-Trak, in a microgravity environment. The experiment on-orbit operations were spread over two International Space Station (ISS) Increments, 10 and 13. The Increment 10 operations were performed by astronaut Leroy Chiao and consisted of the DAFT-1 and -2 implementations, which gave a preliminary look at the P-Trak functionality, but did not provide full validation. However, these tests did provide the first measurement of the particulate air quality on the ISS. The Increment 13 operations were conducted by astronaut Jeff Williams and utilized the full DAFT-3 and DAFT-4 implementation. In all, three Sample Bags were tested. The results of both test sequences demonstrated the overall functionality of the modified Ptrak in a low-gravity environment, successfully mitigating the risk of the SAME experiment.
B. Hypothesis
Given the gravitational sensitivity of the P-Trak, two potential failure modes were identified for the device: 1) that the particulate counting system, containing a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or beco

nsitivity of the P-Trak, two potential failure modes were identified for the device: 1) that the particulate counting system, containing a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or become obscured by the working fluid (isopropanol) and 2) that the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device would cause an over counting of the particulates and give unreliable (high) readings. In order to mitigate the potential condensate control problems, the condensing section was re-designed to enhance capillary fluid motion to replace the missing gravitational force. In order to evaluate this design in low-gravity, an experiment was designed that would use a functionally flight-like design and test it against an aerosol standard and another device (the TSI DustTrak), that was analyzed and determined to be unaffected by the lack of gravity.
The choice of the aerosol and the method used to create it were key items. Ideally, a mono-disperse aerosol would be used (0.7 – 1.3 microns), which would allow an easy comparison of the readings from the devices. However, due to the lack of development time, it was proposed to use Arizona Road Dust (ARD, Fine), a reference par

1.3 microns), which would allow an easy comparison of the readings from the devices. However, due to the lack of development time, it was proposed to use Arizona Road Dust (ARD, Fine), a reference particulate material, in combination with ISS Gaseous Nitrogen (GN2) to create an aerosol for measurement purposes.
Therefore, there are two basic hypothesis in DAFT: 1) that the TSI P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity, and 2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices
C. Objectives of Investigation
The objective of DAFT was to minimize the risks of its parent experiment, SAME, by demonstrating that the modified TSI P-Trak functioned effectively and predictably in low-gravity.
Background
The Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) is a risk mitigation experiment, created in support of its parent experiment, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The purpose of SAME is to create and measure the smokes of typical spacecraft materials when created in a microgravity environment, with the expressed goal of providing the data required for the deve

The purpose of SAME is to create and measure the smokes of typical spacecraft materials when created in a microgravity environment, with the expressed goal of providing the data required for the development of the next generation of spacecraft smoke and fire detectors.
The design of the smoke detectors currently in use aboard the ISS and the NASA Space Shuttle are based on test results from the measurement of the smoke particulate created in a 1-g environment. Previous experimental evidence, acquired by the Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment on board the Space Shuttle, showed that there can be an appreciable difference in the quality of the smokes created in microgravity versus those created on earth. Although it was highly successful, CSD was not designed to have the ability to thoroughly characterize the aerosols created on-orbit. SAME does have this ability.
SAME relies on a COTS device, the TSI P-Trak (a Condensate Nuclei Counter or CNC), to quantify the number concentration of the smoke aerosol, a critical measurement for the success of the SAME experiment. The P-Trak, as designed by the manufacturer, relies on gravity to aid in the recycling of the isopropyl alcoh

II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
In order to prepare the P-Trak for use in microgravity, an analysis of its operation was performed. The P-Trak uses a small pump to draw the sample aerosol through a chamber which is saturated with alcohol vapor by means of a wick. That vapor/aerosol mixture then passes through a condenser tube that causes the alcohol to condense on the particles in the aerosol, making droplets that are large enough to count with a focused laser/photo cell combination. The condenser in the COTS device slopes downward, enabling the alcohol from the droplets that adhere to the tube wall to be recycled back to the evaporator.
Based on analysis and testing performed by the Microgravity Fluids Branch at the NASA Glenn Research Center, a modification to the condenser tube was developed that effectively moves liquid alcohol from the tip of the tube back upstream to the evaporator using capillary forces. This was the major modification made to the device. Other alterations involved the removal of the mercury switch (which was used to sense gravitational orientation), flight-hardening and covering the device with foil tape for flamma

made to the device. Other alterations involved the removal of the mercury switch (which was used to sense gravitational orientation), flight-hardening and covering the device with foil tape for flammability concerns.
The TSI DustTrak, a laser scattering device based on Mie scattering and included as a measurement standard, was hardened in a similar fashion. As designed, the device did not include a mercury switch.
After some consideration, it was decided that a 15 liter Mylar bag would be used for the containment of the aerosol. Several issues revolving around the safety and the atomizing of the particulates (and the fluid that contained them) precluded the use of commercially available mono-disperse particles. Therefore, Arizona Road Dust (ARD) (fine), a NIST standard, was selected due to its known constitution and ease of dispersion into a pressurized gas stream.
A flight design was created, the parameters were tested and determined and flight-like hardware was created and tested with the measurement instruments in order to develop the correlation curves discussed in the results section.
One problem that exists with the ARD sample material is that it contains a substantial number

One problem that exists with the ARD sample material is that it contains a substantial number of particles of sizes above 2.5 microns, which is above the measurement limit of the P-Trak. To mitigate this factor, the hardware included the DAFT Impactor which was developed by the project team based on particle impaction theory. The DAFT Impactor is a particle separator for large particles (only) that was designed specifically for the given combined flow rate of the test devices.
The P-Trak gives a number count of the particles in an aerosol, in readings of particles/cm3. DustTrak gives measurements of the total mass, in mg/m3. Since the distribution of the particulates in the aerosol is known to a certain confidence level, and the units had been correlated through testing on the ground, the experiment was conceived to create a similar aerosol on-orbit and to determine the device correlation in a microgravity environment in order to quantify the P-Trak’s measurement effectiveness.

This indicates then, that the mass of the average particle counted on-orbit is higher than that determined on Earth. This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.
It should be noted that, although the DAFT Impactor is designed to filter out the larger particles, it is only about 50% efficient; which implies that it is allowing a considerable number of larger particles to be drawn into the devices.
If the data collected on-orbit had been to the lower right of the ground based testing line on the graph in

that it is allowing a considerable number of larger particles to be drawn into the devices.
If the data collected on-orbit had been to the lower right of the ground based testing line on the graph in Appendix D, it would have meant that more smaller particles would have been present; which is counter intuitive and would have indicated that the P-Trak may have been over counting the particles, one of the postulated failure modes.
The analysis of the average particulate size and mass shown on the spreadsheet in Figure 5 shows a good uniformity between the particulates sampled from the various bags. The average mass (assuming a material density of water) is 2.5 E-12 grams, with a range from 2 – 3 E-12. The calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron.
The sample material, Arizona Road Dust (Fine) is a standardized, homogenous material; but since it contains a wide distribution of sizes, it is a mixture. The amount of the material that is enclosed in each Dust Holder is small (0.25 gram). From ground testing, it is estimated that only about 10% of the material contained within the Dust Holder is introduced into the aerosol, due to the irregular interior s

t Holder is small (0.25 gram). From ground testing, it is estimated that only about 10% of the material contained within the Dust Holder is introduced into the aerosol, due to the irregular interior surfaces within it, the surface adhesion of the dust and other factors. Therefore, the net amount of sample delivered to the Sample Bags is about 25 milligrams. Since this amount is so small and is coming from a mixture, some variation in the average particle size between samples is expected.

E. Status of Data Analysis
As detailed in the session log above, the data analysis is complete.
F. Final Investigation results
Ideally, DAFT would have collected electronic data from all of the planned 15 test points in order to establish a large body of consistent, repeated data. Several factors contributed to the decision to not pursue additional test points. They were:
Crew Time: Although DAFT was planned for Increment 13, there was not enough crew time available to support all of the desired Payload activities and the prospects for actually performing the experiment at all were extremely uncertain. Fortunately for DAFT, ALTEA had some problems with their hardware and a small block of time came open. DAFT was allowed the opportunity to schedule 3 test points, with very little chance for another session.
Isopropyl Alcohol: As mentioned in the Results section, Jeff Williams was unable to open the DAFT Alcohol Wick container -02. This limited the amount of alcohol availa

ttle chance for another session.
Isopropyl Alcohol: As mentioned in the Results section, Jeff Williams was unable to open the DAFT Alcohol Wick container -02. This limited the amount of alcohol available to support the operation of the P-Trak. Leroy Chiao used this alcohol wick when he performed DAFT-1 and -2 and both of those units were loaded with alcohol over 3 years ago, so the amount that is remaining is highly questionable.
Sample Build Up: Testing in the lab has shown that under some circumstances, especially when a significant amount of the larger ARD particles is sent to the devices, a buildup of particles can occur within the optics chamber of the P-Trak. Clearly, the data shows that the sample aerosol contained a greater proportion of larger particles than is experienced on Earth. It also shows that as the run time on the P-Trak is increasing, especially during Bag #3, the count/mass ratio is declining. Although it is not certain that this build up is occurring, the symptoms of that condition are consistent with the data.
The lack of the electronic data collection initially limited the ability of the project team to perform a more detailed analysis of the data. However w

of that condition are consistent with the data.
The lack of the electronic data collection initially limited the ability of the project team to perform a more detailed analysis of the data. However when the Ptrak and Dusttrak were returned, the data sets were intact in their memory. The stored data reproduced the read downs very closely giving confidence to the earlier conclusions.
Based on the limited availability of the crew, it did not seem reasonable to think that time and procedures could be made available for Jeff or the follow-on Increment 14 crew to troubleshoot the devices.
That being said, DAFT was conceived and built as a Risk Mitigation experiment, not necessarily a Science experiment. It was delivered only 6 months after being proposed and accepted, and it was understood that in some respects, the sample material (the ARD, a poly disperse particulate) was less than ideal.
(Note: For those unfamiliar with the experiment, ideally, a mono-disperse aerosol with particulates about 0.7 microns in size would have been created in a density of about 50,000 pt/cc in order to provide a more quantifiable relationship between the readings from the DustTrak and P-Trak. Unfortunatel

bout 0.7 microns in size would have been created in a density of about 50,000 pt/cc in order to provide a more quantifiable relationship between the readings from the DustTrak and P-Trak. Unfortunately, an aerosol of this type is difficult to manufacture, and the project did not have time or resources to attempt such a development.)
The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with no apparent failure. One of the major concerns was that the P-Trak would accumulate alcohol in the optics chamber and obscure them, causing the unit to either read ‘0’ or display and error code. This did not happen. The units gave readings from zero well up into the middle of their operational ranges, and then back; in short, they performed as expected.
DAFT-1 and -2 showed that the units were ‘apparently working’ and that the air aboard the ISS is almost unbelievably clean. The readings from the devices during that part of the overall experiment though, never crossed the 20% of the operational range threshold, leaving the results somewhat suspect.
This latest experimental run, however, did. The project team believes that the optimal reading range fo

never crossed the 20% of the operational range threshold, leaving the results somewhat suspect.
This latest experimental run, however, did. The project team believes that the optimal reading range for the P-Trak is from 30,000 – 100,000 pt/cc (although the published range goes up to 500,000 pt/cc) and for the DustTrak; 20 – 80 mg/m3. Clearly, the latest data was within this range.
The count/mass ratio between the devices as measured on-orbit, although well outside of the value determined on Earth, is both explainable and credible; and to the best of the team’s ability to analyze the data, seems very consistent.
The problems with the equipment and the data have been discussed at some length, and although they do leave something to be desired, it does appear that there is enough consistency to determine that the readings recorded are believable and representative of the aerosol created, implying that the units both functioned nominally. Further discussion of the low-alcohol readings and the impact of the accumulated ARD in the P-Trak can be found in SAME-RPT-019: “DAFT Final Mission Test Report.”
Due to the constraints listed above, DAFT-4, using the ‘unmodified’ P-Trak, was not per

the impact of the accumulated ARD in the P-Trak can be found in SAME-RPT-019: “DAFT Final Mission Test Report.”
Due to the constraints listed above, DAFT-4, using the ‘unmodified’ P-Trak, was not performed. Since the flight hardware for SAME has been manufactured to the same specifications as the unit that was tested (P-Trak-01), this is not considered to be a factor.
The Science team has examined the data and compared the results against the empirical data accumulated for polydisperse aerosols; and determined that the results do have a good basis for acceptance within the bounds of that analysis.
For these reasons, the SAME (DAFT) project team believes that the DAFT experiment has been a complete success, and that it has confidence that the P-Traks as designed and manufactured for SAME will perform as accurately and effectively on-orbit as they have in the labs.
G. Conclusion
The DAFT experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified Ptrak as operated in low-gravity. This retired a significant risk that was being carried by the SAME project. It should be added at this point that SAME flew successfully in Increment 15 with flawless operation of the PTraks over the

This retired a significant risk that was being carried by the SAME project. It should be added at this point that SAME flew successfully in Increment 15 with flawless operation of the PTraks over the entire test matrix.
Earth Benefits / Spin-off Applications
There are no tangible Earth benefits from this experiment.

FLEX-2 (The Flame Extinguishment - 2) experiment is the second experiment to fly on the ISS which uses small droplets of fuel to study the special spherical characteristics of burning fuel droplets in space. 1.0 Introduction FLEX-2 SRD Rev. 1
1 Introduction
Combustion, which has been both friend and foe to mankind since antiquity, still deﬁes compre-
hension in many important respects. Needs therefore exist to advance fundamental knowledge
in combustion science. Practical consequences of such advancement of knowledge are improve-
ments in strategies for energy production, since most of the energy that is used by society
will continue to be provided by combustion for many years, and mitigation of ﬁre losses, ﬁre
safety being a continuing concern in all sectors. The NASA Microgravity Combustion Science
Program, which was established through recognition of these needs, did much to increase our
fundamental understanding of combustion processes Ronney (1988),Williams (2007). Droplet
combustion experiments had a great deal to do with the advancements in knowledge through
this program. Such experiments, in eﬀect, focus on a microcosm of the ﬁeld of combustion
that can be used to study most aspects of the topic. In addition, droplet combustion is of
practical interest in itself, since liquid fuels possess high energy content per unit mass and are
relatively safe to store and transport, making

id: PSI-68:doc:PSI-68_Science Documents_FLEX-2 SRD Final _ No Hypertext .pdf:7:1
file: PSI-68_Science Documents_FLEX-2 SRD Final _ No Hypertext .pdf
text:
s of the topic. In addition, droplet combustion is of
practical interest in itself, since liquid fuels possess high energy content per unit mass and are
relatively safe to store and transport, making them valuable to the transportation industry for
the foreseeable future. Phenomena of ﬁnite-rate gas-phase chemistry, multicomponent-species
gas-phase transport processes, production of soot and other pollutants, phase-change processes,
liquid-phase species separation and ﬂuid motion, natural and force convection, radiation and
conductive energy transfer and interactions of diﬀerent burning fuel elements, for example, all
are involved in droplet combustion (and, in fact, all are aspects of the subject of the present
SRD). By oﬀering a well-controlled arena in which to investigate these combustion phenomena,
microgravity droplet combustion research provides valuable data that help develop detailed
chemical and physical models of combustion phenomena.
The NASA program in the area of microgravity droplet combustion has employed laboratory
experiments, low-gravity facilities, aircraft ﬂying parabolic trajectories and space-based research
to reduce or eliminate buoyancy, thereby increasing

text:
vity droplet combustion has employed laboratory
experiments, low-gravity facilities, aircraft ﬂying parabolic trajectories and space-based research
to reduce or eliminate buoyancy, thereby increasing the ﬁdelity of the descriptions of the com-
bustion processes. Following glovebox space-shuttle experiments on a ﬁber-supported droplet
combustion, FSDC, the freely deployed droplet-combustion experiment DCE was ﬂown on the
MSL-1 missions, providing a number of new insights into the fundamentals of droplet com-
bustion. Among the DCE results was the demonstration of boundaries between radiative and
diﬀusive extinction of combustion in droplet burning and the establishment of atmospheres in
which the dilution was great enough that the oxygen concentration was too low for combustion
to occur Nayagam et al. (1998), Ackerman et al. (2003). This last observation demonstrated
how droplet-combustion studies could be used to investigate the limiting oxygen index, LOI,
needed to prevent combustion, and so the Flammability-limit experiment FLEX, was designed
for the International Space Station, ISS, to be run using the multiuser droplet combustion ap-
paratus, MDCA, in the combustion integrated

id: PSI-68:doc:PSI-68_Science Documents_FLEX-2 SRD Final _ No Hypertext .pdf:7:3
